teile.einleitung: Class rules make sure that things are calm and fair in the class. They help all children to learn well together and to treat each other kindly.
wichtigste: If you want to say something, you put your hand up first.
When someone is speaking, the others listen.
An Ämtli is a small job for the class.
Many classes make their rules together with the teacher.
“Please” and “thank you” are part of being friendly.
If you make a mistake, you apologise.

abschnitte.titel: Putting your hand up and listening
abschnitte.text: In class you put your hand up when you want to say something. Then you wait until it is **your turn**. That way everyone can speak in turn. When another child is speaking, you **listen**. Listening shows **respect**, and afterwards you may say something yourself.

In Switzerland children often take on an **Ämtli**. This is a small job for the whole class, for example cleaning the blackboard, watering the plants or sweeping the floor. The jobs often change every week. That way every child helps to keep the classroom nice. Shared tasks strengthen the **class community**.

Many classes make their rules together with the teacher. The children may make suggestions and **have a say**. People are often happier to keep rules they helped to make. New rules can be discussed, for example, in the **class council**. There all the children talk about how the class gets on together.

If you want something from another child, you ask politely with **“please”** and say **“thank you”** afterwards. If you have hurt someone by accident, you **apologise**. An apology shows that you are sorry. Then you can make friends again. Rules like these help everyone in the class to feel comfortable.

gewusst: The word “Ämtli” is typically Swiss and means “little office” or small job.
Adults also have rules for living together: in a municipality or in the state they are called laws.

teile.einleitung: A law is a rule that everyone has to follow. Laws make sure that people can live together peacefully and that nobody can simply do whatever they want. In Switzerland laws are passed by parliaments, and the people often have the last word.
wichtigste: A law is a rule that everyone has to follow.
The most important law in Switzerland is the Federal Constitution.
In Switzerland laws are passed by parliaments, and the people can call a referendum.
The police make sure that laws are obeyed.
In court, a judge decides whether someone has broken a law.
There are laws in road traffic too; for example, you need lights on your bike at night.
In Switzerland children must go to school until about the age of 15.

abschnitte.text: A **law** is a binding rule that applies to everyone in a country. Unlike house rules or the rules of a game, a law is passed by the state, and anyone who breaks it can be punished. Laws protect, for example, life, property and freedom. Almost 4000 years ago, the Babylonian king Hammurabi had laws carved into a stone.

The most important law in Switzerland is the **Federal Constitution**. It sets out people's fundamental rights and how the state is organised. The first Federal Constitution dates from 1848; the current one has applied since 2000. All other laws must fit with the Constitution, and every change to the Constitution needs a yes from the people and the cantons.

At federal level, the **National Council** and the Council of States pass new laws; both chambers must agree. After that, 50,000 voters can demand a **referendum** with their signatures within 100 days. Then the whole people votes on it. The 26 cantons and many municipalities also have their own laws and regulations.

The **police** make sure that laws are obeyed and help people in need. If someone is suspected of having broken a law, a **court** decides. A judge examines the evidence and listens to both sides. Only then is it decided whether someone is guilty and what punishment they get.

We come across many laws every day, especially in **road traffic**. Anyone cycling at night needs a white light at the front and a red light at the back. In town, pedestrians walk safely on the pavement. If someone wants to cross the road at a **pedestrian crossing**, cars must stop.

There are also special laws for children. **Compulsory schooling** makes sure that all children may and must learn, in most cantons for eleven years including nursery school, so until about the age of 15. Other laws protect children from violence and from work that is too hard. In Switzerland children aged 10 and over can be punished under juvenile criminal law, although education and protection are more important than punishment.

begriffe.erklaerung: The most important law in Switzerland, which sets out fundamental rights and how the state is organised.
The right of the people to vote on a new law.
An authority that decides in disputes or criminal cases.
More detailed rules that the government issues for a law.

gewusst: Swiss federal laws can be read by everyone free of charge on the internet, in the so-called Classified Compilation of Federal Legislation.
The Swiss Civil Code, which regulates matters such as family and property, has applied since 1912.
Federal laws are published in the three official languages German, French and Italian, and all three versions are equally valid.

teile.einleitung: A canton is a member state or administrative area within a country. In Switzerland the cantons are the building blocks of the country, each with its own government, its own laws and its own coat of arms. But the word also exists in other countries, such as France, Luxembourg or Bosnia and Herzegovina.
wichtigste: A canton is an area with its own authorities within a country.
The word comes from French and Italian and originally means “corner” or “district”.
In Switzerland every canton has its own coat of arms.
The coat of arms of the canton of Bern shows a bear, that of the Grisons an ibex.
In many cantons, the government of a canton is called the Regierungsrat.
A Landsgemeinde is an open-air vote that still exists today in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
Luxembourg, France and Bosnia and Herzegovina also have cantons, but there they have much less power.

abschnitte.text: The word **canton** comes from the French “canton” and the Italian “cantone”, which mean something like “corner” or “stretch of land”. In the Confederation, the members used to be called “Orte” (places) or “Stände” (estates). Only around 1800 did the word canton become established. Today most people think of Switzerland straight away when they hear it.

Every Swiss canton has its own **coat of arms**. Many show animals: Bern a black bear, Uri a bull's head, Schaffhausen a ram and Thurgau two lions. The coat of arms of the Grisons shows an ibex, which is also the canton's heraldic animal. Other coats of arms are simply divided, like the blue and white one of Zurich or the red and blue one of Ticino.

Every Swiss canton has its own government, which in many cantons is called the **Regierungsrat**. In French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino it is called the Council of State. There is also a cantonal parliament, which depending on the canton is called the Kantonsrat, Grand Council or Landrat. Each canton also has its own courts and its own police.

A **Landsgemeinde** is an open-air assembly and vote. Voters meet in a square and vote by raising their hands. In the past it existed in many cantons in central and eastern Switzerland. Today it only takes place in the canton of Glarus and the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, both in spring.

Other countries have cantons too. **Luxembourg** is divided into 12 cantons, and in France cantons are electoral districts for elections to the departmental councils. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, one part of the country consists of 10 cantons with their own governments. But nowhere are cantons as independent as in **Switzerland**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sign with colours and pictures that stands for a family, a town or a canton.
The government of a canton in many German-speaking cantons.
An open-air assembly of the people at which votes are held.
An old word for canton, still found in the word Ständerat (Council of States).

gewusst: At the Landsgemeinde in Appenzell Innerrhoden, many men carry a sword or a bayonet as proof of their right to vote.
The coat of arms of Glarus is the only cantonal coat of arms that shows a person, Saint Fridolin.
Because the word canton is so typical of Switzerland, in some languages Switzerland is jokingly called the land of cantons.

teile.einleitung: Helvetia is a female figure who embodies Switzerland. You can see her on coins, stamps and monuments. Her name comes from the Helvetii, a Celtic people who lived in the area of present-day Switzerland in Roman times.
wichtigste: Helvetia is a symbolic figure for Switzerland.
On the coins she holds a spear and a shield.
Her shield bears the Swiss cross.
Helvetia stands upright on the 50-centime, 1-franc and 2-franc coins.
The 5-, 10- and 20-centime coins show Libertas, not Helvetia.
In Basel the figure “Helvetia on her travels” sits by the Rhine.

abschnitte.text: Helvetia is a **personification**: a country is shown as a person. The name recalls the **Helvetii**, who lived here in Roman times. Many countries have such figures; France, for example, has Marianne. Helvetia is usually shown as a serious, strong woman in a long robe. She stands for the unity and freedom of the country.

On the **50-centime**, **1-franc** and **2-franc** coins, Helvetia stands upright. In one hand she holds a **spear**, and with the other a **shield** bearing the **Swiss cross**. All around are stars for the cantons. The small 5-, 10- and 20-centime coins, by contrast, show the head of **Libertas**, the figure of freedom. Many people mix the two up.

In **Basel** a well-known Helvetia figure sits on the bank of the Rhine near the **Mittlere Brücke** bridge. It is called “Helvetia on her travels”. The figure has put down her shield and spear, and a **suitcase** stands beside her. She looks out at the river like a traveller. In this way the artist shows Helvetia not as stern for once, but as thoughtful.

Helvetia also appears on **stamps**, posters and in drawings. On Swiss stamps the name of the country is often written as “Helvetia”, because Latin does not favour any of the national languages. For the same reason, the coins say “Confoederatio Helvetica”. This is also where the abbreviation **CH** comes from. In cartoons, Helvetia is often used to show the whole of Switzerland.

gewusst: The abbreviation CH stands for “Confoederatio Helvetica”, Latin for Swiss Confederation.
The franc coins with Helvetia have been minted with almost the same design since the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: Jürgen Habermas is a German philosopher and sociologist, born in Düsseldorf in 1929. He is considered one of the most important thinkers of our time. Above all, he asks how people reach understanding through conversation and how democracy can work fairly.
wichtigste: Habermas is counted as part of the Frankfurt School, more precisely its second generation.
His early work “The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere” was published in 1962.
His main work is “The Theory of Communicative Action” of 1981.
In discourse, only the “unforced force of the better argument” should count.
He shaped the idea of deliberative democracy.

abschnitte.text: Habermas was an assistant to **Theodor W. Adorno** at the Institute for Social Research in Frankfurt am Main. The thinkers of this institute are called the **Frankfurt School**. Their philosophy is called **Critical Theory**, because it examines society critically. Habermas is considered the most important representative of the second generation. He taught for a long time as a professor in Frankfurt and often took part in public debates.

In his 1962 book **“The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere”**, Habermas describes how a new public sphere emerged in the salons and coffee houses of the 18th century. There citizens discussed politics and books. This **public sphere** was meant to keep a check on the powerful. Later Habermas saw it as threatened by mass media and advertising.

In his main work, **“The Theory of Communicative Action”** of 1981, Habermas distinguishes two kinds of action. In action aimed at success, you want to achieve something. In **communicative action**, you want to reach an understanding with others. In an ideal conversation, only the **“unforced force of the better argument”** counts, not power or pressure. The yardstick is the **ideal speech situation**: everyone may speak freely and question every claim.

In **“Between Facts and Norms”** of 1992, Habermas develops his theory of law and democracy. Law becomes legitimate when it comes about through fair democratic procedures. In **deliberative democracy**, decisions are well founded if they are preceded by public, reasoned discussion. Elections alone are not enough for this. He also made famous Dolf Sternberger's term **constitutional patriotism**: an attachment to the values of the constitution rather than to origin.

gewusst: “Deliberation” comes from Latin and means “consultation” or “careful thought”.
In 2001 Habermas received the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade.

teile.einleitung: Child labour is work that harms children or keeps them from going to school. Around the world, many millions of children still have to work. Small jobs to help at home, however, do not count as child labour.
wichtigste: Forbidden child labour is hard or dangerous work instead of school.
Small household chores are not forbidden child labour.
In Switzerland real work is in principle only allowed from the age of 15.
In 2024 the UN estimated that around 138 million children were in child labour.
12 June is the World Day Against Child Labour.
The International Labour Organization has its headquarters in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: People speak of **forbidden child labour** when children have to work and it **harms** them. The work is, for example, too hard, too dangerous or lasts too long. Often these children cannot go to **school**. Without school it is harder to find a good job later. **Small chores** at home, such as washing up or laying the table, do not count. They are short, not dangerous and leave enough time for school and play.

**UN** experts estimated that in 2024 around **138 million** children had to work. That is far fewer than in the past, but still a great many. Many of these children work in **farming**, others in factories, mines or as helpers in other people's households. The reasons are often **poverty** and a lack of schools. The **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child** protects children from work that harms them.

abschnitte.titel: In Switzerland too, in the past
abschnitte.text: More than 150 years ago, many children in Switzerland also worked in **factories**, for example in **spinning mills**. They stood at machines for many hours. Over time, child labour was banned by **laws**. The federal **Factory Act** of 1877 banned factory work for children under 14. Today the **Employment Act** in principle only allows real work from the age of **15**; for younger children there are only exceptions for light work.

The **International Labour Organization**, **ILO** for short, is part of the UN and has its headquarters in **Geneva**. It works for fair work and against child labour. Since 2002, **12 June** has been the **World Day Against Child Labour**. On this day, attention is drawn to the problem all over the world. Many aid organisations also support families so that their children can go to school.

abschnitte.titel: What you can do when shopping
abschnitte.text: You can also pay attention to something when shopping. **Quality labels** such as **Fairtrade** show that rules for fair work have been followed. These include a ban on forbidden child labour. You can find such labels, for example, on **clothes**, chocolate, coffee or bananas. Buying such products supports better working conditions.

gewusst: From the age of 13, young people in Switzerland may do light work, for example running small errands.
The ILO is one of the oldest organisations in the UN family; it was founded in 1919.

teile.einleitung: In the class council, the whole class meets regularly to talk together about how they get on. Here all children may have their say, contribute ideas and help decide.
wichtigste: All the children in the class take part in the class council.
The class often sits in a circle.
Often a child chairs the class council, and this role changes.
Many classes hold the class council about once a week.
People talk about the class's problems, wishes and ideas.
Decisions are often made by vote.

abschnitte.text: In the **class council**, the whole class comes together. Usually everyone sits in a **circle**. That way all the children can see each other and talk to each other better. Every child may have their say and help decide. In many classes the class council takes place **regularly**, often once a week.

Often **a child chairs** the class council. They call up the topics and make sure everyone gets a turn. Another child can write down the decisions; this is called the **minutes**. The roles change, so that every child can practise them once. The teacher helps if needed.

The class council is about **how the class gets on together**. People discuss arguments, wishes and ideas, for example an outing or a new rule. In an argument, everyone involved may tell their side. Then the class looks for a **fair solution** together. Many classes collect the topics beforehand in a letterbox or on a list.

When it is about a proposal, the children often vote. Then what the **majority** wants applies. In a **vote**, every vote counts the same. In the class council, children also learn to say what they think and to listen to others. In this way they practise on a small scale how **democracy** works, much like adults in the municipality.

gewusst: Besides the class council, many Swiss schools also have a pupils' council, where children from all classes have a say.
In the class council you practise the same things as at a municipal assembly: making proposals, discussing and voting.

teile.einleitung: The canton of Schaffhausen is the northernmost canton in Switzerland. It lies north of the Rhine and is almost entirely surrounded by Germany. It is known for the Rhine Falls and the Munot fortress.
wichtigste: The capital is also called Schaffhausen.
The Rhine Falls near Neuhausen are one of the largest waterfalls in Europe.
The Munot is the round landmark of the city.
Every evening at 9 o'clock the Munot bell rings.
Stein am Rhein is known for its painted houses.

abschnitte.titel: A canton north of the Rhine
abschnitte.text: Schaffhausen lies almost entirely **north of the Rhine**. Most of the canton is surrounded by **Germany**. It even consists of several parts that are not directly connected. **German** is spoken, in everyday life Swiss German. You can see the abbreviation **SH** on number plates. Schaffhausen has belonged to the Confederation since 1501.

At **Neuhausen am Rheinfall**, the Rhine plunges down loudly and broadly. The **Rhine Falls** are around 150 metres wide and are among the largest waterfalls in Europe. They lie on the border with the canton of Zurich. You can take a boat to a rock in the middle of the falls. For the National Day they are lit up with a big firework display.

High above the city of Schaffhausen stands the **Munot**. It is a round **fortress** from the 16th century. A **tower keeper** lives in the tower. Every evening at 9 o'clock he rings the **Munot bell** (Munotglöckli). In the past this was a sign that the town gates and inns were closing. The old town has many beautiful oriel windows on its houses.

The little town of **Stein am Rhein** lies where the Rhine leaves the Untersee. Its old town has many brightly **painted house fronts**. They show pictures from history and legends. Above the little town stands **Hohenklingen Castle**. Many tourists visit the town every year.

gewusst: Schaffhausen is one of the few cantons with compulsory voting: anyone who does not vote must pay a small fine.
In the coat of arms of Schaffhausen, a black ram is leaping.

teile.einleitung: Every canton has its own coat of arms. It is the canton's identifying sign and appears on flags, buildings and number plates. Many coats of arms tell something about the canton's history.
wichtigste: Each of the 26 cantons has its own coat of arms.
In the past, coats of arms were mainly used to recognise knights.
The coat of arms of Valais has 13 stars for the old Zenden.
The coat of arms of Vaud bears the words “Liberté et Patrie”.
The coat of arms of the Grisons combines the signs of three old leagues.
On 1 August many people also hang out their cantonal flag.

abschnitte.titel: Where coats of arms come from
abschnitte.text: In the **Middle Ages**, knights wore armour and helmets. That is why they looked very similar. They could be recognised by the picture on their **shield**. These signs became **coats of arms**. Later, families, towns and countries also got their own coats of arms. Today every canton and every municipality in Switzerland has a coat of arms.

The **coat of arms of Valais** is divided vertically into white and red and bears **13 stars**. They recall the **Zenden**, the old districts of Valais. The **coat of arms of Aargau** shows white **waves** on black on the left, which stand for the River **Aare**. On the right are **three white stars** on blue. The **coat of arms of St Gallen** is green with a white **bundle of rods** and an axe; it stands for the unity of the canton.

Some coats of arms are very simple. The **coat of arms of Zurich** is divided **diagonally**, white at the top and blue at the bottom. These colours can also be found on Zurich's trams. The **coat of arms of Lucerne** is divided **vertically**, blue on the left and white on the right. Other coats of arms show animals: Bern has a **bear** and Uri a **bull's head**.

The green and white **coat of arms of Vaud** bears the motto **“Liberté et Patrie”**, meaning “Freedom and Fatherland”. It dates from the time the canton was founded. The **coat of arms of the Grisons** combines the signs of **three old leagues**: the Grey League, the League of God's House and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions. The canton of the Grisons grew out of these leagues.

abschnitte.titel: Coats of arms in everyday life
abschnitte.text: The coats of arms appear as **flags** on buildings and at festivals. On **1 August**, the National Day, many people hang out their **cantonal flag** as well as the Swiss flag. In this way they show where they come from. On **number plates**, the cantonal coat of arms appears next to the abbreviation. You can also often see coats of arms on boundary stones and road signs.

gewusst: The study of coats of arms is called heraldry.
The coats of arms of the cantons can be seen on the dome of the Federal Palace in Bern.

teile.einleitung: An intercantonal concordat is a treaty between several cantons. In this way cantons can solve shared tasks together, without the Confederation regulating everything. Concordats are typical of Swiss federalism.
wichtigste: A concordat is a treaty between cantons.
The right to make them comes from Article 48 of the Federal Constitution.
Law-making concordats apply directly to the population, like a law.
Under Article 48a, the Confederation can declare concordats binding in nine areas.
The IVHSM concentrates highly specialised medicine in a few hospitals.
The gambling concordat regulates lotteries and sports betting.
The 1970 school concordat standardised the start of the school year.

abschnitte.text: The 26 cantons are responsible for many tasks themselves, such as schools or hospitals. But some tasks are better solved together. For this, cantons conclude **concordats**. **Article 48** of the Federal Constitution allows them to make treaties and to create shared institutions. Some concordats concern only two cantons, others the whole of Switzerland.

**Law-making concordats** contain rules like a law. They directly set out rights and duties for citizens. **Administrative agreements**, by contrast, only regulate how authorities work together. Under **Article 48a**, the Confederation can declare treaties **generally binding** in **nine** precisely named areas. These include, for example, the execution of sentences and measures, education and waste management.

The **Intercantonal Agreement on Highly Specialised Medicine** (IVHSM) concentrates rare, expensive treatments such as transplants in a few hospitals. This is meant to secure quality and cost-effectiveness. The **Swiss Gambling Concordat** regulates large-scale games such as lotteries and sports betting. Most of the proceeds go to charitable purposes such as culture and sport. The school concordat **HarmoS** is also an example.

abschnitte.titel: The dispute about the start of school
abschnitte.text: In the past, the school year did not start at the same time everywhere; some cantons started in spring. The **Concordat on School Coordination** of 1970 set the start of the school year between mid-August and mid-October. But some cantons did not join it for a long time. That is why in 1985, after a popular vote, the start was written into the **Federal Constitution**. Since then the school year has begun in **late summer** everywhere.

gewusst: The word “concordat” comes from the Latin “concordare”, which means “to agree”.
The HarmoS concordat came into force in 2009 and sets out, among other things, that children start nursery school at the age of four.

teile.einleitung: The canton of Geneva lies in the far south-west of Switzerland at the end of Lake Geneva. It is almost completely surrounded by France. Geneva is an international city where people from all over the world meet.
wichtigste: The capital is the city of Geneva, in French Genève.
The Jet d'Eau sprays water around 140 metres high.
The UN has its European headquarters in the Palais des Nations.
At the Escalade, Geneva remembers an attack that was fought off in 1602.
At the CERN research centre, scientists study the smallest particles.

abschnitte.text: Geneva's landmark is the **Jet d'Eau**. The fountain sprays water around **140 metres** into the air. In the **English Garden** stands the **Flower Clock**. It is made of thousands of flowers, and its hands show the correct time. Geneva is also known for its **watchmakers**. The Rhône leaves Lake Geneva here.

The **UN** has its European headquarters in the **Palais des Nations**. Many countries meet there for talks. In Geneva in 1863, **Henry Dunant** and others founded the **Red Cross**; the International Committee still has its headquarters here. Many other international organisations also work in Geneva. That is why you hear a great many languages in the city.

On the night of 11 to 12 December **1602**, troops of the Duke of Savoy tried to climb over the city walls with ladders. The people of Geneva fought off the attack. Every December the **Escalade** recalls this. There are processions in old costumes. Children smash a **pot made of chocolate**. According to legend, a woman, the Mère Royaume, poured hot soup over the attackers.

The canton of Geneva is almost entirely surrounded by **France**; the border is over 100 kilometres long. Only a narrow strip links it with the canton of Vaud. Geneva has belonged to the Confederation since **1815**. Near Geneva lies **CERN**, a large research centre for **particle physics**. There is a huge ring underground, part of which also lies under France.

gewusst: The World Wide Web was invented at CERN around 1990.
Geneva's coat of arms shows half an eagle and a key.

teile.einleitung: A half-canton is a canton that historically has only half a cantonal vote. In Switzerland there are six such cantons, which always belong together in pairs because they were once a single canton. Today they have equal rights with the other cantons in almost everything.
wichtigste: In federal votes a half-canton has only half a cantonal vote.
There are six half-cantons, forming three pairs.
The pairs are Obwalden and Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, and Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
Each half-canton sends only one person to the Council of States instead of two.
The Federal Constitution of 1999 no longer speaks of half-cantons but of cantons with half a cantonal vote.
Half-cantons have their own constitution, government and parliament, like all cantons.
Altogether the 26 cantons have 23 cantonal votes.

abschnitte.text: A **half-canton** is a canton that came about when an earlier canton was divided. It is not half a state; it has all the rights of a canton, such as its own government, its own laws and its own taxes. Only when it comes to having a say at federal level does it count as half. Since the new **Federal Constitution** of 1999, the official term has been cantons with half a cantonal vote.

For changes to the Constitution, Switzerland requires a **majority of the cantons**. This means that not only a majority of the people but also a majority of the cantons must agree. A normal canton has a whole **cantonal vote**, a half-canton only half. So the 20 whole and 6 half cantons together have 23 votes.

Obwalden and Nidwalden together formed Unterwalden, one of the three original cantons of 1291. But even in the Middle Ages the two valleys on Lake Lucerne largely had their own authorities. The capital of Obwalden is Sarnen, the capital of Nidwalden **Stans**. Both coats of arms show keys, Nidwalden's a double one.

Appenzell split in 1597 because of the Reformation. The Catholic **Appenzell Innerrhoden**, with its capital Appenzell, and the Protestant **Appenzell Ausserrhoden**, with Herisau as the seat of its government and parliament, went separate ways. Innerrhoden is the canton with the fewest inhabitants in Switzerland. The Landsgemeinde still takes place there every year in April.

The canton of Basel split in 1833 after fierce disputes between the city and the countryside. The rural population wanted more rights and founded the canton of **Basel-Landschaft** with its capital Liestal. Basel-Stadt is the smallest canton in Switzerland, but it consists almost entirely of the large city of Basel and the municipalities of Riehen and Bettingen. Several attempts to reunite the two Basels failed in popular votes, most recently in 2014.

Some people think that the two Basels, with almost 500,000 inhabitants together, have too little weight in the **Council of States**. That is why there have been proposals to give them full cantonal rights. But such a change would need the approval of the people and the cantons. So far nothing has changed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A canton's vote in votes that require a majority of the cantons.
The majority of the cantons, which must agree to changes to the Constitution.
The chamber of Parliament in which the cantons are represented.
Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, which are regarded as the founders of the Confederation.

gewusst: Appenzell Innerrhoden is completely surrounded by Appenzell Ausserrhoden, and Ausserrhoden itself lies in the middle of the canton of St Gallen.
Although it is called a half-canton, Basel-Stadt, with around 200,000 people, is much bigger than several whole cantons, for example Uri.
The term “half-canton” does not appear even once in the current Federal Constitution.

teile.einleitung: The separation of powers means that law-making, government and the courts are kept apart. That way no single person and no single authority has all the power in the state. The idea is several hundred years old and is a foundation of every democracy, including Switzerland.
wichtigste: State power is divided among three branches: legislature, executive and judiciary.
The legislature passes laws, the executive governs, the judiciary administers justice.
The French philosopher Montesquieu described the separation of powers in 1748 in his work “The Spirit of the Laws”.
In Switzerland the Federal Assembly is the legislature and the Federal Council the executive.
The highest judiciary at federal level is the Federal Supreme Court, based in Lausanne.
Because of the separation of powers, a Federal Councillor may not sit in the National Council at the same time.
The media are sometimes called the “fourth estate”.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who has all the power can easily abuse it. That is why, with the **separation of powers**, state power is divided among three branches that check one another. You can imagine it like a game: one person writes the rules, another runs the game and a third is the referee. That way nobody can decide everything alone and judge themselves at the same time.

In the 17th century the English philosopher John Locke was already thinking about dividing power. But the idea became famous through the French philosopher **Montesquieu**. In 1748, in his work “The Spirit of the Laws”, he described how freedom is only possible if the powers are separated. His ideas influenced the US Constitution of 1787 and later also the Swiss Federal Constitution of 1848.

The **legislature** is the law-making power; its task is to pass laws. In Switzerland at federal level, this is the Federal Assembly, with the National Council of 200 members and the Council of States of 46 members. It also decides on the budget and elects the Federal Council and the federal judges. A special feature of Switzerland is that the people also help shape laws and the Constitution through initiatives and referendums.

The **executive** is the power that carries things out; it governs and puts the laws into practice. At federal level this is the Federal Council with its seven members and the federal administration. Each Federal Councillor heads a department, for example for finance or defence. So the difference is: the executive governs, the legislature makes the laws.

The **judiciary** is the judicial power, meaning the courts. The highest court in Switzerland is the **Federal Supreme Court**, based in Lausanne; two divisions work in Lucerne. Other federal courts are the Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona and the Federal Administrative Court in St Gallen. The courts are independent, which means that the government and Parliament may not tell them how to judge.

Because the powers are meant to be separate, nobody may sit in two of them at the same time. A member of the Federal Council therefore may not also be in the National Council, and a federal judge may not be in Parliament. This is called **incompatibility**. The media are sometimes called the “fourth estate”, because they watch those in power and report on mistakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The law-making power, meaning Parliament.
The power that carries things out, meaning the government.
The judicial power, meaning the courts.
The rule that you may not hold two particular offices at the same time.

gewusst: Montesquieu first published his famous work “The Spirit of the Laws” without his name, in Geneva.
In Switzerland the separation of powers exists not only at federal level but also in every canton and in the municipalities.
In dictatorships there is usually no separation of powers, because one person or party seizes all the power.

teile.einleitung: A collective labour agreement, CLA for short (GAV in German), is a contract between employers and employees' associations. It sets wages, working hours and other working conditions for a whole company or industry. In Switzerland CLAs play a big role, because there is no national minimum wage.
wichtigste: The CLA is regulated in the Code of Obligations from Article 356.
The parties are employers or their associations and employees' associations.
A CLA must be concluded in writing.
With a declaration of general applicability, a CLA applies to the whole industry.
For the topics it covers, the peace obligation applies.
Individual employment contracts may only differ from it in favour of employees.
Well-known CLAs are the National Framework Agreement in construction and the L-GAV in hospitality.

abschnitte.text: A **collective labour agreement** is concluded between employers or their associations and **employees' associations**. On the employees' side, these are trade unions or staff associations. The CLA is regulated in the **Code of Obligations** from Article 356. According to Article 356c, it must be concluded **in writing**. It contains, for example, minimum wages, working hours, holidays and rules on dismissal.

Normally a CLA only applies to the members of the contracting parties. With a **declaration of general applicability**, it is extended to all businesses in an industry, including non-members. This prevents companies with lower wages from undercutting others. If the CLA affects several cantons, the **Federal Council** decides. If it applies in only one canton, the cantonal government is responsible.

According to Article 357a of the Code of Obligations, the contracting parties must maintain **industrial peace**. On topics covered by the CLA, they may not take industrial action such as strikes. This is called the **peace obligation**. Normally it is relative, so it only applies to the topics covered. But the parties can also agree on an absolute peace obligation. This rule is part of the Swiss **social partnership**.

An individual employment contract may differ from the CLA, but only **in favour of the employees**. This is set out in Article 357 of the Code of Obligations and is called the **favourability principle**. So a higher wage or more holiday is allowed. Worse conditions than in the CLA, on the other hand, are **void**. Then the rule from the CLA automatically applies.

A well-known example is the **National Framework Agreement (LMV)** for the main construction industry. It sets wages and working conditions on building sites. In the hospitality industry, the **L-GAV** applies. From 2004, with the free movement of persons with the EU, **accompanying measures** were introduced. They allow an easier declaration of general applicability if wages are repeatedly undercut.

gewusst: In Switzerland there is a legal minimum wage only in some cantons; otherwise minimum wages are often set by CLAs.
A CLA can also apply to just one large company; this is then called a company CLA.

teile.einleitung: Zurich is the canton with the most inhabitants in Switzerland. It lies in the north of the country around Lake Zurich. The city of Zurich is the largest city in Switzerland and an important centre for business, education and transport.
wichtigste: The canton of Zurich has the most inhabitants in Switzerland.
The city of Zurich lies at the lower end of Lake Zurich.
The Limmat flows out of the lake right through the city.
Zurich main station is the largest station in Switzerland.
Winterthur is the second-largest town in the canton.
At the Sechseläuten, the Böögg is burned.
The city of Zurich's local mountain is the Uetliberg.

abschnitte.text: The canton of Zurich lies in the north of Switzerland and borders Germany. It has belonged to the Confederation since **1351**. The capital is the city of **Zurich**, the largest city in Switzerland. The second-largest town in the canton is **Winterthur**, with over 110,000 inhabitants. Besides the towns, there are many villages, woods and farms, for example in the **Weinland** and in the **Zurich Oberland**.

The city of Zurich lies at the lower end of **Lake Zurich**. The lake is around 40 kilometres long and reaches into the cantons of Schwyz and St Gallen. The **Limmat** flows out of the lake right through the old town. Later it flows into the Aare. Right next to the city lies the **Uetliberg**, Zurich's local mountain. From the top you can see over the city and the lake as far as the Alps.

**Zurich main station** is the largest station in Switzerland. Around 3000 trains arrive and depart there every day. Under the station there are platforms and shops on several floors. **Zurich Airport**, the largest airport in Switzerland, is also in the canton. Many people commute every day by **S-Bahn** (suburban train) to work or to school.

The **Sechseläuten** is a spring festival of the **guilds** in the city of Zurich. The highlight is the burning of the **Böögg** on the Sechseläutenplatz. The Böögg is a snowman made of cotton wool and firecrackers, and it stands for winter. According to old custom: if its head explodes quickly, the summer will be fine. Guild members ride around the fire on horseback.

Zurich is home to well-known universities such as **ETH Zurich** and the **University of Zurich**. **Zurich Zoo** is a popular place for outings. In the **Masoala Hall** grows a rainforest with plants from Madagascar. Animals from this island also live there, for example **lemurs**. Many museums, theatres and concert halls make Zurich a city of culture.

gewusst: The name Masoala comes from a national park in Madagascar with which the zoo works.
Albert Einstein also studied at ETH Zurich.
The coat of arms of the canton of Zurich is divided diagonally into white and blue.

teile.einleitung: The administration of a municipality works in the municipal hall. Inhabitants deal with many matters here, and the municipal council often meets here too.
wichtigste: In towns the municipal hall is often called the town hall (Stadthaus).
In the past, the town council met in the Rathaus.
The administration is usually open on working days.
Official notices hang on the notice board.
In many municipalities you apply for your identity card there.
You often get your dog tag from the municipal administration too.

abschnitte.text: The building of the municipal administration has different names depending on the place. In villages people usually say **Gemeindehaus** (municipal hall) or municipal administration; in many towns it is the **Stadthaus**. Many old towns have a beautiful **Rathaus** (town hall), where the town council used to meet. Some town halls are still used today.

**Municipal employees** work at the counter. They help with questions and requests. If you move house, you register or deregister here. In many cantons you apply for your **identity card** at your municipality of residence. Dogs must also be registered with the municipality. For this you pay the dog tax and often receive a **dog tag**. The counters are usually open on **working days**, from Monday to Friday.

There is often a **notice board** at the municipal hall. There the municipality publishes official notices, for example planning applications, voting dates or invitations to the municipal assembly. That way everyone can read them. Today many notices are also on the municipality's website.

The **municipal council**, the municipality's government, usually holds its meetings in the municipal hall. There it discusses its tasks and takes decisions. The municipal clerk also has an office here. The municipality is not responsible for everything: you get your **driving licence**, for example, from the cantonal road traffic office.

gewusst: Some town halls in Switzerland are several hundred years old.
In many municipalities you pay a special tax for a dog.

teile.einleitung: The Green Liberal Party of Switzerland, GLP for short, combines environmental protection with liberal economic policy. It was founded in the canton of Zurich in 2004 and became a national party in 2007. In French it is called “Parti vert'libéral”, PVL for short.
wichtigste: The first Green Liberal party was founded in the canton of Zurich in 2004.
Its founders had left the Greens because they thought the Greens were too far to the left.
Its founding figures were Martin Bäumle and Verena Diener.
The national party was founded on 19 July 2007.
The GLP wants to protect the environment and the climate with market-based tools.
It is seen as pro-European.
Its colour is a light green.

abschnitte.text: In **2004** the **Green Liberal Party of the Canton of Zurich** was founded. Its founders had previously left the **Greens**, because they thought the Greens were too far to the left. The most important founding figures were the National Councillor **Martin Bäumle** and the cantonal government member **Verena Diener**. Soon Green Liberal parties were also founded in other cantons.

On **19 July 2007** the cantonal parties of Zurich, Bern, St Gallen and Basel-Landschaft joined together. They founded the **Green Liberal Party of Switzerland**. In French it is called **“Parti vert'libéral”**, **PVL** for short. Since then the party has been represented in many cantons. In the 2019 elections it made big gains together with the Greens.

The GLP wants to **protect the environment and the climate**. But it relies on the **market economy** and **personal responsibility** to do so. An important principle is **true costs**: whoever harms the environment should pay for it. For this, the party proposes **incentive taxes** instead of bans. These make environmentally harmful behaviour more expensive.

The Green Liberals are seen as **pro-European**. They want **closer relations** between Switzerland and the European Union. They believe close cooperation keeps the Swiss economy strong. Other parties are more critical and want more distance from the EU. European policy is a much-debated topic in Switzerland.

In Parliament the GLP forms its own **parliamentary group**. This requires at least **five members** from one of the two chambers. The GLP meets this, while the small EVP, with only two seats, does not. A group has advantages, for example seats on committees. The party's logo is **light green**, combined with a light blue.

gewusst: The name Green Liberals combines two directions that were often seen as opposites in the past: green for environmental protection and liberal for a free economy.
Before moving to the GLP, Verena Diener was a Green member of the cantonal government in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: The canton of Bern stretches from the Jura to the high Alps. After the Grisons, it is the second-largest canton in Switzerland. The Federal Council and Parliament have their seat in the city of Bern.
wichtigste: By area, Bern is the second-largest canton in Switzerland.
German and French are spoken in the canton.
The Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau stand in the Bernese Oberland.
Interlaken lies between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz.
Emmental cheese comes from the Emmental.

abschnitte.text: The city of **Bern** is the capital of the canton and the **federal city** of Switzerland. The Federal Council and Parliament meet in the **Federal Palace**. The **old town**, with its arcades and the **Zytglogge** tower, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The heraldic animal is the **bear**; you can see bears in the Bear Park by the Aare. The canton is **bilingual**: French is spoken in the Bernese Jura, and both languages in Biel.

The mountainous south is called the **Bernese Oberland**. The **Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau** stand there. **Interlaken** means “between the lakes”; the town lies between **Lake Thun** and **Lake Brienz**. The **Lauterbrunnen valley** is also called the “valley of 72 waterfalls”; the **Staubbach Falls** are well known. Near Meiringen, walkways lead through the narrow **Aare Gorge**, which is around 1.4 kilometres long.

The **St Beatus Caves** lie on Lake Thun. According to legend, Saint **Beatus** drove a dragon out of the cave and then lived there himself. Today you can walk through the **stalactite caves**. Stalactites form very slowly when water containing lime drips. Many school classes visit the caves.

**Emmental cheese** is made in the hilly **Emmental**. It is known for its big holes. A famous festive dish is the **Bernese platter** (Berner Platte). It is served with bacon, sausages, beef, sauerkraut and beans. Every November the **Zibelemärit**, a big onion market, takes place in Bern.

gewusst: The canton of Jura used to belong to the canton of Bern and has been a separate canton since 1979.
The town of Biel is considered the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The canton of Glarus is a narrow mountain valley in eastern Switzerland. High mountains surround it on almost all sides. Here voters still decide at the Landsgemeinde in the open air.
wichtigste: The capital is also called Glarus and lies at the foot of the Glärnisch.
The highest mountain is the Tödi, at 3614 metres.
Twice a year the sun shines through the Martinsloch onto the church of Elm.
Green Schabziger is a Glarus speciality.
Braunwald is a car-free holiday resort.

abschnitte.text: Every year in May the **Landsgemeinde** takes place in Glarus. Voters stand in the **Ring** and vote by raising their hands. In 2007 Glarus became the first canton to introduce a **voting age of 16**. Since 2011 the canton has had only three municipalities: **Glarus**, **Glarus Nord** and **Glarus Süd**. The coat of arms shows Saint **Fridolin**.

The highest mountain is the **Tödi**, at 3614 metres, on the border with the Grisons. In the **Klöntal**, below the Glärnisch, lies the **Klöntalersee**, a popular place for outings. The **Walensee** lies between Glarus and St Gallen; on its northern shore the steep **Churfirsten** rise up. Above Linthal, **Braunwald** sits on a sunny terrace. The village is car-free and can be reached by **funicular**.

Above the village of **Elm** there is a large hole in a rocky ridge, the **Martinsloch**. In spring and autumn the sun shines straight through it for a short time onto the church tower of Elm. The area is part of the **Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona**, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. There you can clearly see how older rocks were pushed over younger ones when the Alps were formed.

**Glarner Schabziger** is a green cheese. It is green because it contains dried herbs, blue fenugreek (Zigerklee). It is grated over pasta, for example. The **Glarner Pastete** is made of puff pastry. It is filled half with almond paste and half with plum purée. Glarus used to be known for its **textile industry** too.

gewusst: Before the big municipal merger of 2011, Glarus had 25 municipalities.
Every April the Näfelser Fahrt recalls the Battle of Näfels in 1388.

teile.einleitung: A cantonal hospital is a large hospital that belongs to the canton or is supported by it. In Switzerland the cantons are mainly responsible for healthcare. They plan which hospitals are needed.
wichtigste: A cantonal hospital is a large hospital of the canton.
The cantons plan hospital care in Switzerland.
You call the ambulance on 144.
In an emergency you first go to the A&E department.
Seriously injured people are sometimes flown by helicopter, for example by Rega.
Doctors are also trained in university hospitals.

abschnitte.text: A **cantonal hospital** is a large hospital that belongs to the canton or is supported by it. Many different illnesses and injuries are treated there. In Switzerland **healthcare** is mainly the task of the **cantons**. They plan which hospitals are needed and which treatments they offer. In Aargau the largest hospital is **Aarau Cantonal Hospital**; another is in Baden.

abschnitte.titel: When things need to happen fast
abschnitte.text: In an emergency you call the **ambulance** on **144**. The **rescue service** comes with an ambulance and takes injured people to hospital. There you first go to the **A&E department**, where help is given immediately. Seriously injured people are sometimes flown by **rescue helicopter**. In Switzerland this is done, for example, by **Rega**, the Swiss Air-Rescue.

Many professionals work together in a hospital. **Doctors** examine the patients and decide on their treatment. **Nurses** care for the patients around the clock. There are also, for example, physiotherapists, laboratory staff, cooks and cleaning teams. That is why a large hospital is also an important **employer** in the canton.

A **university hospital** is a hospital where students also learn to be doctors. A lot of **research** is also done there. There are such hospitals in Zurich, Basel, Bern, Geneva and Lausanne. In Bern the university hospital is called the **Inselspital**. University hospitals often treat particularly difficult cases from the whole region.

In Switzerland every person must have **health insurance**, often called a Krankenkasse. It pays a large part of the treatment in hospital. The **cantons** also pay part of the costs of hospital stays. That is why the cantons often discuss how many hospitals are needed and where they should be.

gewusst: Rega's emergency number is 1414, and it also flies people out of the mountains.
The German word “Spital” comes from the Latin “hospitalis”, which means “hospitable”.

teile.einleitung: Equal rights means that all people have the same rights. Nobody may be put at a disadvantage because of their sex, origin, language or religion. In Switzerland, equal rights for women and men have been written into the Federal Constitution since 1981.
wichtigste: Equal rights means: everyone has the same rights.
Since 1981 the Federal Constitution has stated that men and women have equal rights.
Work of equal value gets equal pay.
The Gender Equality Act has applied since 1996.
Nobody may be put at a disadvantage because of their sex.
Women may do military service voluntarily.
All jobs are open to girls and boys.

abschnitte.text: **Equal rights** means that all people have the same rights. The Federal Constitution says: all people are equal before the law. It forbids **discrimination**, meaning putting people at a disadvantage, for example because of their sex, origin, language or religion. This applies in the family, in education and at work.

On **14 June 1981** the people approved the **equality article**. Since then the Federal Constitution has said: **men and women have equal rights.** The law must ensure their equality. Before that, women in Switzerland had only had the right to vote and stand for election at federal level since 1971. Since then, 14 June has been an important day for the women's movement.

The Federal Constitution requires **equal pay for work of equal value**. This applies to women and men. The **Gender Equality Act** of 1996 protects people at work from being disadvantaged because of their sex. Even so, women still earn less on average. This is much discussed in politics.

On **14 June 2019** a big **women's strike** took place all over Switzerland. Many participants wore **purple**, the colour of the women's movement. They campaigned for equal pay and more recognition. A first big women's strike had already taken place on 14 June 1991.

Girls and boys may train for **the same jobs**, for example as a joiner or a nurse. There are differences in the **army**: for Swiss men service is compulsory, while women may serve **voluntarily**. At home, the rule is: housework is everyone's job. In a fair family, **everyone** helps.

gewusst: The canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden only introduced women's suffrage in 1990, after a judgement of the Federal Supreme Court.
The equality article of 1981 is now in Article 8 of the Federal Constitution.

teile.einleitung: Nidwalden is a small canton in central Switzerland on Lake Lucerne. Together with Obwalden, it used to form the old Unterwalden. Its capital is Stans.
wichtigste: Obwalden and Nidwalden together were called Unterwalden.
The CabriO cable car with an open upper deck goes up the Stanserhorn.
In Stans a monument recalls Arnold Winkelried.
At Glasi Hergiswil, glass is blown by hand.
Aircraft are built in Stans.

abschnitte.text: **Obwalden** and **Nidwalden** together formed the old **Unterwalden**. Unterwalden was one of the three **original cantons**, together with Uri and Schwyz. Today Obwalden and Nidwalden are two separate cantons. Nidwalden's coat of arms shows a white **double key** on a red background. The capital is **Stans**. In 1481 the **Stanser Verkommnis** (Covenant of Stans), an important treaty of the old Confederates, was concluded there.

On the village square of Stans stands the monument to **Arnold Winkelried**. According to legend, in 1386 he helped the Confederates to victory over the Habsburgs in the **Battle of Sempach**. Whether he really existed is uncertain. But the story is one of the best-known legends in Switzerland. It tells of one person's commitment to the community.

Since 2012 the **CabriO** cable car has gone up the **Stanserhorn**. You can ride on its roof in the open air. Above **Beckenried** lies the **Klewenalp**, a skiing and hiking area high above Lake Lucerne. The **Bürgenstock** juts out into the lake. At the top stand large hotels with wide views.

At **Glasi Hergiswil**, **glass** is blown by hand. Visitors can watch the glassblowers at work. **Aircraft** have been built in **Stans** for many decades. The company Pilatus is an important employer in the canton. **Buochs airfield** lies right next to it.

gewusst: Nidwalden abolished its Landsgemeinde in 1996.
From the Bürgenstock, the Hammetschwand Lift, a lift on a rock face, goes up to a viewpoint.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland's fundamental rights are listed in the catalogue of fundamental rights of the Federal Constitution, in Articles 7 to 36. They protect people's dignity, freedom and equality against the state. Some apply to all people, a few only to Swiss citizens.
wichtigste: The catalogue of fundamental rights covers Articles 7 to 36 of the Federal Constitution.
It begins with human dignity in Article 7.
Article 10 forbids the death penalty.
Article 17 protects media freedom and forbids censorship.
Freedom of establishment applies only to Swiss citizens.
Anyone carrying out state tasks is bound by fundamental rights.
Because of Article 190, courts must still apply federal acts.

abschnitte.text: The **catalogue of fundamental rights** is in Title 2, Chapter 1 of the Federal Constitution. It runs from **Article 7** to **Article 36**. At the beginning is **human dignity**: “Human dignity must be respected and protected.” It forms the basis of all the other fundamental rights. These are followed by, for example, equality before the law, protection against arbitrary conduct and the **right to life**. Article 10 paragraph 1 states that the **death penalty** is forbidden.

**Article 17** guarantees **media freedom**, meaning the freedom of the press, radio and television. It forbids **censorship** and protects editorial confidentiality. **Article 18** guarantees **freedom of language**. It protects the use of your own language, especially your mother tongue. For a country with four national languages, this is particularly important.

Most fundamental rights forbid the state to interfere. But some require it to **provide** something. **Article 19** guarantees **adequate and free primary education**. The cantons must offer it to all children. The **right to assistance in situations of need** in Article 12 is also a social right. Such rights are called **social fundamental rights**.

Most fundamental rights apply to **all people** in Switzerland. **Freedom of establishment** in **Article 24**, on the other hand, belongs only to Swiss nationals. They may settle anywhere in the country and leave the country. For people from other countries, laws and agreements apply, for example with the EU.

**Article 35** requires fundamental rights to be upheld throughout the legal system. Anyone who carries out **state tasks** is bound by them. **Article 36** sets out when fundamental rights may be restricted. A special feature is **Article 190**: the courts must apply federal acts even if these violate a fundamental right. So Switzerland has no **constitutional review** of federal acts.

gewusst: Many fundamental rights already applied in Switzerland before 1999 as unwritten constitutional law, recognised by the Federal Supreme Court.
The introduction of constitutional review has been discussed in Parliament several times, but so far it has not been introduced.

teile.einleitung: The municipal budget is the plan of how much money a municipality will take in and spend in the coming year. In Switzerland voters have a say in it.
wichtigste: In the budget, also called the estimates, the municipality plans its income and spending.
Most of the money comes from taxes.
The municipal council makes the proposal, and the voters approve the budget.
The budget is usually decided in November or December.
The annual accounts show what was actually spent.
If the municipality spends more than it takes in, there is a deficit.

abschnitte.text: In the **budget**, also called the **estimates**, the municipality plans its **income** and **spending** for the coming year. The figures are in **francs**. Most of the money comes from **taxes** paid by inhabitants and companies. With it, the municipality pays for its tasks, for example schools, roads and the fire brigade.

The **municipal council**, the municipality's government, prepares the budget. It presents it to the **municipal assembly** or the municipal parliament. There the **voters** decide whether to approve it. Because the budget applies to the following year, it is usually decided **towards the end of the year**, in November or December.

The budget is only a plan. What was actually taken in and spent is shown by the **annual accounts**. The voters must approve these too. That way you can see whether the municipality has managed its money well. Sometimes more money comes in than expected, sometimes less.

If spending is greater than income, the budget shows a **minus**. This is called a **deficit**. For big projects, such as a new school building, a municipality often borrows money. Then it has **debts**, which it must pay back later. A careful municipality makes sure that its debts do not get too big.

gewusst: Every Swiss municipality draws up its own budget every year.
In many municipalities, any voter can propose changes to the budget at the assembly.

teile.einleitung: Invalidity insurance, IV for short, helps people who cannot work, or can only work partly, because of an illness, an accident or a disability. Together with the AVS, it is part of the first pillar of the Swiss pension system. Its first aim is to bring those affected back into working life.
wichtigste: The IV has existed since 1 January 1960.
Its principle is: integration before pension.
The IV contribution is 1.4 per cent of wages (as of 2025).
A partial pension is paid from a degree of invalidity of 40 per cent.
A full pension is paid from 70 per cent.
Each canton has an IV office that examines applications.
Since 2012 there has been the assistance contribution.

abschnitte.text: The Federal Act on **Invalidity Insurance** came into force on **1 January 1960**, twelve years after the AVS. Everyone who lives or works in Switzerland is insured. The IV is a **national insurance** and belongs to the **first pillar**. It helps in cases of illness, accident or disability, including for children. The word “invalid” here means that someone can permanently work less.

The most important principle is **integration before pension**. The IV first tries to bring those affected back into **working life** with various measures. These include, for example, retraining, aids or support at the workplace. Only if this does not succeed is a **pension** paid. This is assessed by the **IV office** in each canton.

What counts is the **degree of invalidity**. It shows how much someone's ability to earn a living is limited. A **partial pension** is paid from **40 per cent**. From **70 per cent**, you receive a **full pension**. Below that there is no right to a pension, but integration measures are still possible.

abschnitte.titel: Funding and help in everyday life
abschnitte.text: The IV is funded mainly through **wage contributions** and money from the Confederation. The contribution is **1.4 per cent** of wages; employers and employees each pay half (as of 2025). Because the IV had large debts, the people and the cantons agreed in 2009 to a temporary **increase in VAT**, which applied from 2011 to 2017. Since 2012 there has been the **assistance contribution**. With it, people with disabilities can themselves employ people who help them at home.

gewusst: The IV also pays for aids such as wheelchairs, hearing aids or guide dogs.
For children with certain congenital conditions, the IV covers the medical costs.

teile.einleitung: Municipal autonomy means that municipalities may regulate many matters independently. They do not have to ask the canton or the Confederation about everything. This is an important principle of Swiss democracy and is even written into the Federal Constitution.
wichtigste: Municipal autonomy means that municipalities may regulate many things themselves.
The word autonomy comes from Greek and means self-determination.
The Federal Constitution guarantees municipal autonomy in Article 50.
Exactly how much autonomy there is is decided by the law of each canton.
For example, municipalities set their own tax rate.
If its autonomy is violated, a municipality can go to court.
Municipal autonomy is part of Swiss federalism.

abschnitte.text: **Autonomy** comes from Greek and means something like making your own laws. A municipality with autonomy may make its own rules and decide for itself in certain areas. The canton does not simply interfere there. In this way people locally can decide on things that affect them directly.

Article 50 of the **Federal Constitution** says that municipal autonomy is guaranteed in accordance with cantonal law. This means: the Confederation protects the municipalities, but the cantons decide how much freedom they get. That is why municipalities in some cantons have more room for manoeuvre than in others. Municipalities in German-speaking Switzerland are often considered particularly independent.

Municipalities set their **tax rate** and so decide how much municipal tax their inhabitants pay. With the zoning plan, they decide where building is allowed and where it is not. They organise their administration, elect their authorities and decide on their budget. They often also decide whether a new school building, a gym or a cycle path is built.

If the canton interferes in a matter that actually belongs to the municipality, the municipality can defend itself. It can lodge an **autonomy complaint** and, if necessary, go all the way to the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne. The court then checks whether the municipality really may decide for itself in this area. So municipal autonomy is not just a nice word but a real right.

The people in a municipality often know their needs best. A mountain municipality has different concerns from a city. Thanks to municipal autonomy, both can find suitable solutions. However, small municipalities are sometimes overwhelmed by difficult tasks, which is why they work together or merge.

begriffe.erklaerung: Self-determination, meaning the right to make your own rules.
The most important law in Switzerland, which sets out the basic rules of the state.
A number with which the municipality decides how high its taxes are.
A legal action with which a municipality defends its independence in court.

gewusst: Because each municipality sets its own tax rate, you can pay a lot more or less tax in the next village.
By international comparison, Swiss municipalities are considered particularly independent.
Even a very small municipality with only a few dozen inhabitants has its own authorities.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland the municipality is the smallest political place where people live and can help decide. Together with the Confederation and the 26 cantons, it forms the third level of the state. There are just over 2000 municipalities, about 2100 in 2026.
wichtigste: The municipality is the lowest of Switzerland's three levels of state.
There are just over 2000 municipalities, about 2100 in 2026.
Every municipality belongs to a canton, and the canton sets the rules for its municipalities.
Municipalities have an executive, usually the municipal council, and a legislature.
The legislature is either the municipal assembly or a municipal parliament.
Municipalities raise their own taxes and have a great deal of independence.
Because of mergers, the number of municipalities has been falling for years.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is a **federal state** with three levels: the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities. This division is called **federalism**. Each level has its own tasks and its own authorities. The municipalities are closest to the people, which is why many everyday questions are decided there.

Municipalities vary greatly in size. The largest is the city of Zurich with over 400,000 inhabitants, while some mountain municipalities have only a few dozen people. The number per canton is also uneven: the canton of Bern has several hundred municipalities, while the canton of Glarus has had only three since 2011. Basel-Stadt consists of only three municipalities: Basel, Riehen and Bettingen.

Depending on the place, the **executive** is called the municipal council, town council or municipal executive, and it is elected by the people. In many municipalities, the **legislature** is the municipal assembly of all voters. Larger municipalities have an elected parliament, such as an Einwohnerrat or a Grosser Gemeinderat. In many municipalities, members of the authorities do the work alongside their job.

Municipalities are often responsible for primary and lower secondary schools, the water supply, waste disposal and local roads. With the **zoning plan**, they decide where building is allowed. They look after social assistance, the fire brigade and the register of residents. Exactly which tasks are included is regulated slightly differently by each canton.

Anyone with Swiss citizenship always also has citizenship of a municipality, the so-called **place of origin**. In naturalisations, the municipality has an important say. Around 1850 there were still over 3000 municipalities. Since then many have merged, because larger municipalities can often carry out tasks more easily and cheaply.

begriffe.erklaerung: Power is shared between the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities.
The government, which carries out decisions and runs the administration.
The authority that decides on rules and the budget.
The municipality whose citizenship you hold, no matter where you live.
A plan that sets out where houses, businesses or green spaces are allowed.

gewusst: Many Swiss people have never visited their place of origin, because it comes from their ancestors.
Besides political municipalities, Switzerland also has citizens' communes and church parishes.
In 2011 the canton of Glarus turned 25 municipalities into just three: Glarus Nord, Glarus and Glarus Süd.

teile.einleitung: The Fifth French Republic is France's current form of state. It began in 1958 with a new constitution that gives the President a lot of power.
wichtigste: The constitution was approved by referendum in 1958.
It was triggered by the Algerian crisis, which brought Charles de Gaulle back to power.
France has a semi-presidential system with a President and a Prime Minister.
Since a referendum in 1962, the President has been elected directly.
Since 2002 the term of office has been five years instead of seven.
The Conseil constitutionnel has nine appointed members.

abschnitte.text: The **Fourth Republic** was considered unstable because governments changed often. In 1958 a coup by French military officers in Algiers brought the country to the brink of civil war. This **Algerian crisis** brought **Charles de Gaulle** back to power. He became head of government and had a new constitution drawn up. It was approved by **referendum** in September 1958 and proclaimed on 4 October 1958.

Political scientists usually call the system **semi-presidential**. A directly elected **President** with wide powers stands alongside a **Prime Minister**, who depends on Parliament. Parliament consists of the **National Assembly** and the **Senate**. When the President and the parliamentary majority belong to different camps, this is called **cohabitation**.

At first, an electoral college chose the President. In **1962** de Gaulle pushed through **direct election** by referendum; it first took place in 1965. With the referendum of 2000, the term of office was shortened from seven to **five years**, the so-called **quinquennat**. It has applied since 2002. Since 2008 no more than two consecutive terms have been allowed.

**Article 16** gives the President emergency powers in a serious crisis. So far it has only been used once, by de Gaulle in 1961 after the generals' coup in Algiers. With **Article 49 paragraph 3**, “49.3” for short, the government can push a law through without a vote if no motion of no confidence succeeds. The constitution is watched over by the **Conseil constitutionnel**. Its nine members are appointed for nine years, three each by the President of the Republic, the President of the National Assembly and the President of the Senate.

gewusst: Former Presidents of the Republic are members of the Conseil constitutionnel by right.
The 1958 constitution still applies today, making it one of France's longest-lasting constitutions.

teile.einleitung: At the children's conference, children from several cantons met to talk about their rights. It took place in Trogen in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. The children chose the topics themselves and wrote demands to politicians.
wichtigste: At the children's conference, children discussed their own concerns.
It took place in Trogen in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden.
Until 2021 the Pestalozzi Children's Village was the venue.
Children from the 4th to 6th years of primary school took part.
It was mainly about children's rights.
At the end, the children wrote demands to politicians.

abschnitte.text: The **children's conference** took place in **Trogen**. Trogen lies in the canton of **Appenzell Ausserrhoden** in eastern Switzerland. Until 2021 the **Pestalozzi Children's Village** was the venue of the conference. It is named after the educator **Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi**. At the conference, **children** from several cantons met to talk about their concerns.

Children from the **4th to 6th years of primary school** took part in the children's conference. They were about **10 to 13 years** old. The conference lasted **a few days**, most recently five. During this time the children stayed at the conference venue. In this way they also got to know children from other regions.

The children's conference was mainly about **children's rights**. These are set out in the **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child**, which also applies to Switzerland. The children thought about how these rights could be better put into practice in Switzerland. The children chose the **topics** of the workshops **themselves**. So it was about what really mattered to them.

The children talked about their topics in **workshops**. Then they wrote down **demands**. They passed these on to adults in **politics**. In this way politicians found out what was on children's minds. For the children it was a chance to use their **right to have a say**.

gewusst: The Pestalozzi Children's Village was founded after the Second World War to give a home to children from countries affected by the war.

teile.einleitung: Obwalden is a canton in central Switzerland with lakes, mountains and the holiday resort of Engelberg. Together with Nidwalden, it used to form Unterwalden. Its capital is Sarnen.
wichtigste: Lake Sarnen lies in the middle of the canton near the capital, Sarnen.
Engelberg belongs to Obwalden but is separated from the rest of the canton.
The Rotair revolving gondola goes up the Titlis.
Brother Klaus from Obwalden is considered the patron saint of Switzerland.
The Brünig Pass links Obwalden with the Bernese Oberland.

abschnitte.titel: Sarnen and the coat of arms
abschnitte.text: The capital is **Sarnen** on **Lake Sarnen**. Obwalden and Nidwalden used to form **Unterwalden** together, one of the three original cantons. Both coats of arms show a **double key**, the sign of Saint **Peter**. The state archive in Sarnen holds the **White Book of Sarnen**. It contains one of the oldest versions of the legend of William Tell.

**Niklaus von Flüe** lived in the 15th century. He was a farmer and father of a family, and later withdrew as a hermit to the **Ranft** near Flüeli. He is called **Brother Klaus**. Many people came to him for advice. He is said to have helped settle a dispute among the Confederates in 1481. He is considered the **patron saint of Switzerland** and was canonised in 1947.

The holiday resort of **Engelberg** belongs to Obwalden but is separated from the rest of the canton. You travel there through Nidwalden. Engelberg has an old **monastery**. Above the village rises the glacier mountain **Titlis**. The **Rotair** revolving gondola turns a full circle during the ride, so you can see in all directions.

In the south lies **Lake Lungern**, near the village of Lungern. Its water is used for a **hydroelectric power station**. The **Brünig Pass** leads from Lungern to Brienzwiler in the canton of Bern. It is only just over 1000 metres high. Trains of the Zentralbahn also cross it on the way to the Bernese Oberland.

gewusst: An area that is separated from the rest of its canton is called an exclave. Engelberg is such an exclave.
Obwalden abolished its Landsgemeinde in 1998.

teile.einleitung: A popular initiative always starts with a small group of people: the initiative committee. It writes the text, collects signatures and campaigns for a yes. The committee is responsible for the initiative.
wichtigste: An initiative committee launches a popular initiative.
It has at least 7 and at most 27 members.
All members must be entitled to vote.
A federal initiative needs 100,000 valid signatures in 18 months.
The names of the members are on the signature form.
A majority of the committee decides on a withdrawal.

abschnitte.text: An **initiative committee** consists of at least **7** and at most **27** people. This is required by the Federal Act on Political Rights. All members must be **entitled to vote**, meaning Swiss citizens aged 18 or over. They often come from parties, associations or clubs. The law calls them the **originators** of the initiative.

First, the committee writes down exactly what the initiative wants. This **initiative text** is meant to go into the Federal Constitution later. The **Federal Chancellery** then checks whether the signature list meets the rules. After that, the initiative is published in the **Federal Gazette**. From that day, the collection period begins.

The committee has **18 months** to collect **100,000** valid signatures. Each **signature form** shows the names of the committee members. That way you can see who is behind the initiative. Signatures are collected in the street, at events or by post. At the end, the committee submits the signatures to the Federal Chancellery.

Before the vote, the committee **campaigns** for a yes, for example with posters, leaflets and media appearances. Sometimes Parliament makes a **counter-proposal**. Then the committee can **withdraw** the initiative. For this, a **majority** of the committee members must agree; one member alone cannot decide. That is why the form includes a **withdrawal clause**.

gewusst: There are also initiatives in the cantons and municipalities, but different numbers and deadlines apply there.
The first federal popular initiative went to the vote in 1893.
