teile.einleitung: In most villages the municipal council is the government of the municipality. It runs the municipality, prepares business and carries out decisions.
wichtigste: The municipal council is the government of the village.
It usually has three to nine members.
An odd number prevents a tie.
Each member looks after their own department.
The meetings are usually not public.
The municipal council must also obey the law.

abschnitte.text: In most villages the **municipal council** runs the municipality. It is like a small **government** for the village. It usually has between **three and nine members**. The number is often **odd**, for example five. That way there can be no tie when everyone votes. Anyone who wants to be elected to the municipal council usually has to **live in the same municipality**.

The work is shared out. Each member is responsible for a **department**, an area of tasks such as finance, building or schools. In many municipalities, the municipal council or a committee grants **planning permission** when someone wants to build a house. The municipal council is led by the mayor.

The municipal council prepares the **business** for the **municipal assembly** and makes proposals. The voters then decide there. Its own **meetings** are usually **not public**. Afterwards it informs the population about its decisions, for example in the municipal newsletter.

Under the **rule of law**, the laws apply to everyone, including the government of a municipality. Anyone who disagrees with a decision of the municipal council can challenge it. In other parts of the country the municipal government has a different name; in the canton of **Vaud**, for example, it is the **Municipalité**, led by the **Syndic**.

gewusst: In the city of Zurich it is the parliament, not the government, that is called the Gemeinderat.
Many municipal councillors in small villages hold their office alongside their job.

t1dko0eo.t: Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany

teile.einleitung: The Basic Law is the constitution of the Federal Republic of Germany. It was proclaimed on 23 May 1949. Originally it was meant as a temporary arrangement, but since 1990 it has applied to the whole of Germany.
wichtigste: The Basic Law was proclaimed in Bonn on 23 May 1949.
It was drawn up by the Parliamentary Council under Konrad Adenauer.
Article 1 begins with the sentence: “Human dignity shall be inviolable.”
Article 20 establishes democracy, the welfare state, the federal state and the rule of law.
The eternity clause protects the most important principles from any change.
A change needs a two-thirds majority in the Bundestag and the Bundesrat.
Since 3 October 1990 it has applied to the whole of Germany.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, Germany was divided. In the western zones of occupation, the **Parliamentary Council** in Bonn drew up a constitution. It had 65 voting members, sent by the state parliaments. Its president was **Konrad Adenauer**. On **23 May 1949** the Basic Law was proclaimed. This day is regarded as the birthday of the Federal Republic.

abschnitte.titel: Why Basic Law and not constitution
abschnitte.text: The founding fathers and mothers of the Basic Law deliberately did not choose the word “constitution”. Because Germany was divided, the Basic Law was meant to be **provisional**, a temporary arrangement until reunification. **Article 146** still provides that it can be replaced by a constitution adopted by the people. But the Basic Law proved its worth and remained.

**Article 1** begins with the sentence: **“Human dignity shall be inviolable.”** Human dignity is deliberately placed right at the start. This is a response to the crimes of **National Socialism**. Then come the fundamental rights, for example freedom of expression. **Article 20** states that Germany is a democratic and social federal state and a state under the rule of law.

An amendment to the Basic Law needs **two thirds** of the members of the Bundestag and two thirds of the votes of the **Bundesrat**. No popular vote is planned for this, unlike in Switzerland. Some principles may not be changed at all. This is set out in **Article 79 paragraph 3**, the so-called **eternity clause**. It protects the division into states (Länder) and the principles of Articles 1 and 20.

In 1990 the People's Chamber of the GDR decided to join the Federal Republic. For this it used **Article 23** in its old version, which allowed other parts of Germany to join. Since **3 October 1990** the Basic Law has applied to the whole of Germany. Compliance with the Basic Law is watched over by the **Federal Constitutional Court** in Karlsruhe.

gewusst: Article 20 paragraph 4 gives all Germans a right to resist anyone who seeks to abolish the democratic order, if no other remedy is available.
In Germany, 3 October is a public holiday, the Day of German Unity.

teile.einleitung: An illiberal democracy is a state in which there are elections, but fundamental rights and the rule of law are poorly protected. The term is used in political science and is politically disputed. It helps to describe states between democracy and dictatorship.
wichtigste: In an illiberal democracy there are elections but little protection of fundamental rights.
Fareed Zakaria made the term well known in 1997.
Above all, the independent judiciary is often weakened.
In 2014 Viktor Orbán spoke openly about building an “illiberal state”.
Critical media often come under the influence of owners close to the government.
In 2018 the European Parliament launched an Article 7 procedure against Hungary.

abschnitte.text: A **liberal democracy** combines two things: the majority decides, and at the same time the **rule of law** and **fundamental rights** protect every person. This includes free media, independent courts and rights for minorities. In an **illiberal democracy**, elections do take place. But the other parts are restricted. Alexis de Tocqueville and John Stuart Mill already warned against a **tyranny of the majority**.

The writer **Fareed Zakaria** made the term well known in 1997 with an essay in the journal “Foreign Affairs”. He described states with free elections but without protection of civil liberties. The political scientists **Steven Levitsky** and **Lucan Way** speak of **competitive authoritarianism**. By this they mean regimes in which the opposition may stand for election but the elections are not fair. Experts argue about which term fits better.

Often the **independent judiciary** is weakened first, for example through new rules for electing judges. Critical **media** are rarely banned openly. More often, businesspeople close to the government buy them up. The government justifies this by appealing to the will of the majority. Supporters say they are only doing what the voters want.

In 2014 the Hungarian Prime Minister **Viktor Orbán** said in a speech in Romania that he wanted to build an **illiberal state**. In Hungary, many media outlets were brought together in a foundation close to the government in 2018. In 2018 the **European Parliament** voted for an **Article 7 procedure** against Hungary. It concerns the risk of serious breaches of the EU's values. The Hungarian government rejected the accusations.

gewusst: Zakaria's 1997 essay was called “The Rise of Illiberal Democracy”.
Orbán gave his well-known speech in Băile Tușnad, a spa town in Romania with many Hungarian-speaking inhabitants.

teile.einleitung: At the lost property office, things that have been found are kept until their owners collect them. In Switzerland the law sets out exactly what you must do with something you find.
wichtigste: At the lost property office you can find lost things again.
You take things you find to the lost property office or to the police.
Lost property offices are often run by the municipality or the police.
Things left on the train end up at the railway's lost property office.
Honest finders may ask for a finder's reward.
If nobody comes forward for five years, the thing belongs to the finder.

abschnitte.titel: What a lost property office does
abschnitte.text: The **lost property office** collects things that someone has lost: keys, mobile phones, jackets, purses or umbrellas. If you are missing something, you can ask there. In Switzerland a lost property office is usually run by the **municipality** or the **police**. The **railway** also has its own lost property office for things left behind on trains or at stations.

abschnitte.titel: What to do with something you find
abschnitte.text: If you find a purse in the street, it belongs to someone else. You take it to the **lost property office** or the **police**. Simply keeping it is **forbidden** and a criminal offence. The law requires you to report or hand in what you find. That way the owner has a chance of getting their thing back.

The **Civil Code** sets out the finder's rights. If you return something that was lost, you may ask for a reasonable **finder's reward**. If you report what you found correctly and the owner has not been found after **five years**, you become the owner yourself. So honesty can pay off.

abschnitte.titel: Helping things find their way back
abschnitte.text: The easiest way for something to come back is if your **name** is on it. So write it in your exercise books, pencil cases and gym bags. For keys, a tag with your parents' phone number helps. Then the finder or the lost property office knows straight away who the thing belongs to.

gewusst: Every year many thousands of umbrellas, gloves and hats end up in lost property offices.
After five years, something that was found and correctly reported can belong to the finder.

teile.einleitung: In many Swiss municipalities the municipal clerk runs the administration. This person works closely with the municipal council and makes sure that everything is properly recorded.
wichtigste: The municipal clerk runs the municipality's administration.
They write the minutes of the municipal council's meetings.
They are usually employed by the municipal council.
They advise the municipal council but do not vote.
In a town the office is called town clerk.
At cantonal level, the equivalent is the state chancellor.

abschnitte.text: The **municipal clerk** is the head of the administration of a political municipality. They carry the main administrative responsibility and in many municipalities manage the administration's **staff**. Their office is in the **municipal hall**. In a town the office is called **town clerk**; the tasks are similar.

At the meetings of the municipal council, the municipal clerk records what was discussed and decided. This document is called the **minutes**. Important letters and documents of the municipality often bear two signatures: that of the **mayor** and that of the municipal clerk. That way it is clear that everything is in order.

Today the municipal clerk is usually **employed by the municipal council**. They attend the meetings and give **advice**, because they know the laws and procedures well. But only the elected members of the municipal council may vote. So the clerk is not a politician but an expert in administration.

Old minutes and documents are kept in the **municipal archive**. The municipal clerk is often responsible for it. That way you can look up what the municipality decided even many years later. There is a similar role at cantonal level: the **state chancellor** heads the **State Chancellery**. At federal level, the equivalent office is the Federal Chancellery.

gewusst: Many municipal archives contain documents that are hundreds of years old.
The municipal clerk often knows the procedures for longer than the elected councillors, who change.

teile.einleitung: The municipal administration is the team that does the day-to-day work in a municipality. It usually works in the municipal hall, the building where the municipality's administration is housed. If you move house, register a dog or need planning permission, you deal with the municipal administration.
wichtigste: The municipal administration carries out what the municipal council and the voters decide.
The municipal hall is the building where the municipality's administration works.
In towns it is often called the Stadthaus or Rathaus.
The administration is often led by the municipal clerk.
Important departments are the residents' registration office, tax office, building office and finance.
Many services can now also be dealt with online.
Municipal administrations train apprentices, for example in business administration.

abschnitte.text: The **municipal administration** consists of a municipality's employees. They work for the population and carry out the decisions of politicians. While the **municipal council** is elected and makes decisions, the administrative staff are employed and do the specialist tasks. In small villages there are only a few people; in big cities there are several thousand.

The **municipal hall** is the building where the municipality's administration works. There is a counter where you can ask questions and collect documents. The municipal council often meets in the same building. In towns the building is called the Stadthaus or Rathaus, and some of them are several hundred years old, like the town hall in Basel with its red façade.

At the **residents' registration office**, you register when you move to the municipality and deregister when you move away. The tax office deals with taxes, and the building office checks planning applications. The municipal works depot makes sure that roads are cleaned, snow is cleared in winter and rubbish is disposed of. There are often also social services, school administration and finance administration.

The **municipal clerk** plays a central role. This person writes the minutes of the municipal council's meetings and of the municipal assembly. They know the laws well and advise the municipal council. In many municipalities they also run the whole administration.

In the past you had to go to the counter in person for almost everything. Today many municipalities offer an **online counter**, where you can, for example, fill in forms or report a move. This saves time and paper. Even so, personal contact remains important, especially for older people.

Municipal administrations are popular **training companies**. Young people can do a commercial apprenticeship there, for example. They learn how taxes, residents' data or planning applications are handled. In this way they get to know Swiss democracy from the inside.

begriffe.erklaerung: Office that records who lives in the municipality.
Permission to build or convert a house.
The municipality's service for roads, rubbish and maintenance.
A written record of what was discussed at a meeting.

gewusst: Anyone who moves house in Switzerland usually has to register with the new municipality within 14 days.
Many municipal halls used to be schools or inns and were converted later.
On some municipal halls hangs the municipal coat of arms, which often shows animals, plants or tools.

teile.einleitung: Appenzell Ausserrhoden is a canton in eastern Switzerland with green hills and scattered farms. It borders Appenzell Innerrhoden and St Gallen. Its capital is Herisau.
wichtigste: Herisau is the capital and the largest village in the canton.
Appenzell Ausserrhoden came about in 1597 when Appenzell was divided.
At the time of the division, Ausserrhoden was Protestant.
The coat of arms shows a black bear and the letters V and R.
The canton's abbreviation is AR.

abschnitte.text: In the past there was only the **land of Appenzell**. After the **Reformation**, people there disagreed about their faith. In **1597** Appenzell therefore split into two parts. The **Protestants** lived in Ausserrhoden, the **Catholics** in Innerrhoden. In this way two separate half-cantons came about, which today count as cantons with half a cantonal vote.

The capital is **Herisau**. The government and the parliament, the cantonal council, meet there. The **coat of arms** shows an upright black **bear**. Beside it are the letters **V** and **R**. They stand for “Ussere Rhode”, the outer Rhoden. A Rhode used to be a district in the land of Appenzell. You can see the abbreviation **AR** on number plates.

A famous custom is the **Silvesterchläuse**, above all in **Urnäsch**. They go from house to house with big bells and sing a Zäuerli, a yodel without words. There are “schöne” (beautiful), “wüeschti” (ugly) and “schö-wüeschti” (beautiful-ugly) Chläuse. This happens on 31 December and on 13 January, the old New Year's Eve according to the former calendar.

The **Pestalozzi Children's Village** was founded in **Trogen** in **1946**. Children who had lost their homes in the Second World War lived there. They came from various countries in Europe. The children's village is named after the educator **Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi**. Today the foundation works for children's education in many countries.

gewusst: Appenzell Ausserrhoden abolished the Landsgemeinde in 1997.
Textile work used to be important in Ausserrhoden: many families wove and embroidered at home.

teile.einleitung: A community is a group of people who belong together and feel connected to each other. The first community that almost all children know is their family. Later come the school class, friends, clubs, the neighbourhood and the municipality.
wichtigste: A community is a group of people who belong together.
The family is the first community that almost all children know.
A school class is a community of children who go to school together.
A club is a group of people with the same hobby or goal.
Helping each other strengthens a community.
Help given voluntarily and without pay is called voluntary work.
A community needs rules so that living together works.

abschnitte.text: A **community** comes about when people share something, for example a place to live, a hobby, a language or a goal. The **family** is the first community in which a child experiences love, protection and rules. People need community, because alone many things would be difficult. Every person belongs to several communities at the same time.

The **school class** is a community of children who go to school together. There you learn to be considerate, to settle arguments and to work together. Many classes have a **class council**, a regular class meeting. There all children can raise issues, and the class decides together, for example about an outing or new rules.

A **club** is a group of people with the same hobby or goal. There are a great many clubs in Switzerland, such as football clubs, gymnastics clubs, bands, Scouts or fire brigade associations. A club has statutes, meaning rules, and a committee that runs it. Once a year the members meet at the annual general meeting and vote on important matters.

Help given voluntarily and without pay is called **voluntary work**. Millions of people in Switzerland do such work, for example as a coach in a sports club, as a leader in a youth group or by shopping for elderly neighbours. Without this work, many clubs, festivals and support services would not exist at all. Those who help make the community stronger and often find new friends themselves.

Neighbours form a community too. At a **neighbourhood party**, you meet your neighbours and celebrate together, often with games, music and a buffet to which everyone brings something. In some mountain villages there is still communal work, where everyone repairs paths or clears alpine pastures together. The political municipality is also a community, in which everyone decides together about the village.

A community becomes strong when people help each other, listen and treat each other fairly. Shared **rules** that everyone keeps are important. Shared experiences such as camps, festivals or projects also bring people together. Anyone who excludes or laughs at others, on the other hand, weakens the community.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of people with the same hobby or goal and their own rules.
Work that you do for others voluntarily and without pay.
A regular class meeting at which everyone may have their say.
The written rules of a club.

gewusst: There are an estimated 100,000 clubs in Switzerland, roughly one club for every 90 inhabitants.
Many fire brigades in Swiss villages are made up of people who do this alongside their job.
Humans are considered social beings, because they cannot live well without other people.

teile.einleitung: In football, the yellow card is a caution from the referee. It shows everyone at a glance that a player has played unfairly.
wichtigste: The yellow card is a caution.
Only the referee shows cards.
Two yellow cards in the same match mean a second yellow and a sending-off.
The idea comes from the Englishman Ken Aston, who thought of traffic lights.
Cards have been used since the 1970 World Cup in Mexico.

abschnitte.text: With the **yellow card**, the **referee** cautions a player. This happens, for example, after an **unfair foul** or for unsporting behaviour. Only the referee may show cards during the match; he keeps them in his pocket. Of course, there is no card for good moves.

If a player gets a **second yellow card** in the same match, the referee first shows yellow and then red. This penalty is called a **second yellow card** (yellow-red card). The player must leave **the pitch** and may not play any more. His team then plays on with one player fewer. For particularly bad fouls there is a straight **red card**.

In the past, the referee only gave cautions verbally. This led to misunderstandings when players and referees did not speak the same language. The English referee **Ken Aston** was driving and stopped at a set of **traffic lights** that changed from yellow to red. That gave him the idea for the cards. They were shown for the first time at the **1970 World Cup in Mexico**.

Since then, the cards have been understood in every language. Spectators in the stadium can also see immediately what has happened. Today cards are used in other sports too, for example in **handball** and **hockey**. We also know yellow as a warning from road traffic.

gewusst: At the first World Cup with cards in 1970, not a single red card was shown.
The idea for the cards came about while waiting at traffic lights.

teile.einleitung: Appenzell Innerrhoden is the canton with the fewest inhabitants in Switzerland. It lies at the foot of the Alpstein in eastern Switzerland. Old customs such as the Landsgemeinde are still alive here.
wichtigste: The capital is called Appenzell and is known for its colourful houses.
In 2024 only around 16,000 people lived in the canton.
The Säntis is the highest mountain in the Alpstein.
Biberli are filled honey gingerbreads from Appenzell.
The canton's abbreviation is AI.

abschnitte.text: The capital is the village of **Appenzell**. Its houses are brightly painted and have curved gables. Innerrhoden came about in **1597**, when the land of Appenzell split. The **Catholics** lived in Innerrhoden, the Protestants in Ausserrhoden. Instead of municipalities, Innerrhoden has **districts**. The abbreviation **AI** appears on number plates.

Every year at the end of April the **Landsgemeinde** takes place in Appenzell. Voters gather in the open air on the Landsgemeinde square. They vote by raising their hands. This is a very old form of **direct democracy**. Only two cantons, Appenzell Innerrhoden and Glarus, still have the Landsgemeinde.

The **Alpstein** is a mountain range with steep limestone cliffs. Its highest mountain is the **Säntis**, at around 2502 metres. A cable car goes up to the summit. Below the **Ebenalp** lies the **Wildkirchli**, caves in a rock face with a small chapel. Hermits used to live there. A little lower down lies the **Seealpsee**, a popular hiking destination.

**Appenzeller cheese**, with its spicy rind, is well known. A sweet speciality is **Biberli**. These are gingerbreads made with honey and spices and filled with almond paste. Traditional costumes, the procession of cattle up to the alpine pastures and folk music with the dulcimer are also part of Innerrhoden. Many customs are kept up with particular care here.

gewusst: Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton to introduce women's suffrage at cantonal level: in 1990, after a decision of the Federal Supreme Court.
On the Säntis there is a weather station that has been collecting data since the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: Children's and youth representatives stand up for children's concerns in a municipality, a town or a canton. They listen to children and take their wishes into politics. That way children can have a say too.
wichtigste: Children's representatives stand up for children and young people.
They ask children about their wishes and ideas.
They take children's concerns to the municipality's politicians.
They support places for children, for example playgrounds or youth centres.
At an ombudsman's office you can complain if rights are violated.
In 1981 Norway became the first country to create an ombudsman for children.

abschnitte.text: **Children's and youth representatives** make sure that a municipality thinks about children. As the name says, they are there for **children and young people**. These can turn to them directly. In some municipalities this is a separate post; in others it is a task within the administration. An important quality is that they **listen well** and take children's concerns seriously.

Children's representatives ask **children** about their wishes and ideas. This can happen at school, in surveys or at meetings. It is often about **places for children**, for example a new **playground**, a **youth centre** or a skate park. Safe routes to school are also a common topic. In this way the municipality finds out what really matters to children.

Children's representatives take children's concerns into **municipal politics**. They bring the wishes to the municipality's **politicians**. That way the **municipal council** can take children into account in its decisions. This fits with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child: it says that children should be **heard** on matters that affect them.

An **ombudsman's office** is an office where you can **complain**. It hears the complaint and helps to find a **fair solution**. There are also ombudsman's offices just for **children's rights**. Children can turn to them if they think their rights are being violated. In **1981** **Norway** became the first country in the world to create an ombudsman for children; many other countries followed later.

gewusst: The word ombudsman comes from Swedish and means something like “representative” or “agent”.
In some countries there is an ombudsman for children who reports directly to parliament.

teile.einleitung: The municipal library is a place where you can borrow books and other media. Many Swiss municipalities run their own library for their inhabitants.
wichtigste: At the library you borrow books and bring them back later.
You usually need a library card, which is often free for children.
If you bring something back late, you often pay a small fine.
You are quiet in the library.
You can often renew a loan.
At the toy library you borrow games and toys.

abschnitte.text: At the **municipal library** you can borrow **books**, read them and bring them back later. There are often also audiobooks, films, magazines and games. To borrow things you usually need a **library card**. That way the library knows who has which book. For children the card is often free.

The books are arranged **by subject** and often alphabetically by the author's name. That way you can find them quickly. If you are stuck, **librarians** will help. They know the books well and give tips. Because many people read and study there, you are **quiet** in the library.

Every book has a return date. If you are late, you often pay a small **fine**. If you want to read a book for longer, you can often **renew** the loan, at the desk or online. If the library is closed, you put books in the **returns box**.

Many libraries offer **story times**, when someone reads exciting stories aloud to children. In Switzerland there is also the **Ludothek**, a toy library. There you can borrow board games, ride-on toys and other toys for a few weeks. The word comes from the Latin “ludus”, which means game.

gewusst: A single library book can be read by dozens of people.
Toy libraries exist in many Swiss municipalities.

teile.einleitung: A compromise is a solution in which both sides give way a little. Nobody gets everything they wanted, but everyone is reasonably satisfied.
wichtigste: In a compromise, both sides give way a little.
To find a compromise, you have to talk to each other.
A compromise can settle an argument.
A compromise is often in the middle, for example 15 minutes between 10 and 20.
You can also do both, one after the other.
Compromises are very important in Swiss politics.

abschnitte.text: When two sides want different things, there is often an **argument**. A **compromise** is a solution that takes both wishes into account to some extent. Nobody gets everything they wanted. But in the end everyone is **reasonably satisfied**. A good compromise feels fair.

You can only find a compromise if you **talk to each other**. That way you find out what the others want and why. Friendly sentences help, for example: **“How about doing both?”** A sentence like this makes a suggestion for both sides. Insults or threats, on the other hand, only make an argument bigger.

Half the class wants to play football, the other half basketball. A compromise: first football, then basketball. Lisa wants a 10-minute break, Tim 20 minutes. A compromise is **15 minutes**, which is in the **middle**. If the class wants to sing three songs and only two children would like rock songs, you can sing one rock song and two folk songs. That way the smaller group's wish is included too.

In **Switzerland** several parties govern together in the Federal Council. For laws to come about, the National Council and the Council of States must agree. Often this only works with **compromises**. That is why Switzerland is seen as a country where people negotiate a lot. This is also called **concordance**.

gewusst: The word “compromise” comes from Latin and originally meant “a mutual promise”.
If the National Council and the Council of States pass different versions of a law, they look for a joint solution over several rounds, if necessary in a conciliation conference.

teile.einleitung: A class representative represents the whole class, for example to the head teacher. The children in the class elect this person themselves, just as adults elect their representatives in politics.
wichtigste: The class representative speaks for the whole class.
The children in the class elect the class representative themselves.
Anyone who stands for election is a candidate.
You may also put yourself forward.
Whoever has the most votes is elected.
A deputy steps in when the class representative is absent.

abschnitte.text: The **class representative** passes on the class's wishes and ideas, for example to the teacher or the head teacher. For this, the person must know what the class wants. That is why **listening well** is especially important. They do not speak only for themselves, but for everyone.

Anyone who would like to be elected is a **candidate**. You may put yourself forward or be suggested by others. The candidates often say briefly why they would like to take on the role. Then the **election** decides. It is the same in elections in the municipality or the canton.

Every child has one **vote** and should choose freely. People often vote secretly on a slip of paper. Whoever gets **the most votes** is elected. If, for example, Anna has 8 votes, Ben 6 and Lea 5, then Anna is elected. Buying votes with sweets or presents is unfair and not allowed.

The class often also elects a **deputy**. This person takes over the job when the class representative is ill or absent. Many Swiss schools also have a **pupils' council**. There representatives from all classes meet and discuss ideas for the whole school.

gewusst: Elected representatives also sit in the Federal Palace in Bern: the members of the National Council speak for the population, much as a class representative speaks for the class.
Secret elections on slips of paper exist so that nobody is put under pressure.

teile.einleitung: The canton of Basel-Landschaft lies in the north-west of Switzerland around the city of Basel. It is also called the Baselbiet. Its capital is Liestal.
wichtigste: Basel-Landschaft has been a separate canton since 1833.
Since 1994 the Laufental has belonged to Basel-Landschaft.
The coat of arms shows a red Basel crozier on a white background.
The Roman town of Augusta Raurica is in Augst.
The canton is known for its many cherry trees.

abschnitte.text: In the past, the countryside belonged to the city of **Basel**. But the people in the countryside had fewer rights than the townspeople. After a fierce dispute, the countryside separated from the city in **1833**. This created two half-cantons: **Basel-Stadt** and **Basel-Landschaft**. Later there were several attempts to reunite the two, but they were rejected.

abschnitte.titel: Liestal, coat of arms and Laufental
abschnitte.text: The capital is **Liestal**. The **coat of arms** shows a red **Basel crozier** on a white background. The Basel crozier recalls the staff of the Bishop of Basel. The **Laufental** belonged to the canton of Bern for a long time. The people there voted to change canton, and since **1994** it has belonged to Basel-Landschaft. The cantonal anthem is the **Baselbieterlied**.

**Augusta Raurica** was a Roman town. Its remains lie mainly in **Augst** and partly in Kaiseraugst in Aargau. You can see a large **Roman theatre** and parts of temples there. A museum displays a famous silver treasure. A reconstructed Roman house shows how people lived at that time.

There are a great many **cherry trees** in the Baselbiet. In spring they blossom white, and in summer the **Chriesi** (cherries) are harvested. They are also used to make kirsch, a spirit. In **Liestal**, the **Chienbäse** takes place on the Sunday of carnival: people carry burning bundles of wood through the old town. Burning carts also drive through the town gate. The fire brigade keeps a close watch.

gewusst: The word “Chienbäse” comes from “Chien”, resinous pine wood that burns especially well.
The Basel crozier in the coat of arms of Basel-Landschaft is red; that of Basel-Stadt is black.

teile.einleitung: Many families keep a pet, for example a dog, a cat or rabbits. An animal is lovely, but also a big responsibility. In Switzerland the Animal Protection Act sets out how to keep animals well.
wichtigste: A pet needs fresh water and suitable food every day.
You take a dog outside several times a day.
Guinea pigs and rabbits need the company of their own kind.
You pick up dog poo with a little bag.
You take a sick animal to the vet.
Chocolate is poisonous for dogs.
Before buying, it must be clear who will look after the animal every day.

abschnitte.text: A pet often lives for many years and needs care **every day**. That is why a family must first decide who will feed it, clean it out and take it for walks. Holidays, costs and space in the home also play a part. Not every animal suits every family. In a rented flat, you also need to ask whether pets are allowed.

Every animal needs **fresh water** and the right food every day. For rabbits, **hay** is the most important thing, plus fresh greens. Hay is good for digestion and wears down their teeth, which keep growing. You must **muck out** the hutch regularly and put in fresh bedding. Some foods are dangerous: **chocolate** is poisonous for dogs.

In the wild, many animals live in groups. That is why the Swiss **Animal Protection Ordinance** requires sociable animals such as **guinea pigs** to live with at least one of their own kind. Rabbits and budgerigars also do not feel well on their own. Dogs need a lot of contact with people and **exercise** outside several times a day. An animal that is bored can become ill.

If an animal becomes ill, you take it to the **vet**. There it is examined, treated and often vaccinated too. In Switzerland dogs must be identified with a **microchip** and registered. On a walk, you pick up **dog poo** with a little bag and throw it in a bin. That way paths and fields stay clean.

gewusst: The teeth of rabbits and guinea pigs keep growing throughout their lives.
Switzerland has one of the strictest animal protection laws in the world.

teile.einleitung: In a children's and youth parliament, young people meet to talk about their concerns. They present ideas, discuss them and vote. In this way they practise democracy and can have a say in their municipality.
wichtigste: In a children's and youth parliament you practise democracy.
The members present ideas, discuss them and vote.
The idea with the most votes wins.
Whoever is speaking deserves for the others to listen carefully.
With a proposal, a youth parliament asks the municipality to examine or do something.
Some children's parliaments meet in the town's real council chamber.

abschnitte.text: In a **children's and youth parliament**, young people learn how **democracy** works. They present **ideas**, **discuss** them and **vote**. The idea with the most votes wins. Children's parliaments are usually for younger children, **youth parliaments** for teenagers. They exist in many Swiss municipalities, towns and cantons.

In a parliament, people **listen carefully** to each other. Only then can good decisions be made. Different **opinions** are normal. You exchange **arguments** and look for a good solution together. At the end there is a vote, and even those who lose accept the result.

Youth parliaments campaign for things that matter to young people. A typical example is a **skate park**. Other ideas are a youth centre, safe cycle paths or more benches in the playground. With a **proposal**, the youth parliament asks the **municipality** to examine or do something. The authorities then reply to it.

Some children's parliaments may meet in the town's real **council chamber**. That way the members feel like real politicians. There is a chair, an **agenda** and fixed rules about who may speak when. Adults support the parliament but do not decide for the children. At federal level, the **Youth Session** takes place every year in the Federal Palace in Bern.

gewusst: In Switzerland there is an umbrella organisation that links the many youth parliaments with each other.
Some adults who are in politics today started out in a youth parliament.

teile.einleitung: The Conference of Cantonal Governments, KdK for short, is an association of all 26 cantonal governments of Switzerland. It helps the cantons to act together towards the Confederation, especially in European policy.
wichtigste: The governments of all 26 cantons are represented in the KdK.
The KdK was founded in 1993.
It is based in the House of the Cantons in Bern.
It represents the interests of the cantons towards the Confederation.
European policy is one of its most important priorities.
For a joint statement, at least 18 cantons must agree.

abschnitte.text: Each of the **26 cantonal governments** has a seat in the KdK. The KdK is therefore a body of the **executives**, that is the governments, and not of the cantonal parliaments. This allows the cantons to speak with one voice. Besides the KdK there are many **specialist conferences**, for example the **GDK**, in which the cantonal health directors work together.

The KdK was founded in **1993**. The main impulse came from **European and integration policy**: after the vote on the European Economic Area (EEA) in December 1992, the cantons wanted to have a greater say in the Confederation's foreign policy. Treaties with the **European Union** often affect tasks of the cantons. To this day the KdK is an important partner of the Confederation in European policy.

The KdK is based in the **House of the Cantons** in Bern. Many specialist conferences of the cantons also work there. The general secretariat of the KdK is run by the **ch Foundation for Federal Cooperation**. This foundation is supported by the cantons and promotes cooperation within the federal state.

The KdK issues **statements** on plans of the Confederation. A statement counts as the joint position of the cantonal governments if at least **18 of 26** cantons agree. Individual cantons may still submit a different opinion. In this way the KdK shows the Confederation what the cantons think, without any canton having to give up its own position.

gewusst: Switzerland is a federal state: many tasks such as schools, police and hospitals lie with the cantons, which is why their cooperation is so important.
The ch Foundation also organises exchange programmes in which young people get to know another language region of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A youth parliament is a place where young people talk about politics and contribute ideas. There, young people discuss topics that affect them and make proposals to the municipality, the canton or the Confederation. In this way you can try out democracy yourself even before the voting age of 18.
wichtigste: A youth parliament is a place where young people talk about politics and contribute ideas.
In Switzerland there are youth parliaments in many municipalities, regions and cantons.
The members are usually around 14 to 25 years old.
Youth parliaments can carry out projects and make proposals to the authorities.
At federal level, the Federal Youth Session takes place every year in the Federal Palace in Bern.
The umbrella organisation of Swiss youth parliaments supports youth parliaments throughout the country.
Those who take part learn to discuss, argue and vote.

abschnitte.text: In a **youth parliament**, young people meet regularly to talk about politics and their concerns. They can call, for example, for a new skate park, better bus links or more climate protection. Unlike a real parliament, a youth parliament usually cannot pass laws. But it can make proposals that adults must or should listen to.

There are many **youth parliaments**, youth councils and youth commissions in Switzerland. Some belong to a municipality or town, others to a region or a whole canton. They are supported by the **Swiss umbrella organisation of youth parliaments**, DSJ for short. If you want to take part, you can often simply sign up; sometimes there are elections.

Since 1991 the **Federal Youth Session** has taken place every year. Around 200 young people from all over Switzerland meet for a few days in the Federal Palace in Bern. They sit in the seats of the members of the National Council and debate in German, French and Italian. At the end, they pass on their demands to the federal Parliament as a **petition**.

Youth parliaments often organise their own projects, for example concerts, panel discussions before votes or campaigns against litter. In some municipalities they have their own small **budget**. Some may even submit proposals to the municipal parliament. In this way young people's ideas become visible.

If you take part in a youth parliament, you learn to form your own **opinion** and to give good reasons for it. You practise listening to others and finding compromises. Many politicians gained their first experience in a youth parliament. You also get to know people of your own age with very different views.

begriffe.erklaerung: A written request to an authority that anyone may submit, including children.
A yearly meeting of young people in the Federal Palace, where they debate like a parliament.
The age from which you may vote in elections and referendums; in Switzerland usually 18.
A solution in which each side gives way a little.

gewusst: The first Federal Youth Session took place in 1991 for the 700th anniversary of the Confederation.
In 2007 the canton of Glarus became the first canton to introduce a voting age of 16 at cantonal and municipal level.
Anyone may submit a petition, no matter how old they are or what passport they hold.

teile.einleitung: Uri is one of the three original cantons in central Switzerland. It consists mainly of the valley of the Reuss and high mountains. The legend of William Tell takes place here, and important routes lead over and under the Gotthard.
wichtigste: The Tell Monument stands on the village square of Altdorf.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel begins in the north at Erstfeld.
The southernmost part of Lake Lucerne is called Lake Uri.
The coat of arms shows a black bull's head on a yellow background.
The Reuss flows through the canton of Uri.

abschnitte.text: The capital is **Altdorf**. The **Tell Monument** stands on the village square. It shows **William Tell** with his son. According to the legend, Tell shot an apple off his son's head in Altdorf. The **Rütli meadow** lies on Lake Uri. According to tradition, representatives of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden formed an alliance there. Uri was one of the three **original cantons**.

abschnitte.titel: Coat of arms, Reuss and Lake Uri
abschnitte.text: The **coat of arms of Uri** is yellow with a black **bull's head**. The bull has a red ring in its nose. The **Reuss** rises in the Gotthard area and flows through the whole of Uri. At Flüelen it flows into **Lake Uri**, the southernmost part of Lake Lucerne. It stretches from Flüelen to Brunnen and is surrounded by steep mountains.

An important north-south route runs through Uri. The **Gotthard Base Tunnel** is 57 kilometres long. Its northern entrance is at **Erstfeld**. In the **Schöllenen Gorge** near Andermatt, the **Devil's Bridge** crosses the Reuss. A legend says that the devil built the first bridge. As payment he wanted the first soul to cross it, but the people of Uri sent a billy goat.

Several passes link Uri with other cantons. The **Susten Pass** leads from Wassen to Innertkirchen in the canton of Bern. At the top you can see the Stein Glacier. The **Klausen Pass** leads from Altdorf to Linthal in the canton of Glarus. The **Gotthard Pass** leads to Ticino, the Furka Pass to Valais. In winter many pass roads are closed.

gewusst: Since its opening in 2016, the Gotthard Base Tunnel has been the longest railway tunnel in the world.
In 1804 Friedrich Schiller wrote the play “William Tell”, which made the legend world-famous.

teile.einleitung: The Justice Initiative was a federal popular initiative. It wanted the judges of the Federal Supreme Court no longer to be elected by Parliament but chosen by lot. The people and the cantons clearly rejected it in November 2021.
wichtigste: Its official title was “Appointment of federal judges by drawing lots”.
The main initiator was the businessman Adrian Gasser.
An expert commission would have checked who was professionally and personally suitable.
The term of office would have ended five years after the normal retirement age, with no re-election.
The initiative was rejected with around 68 per cent voting no, and in all cantons.

abschnitte.titel: How federal judges are elected today
abschnitte.text: The **Federal Supreme Court** is the highest court in Switzerland. Its judges are elected by the **Federal Assembly**, meaning the National Council and the Council of States together. Care is taken that the parties are represented roughly according to their strength. The judges must regularly stand for **re-election**. Critics think that this could make judges dependent on their party.

The initiative wanted to introduce **selection by lot**. First, an independent **expert commission** elected by the Federal Council would have checked who was suitable for the office. Only these people would have gone into the draw. The national languages were also to be fairly represented. The term of office would have lasted until five years after retirement age. There would no longer have been re-election, but **removal from office** would have been possible.

The initiative was submitted on 26 August 2019 with 130,100 valid **signatures**. A popular initiative needs 100,000. Behind the initiative was the businessman **Adrian Gasser** with a committee. The Federal Council and Parliament recommended a no. In the National Council and the Council of States, several ideas for a **counter-proposal** failed, so the initiative went to the people without a counter-proposal.

On 28 November 2021 the Swiss people voted. The initiative was rejected with **68.07 per cent voting no**, just over two thirds. There was not a majority in a single canton, so the **majority of the cantons** was also missing. Supporters wanted more independent judges. Opponents thought that drawing lots was not democratic and that the existing system worked well.

gewusst: In ancient Athens, many offices were given out by lot, because this was considered particularly fair.
The Federal Supreme Court has its headquarters in Lausanne; one division works in Lucerne.

teile.einleitung: Impeachment is a procedure in the USA by which high officials can be charged with serious offences and removed from office. It also applies to the President. So far, however, no US President has ever been removed in this way.
wichtigste: The House of Representatives brings the charges by a simple majority.
The Senate decides and needs two thirds of those present for removal.
If the President is charged, the Chief Justice presides over the trial.
Grounds are treason, bribery and other serious offences.
Andrew Johnson was the first President to be impeached, in 1868.
Donald Trump is the only one to have been impeached twice (as of 2025).
Richard Nixon resigned in 1974 before proceedings began.

abschnitte.text: The **US Constitution** allows the President and other high officials to be removed from office. As grounds, Article II names **treason**, **bribery** and other high crimes and misdemeanours. What exactly falls under this is ultimately decided by **Congress**. So the procedure is both political and legal. It is meant to prevent someone from seriously abusing their power.

First, the **House of Representatives** votes on the articles of impeachment. A simple majority is enough for this. Then comes a kind of trial in the **Senate**. Removal requires **two thirds** of the senators present. If the President is charged, the **Chief Justice**, the head of the Supreme Court, presides over the trial.

The first President to be impeached was **Andrew Johnson**, in 1868. After the Civil War he had quarrelled with Congress about rebuilding the country. In the Senate, just one vote was missing for his removal. **Richard Nixon** faced certain impeachment because of the **Watergate scandal**. He resigned in 1974, the only US President so far to do so.

**Bill Clinton** was impeached in 1998 for lying under oath and obstruction of justice. The Senate acquitted him in 1999, and he stayed in office until 2001. **Donald Trump** was impeached in 2019 over the Ukraine affair and in 2021 after the storming of the Capitol. In both cases the necessary two-thirds majority was not reached in the Senate. This makes him the only President to have been impeached twice (as of 2025).

gewusst: The word “impeachment” means the charge, not yet the removal from office.
The Vice-President does not preside over the trial of the President, because he could benefit from the result himself.

teile.einleitung: The Green Party of Switzerland, the Greens for short, is a political party that campaigns above all for environmental and climate protection. It grew out of the environmental movement of the 1970s. It was founded as a national party in Fribourg in 1983.
wichtigste: The national Green Party was founded in Fribourg on 28 May 1983.
Switzerland's first green party was founded in Neuchâtel in 1971.
In 1979 Daniel Brélaz became the first Green elected to the National Council.
Environmental and climate protection are at the centre of its policies.
In the 2019 election the Greens won 13.2 per cent.
In 2023 they won 23 seats in the National Council.
The Greens have never been represented in the Federal Council so far (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: Switzerland's first green party was the **“Mouvement populaire pour l'environnement” (MPE)**. It was founded in 1971 as a local party in **Neuchâtel**. In 1979 **Daniel Brélaz** from the canton of Vaud was elected to the National Council. He was the first Green in a national parliament anywhere in the world. He remained active in politics for many years.

On **28 May 1983** several cantonal and local green groups met in **Fribourg**. They founded a national umbrella organisation. This became the **Green Party of Switzerland**. In French it is called “Les Vert-e-s”. Since then the party has been active in many cantons and municipalities.

The Greens grew out of the **environmental movement**. Their core issues are **climate protection**, nature and **public transport**. They also campaign for social justice and equality. On the political spectrum they are seen as left-wing. Other parties share some of their goals but often have different ideas about how to reach them.

In the **2019** elections, climate protection was a main issue. Before that, many young people had demonstrated in the **climate strikes**. The Greens won **13.2 per cent**, their best result, and 28 seats. The Green Liberals also made big gains. The media therefore spoke of a **green wave**. In the **2023** elections the Greens fell to **23 seats**.

In 2012/13 **Maya Graf** of the Greens, from the canton of Basel-Landschaft, became the first member of her party to be **President of the National Council**. In 2021/22 **Irène Kälin** became the second Green to hold the office. The Greens, however, have never been represented in the **Federal Council** so far (as of 2025). They have stood several times but were not elected.

gewusst: Daniel Brélaz was mayor of Lausanne from 2002 to 2016.
In the 2019 elections the Greens grew from 11 to 28 seats in the National Council.

teile.einleitung: On the evening of 1 August, large fires burn on many hills and mountains in Switzerland. They are called hilltop bonfires. They are part of the National Day celebrations and recall old warning fires.
wichtigste: Hilltop bonfires burn on the evening of 1 August, when it gets dark.
For the fire, people collect wood and branches into a big pile.
Because it burns high up, it can be seen from far away.
In the past, fires on hills passed on messages and warnings.
Such lookout posts were called Hochwachten.
In very dry weather a fire ban often applies.
At the end, the fire must be put out properly.

abschnitte.text: **1 August** is Switzerland's National Day. On this day people remember the alliance of the Confederates in 1291. In the evening, when it gets dark, **hilltop bonfires** are lit on hills. There are often speeches, lanterns and fireworks too. Because the fire burns **high up** and is not hidden, it can be seen from far away.

In the days before the celebration, clubs, families or municipalities collect **wood and branches**. They stack them into a big pile. Children often help too. The spot is chosen so that the fire does not endanger trees or houses. Adults keep watch for as long as it burns.

Centuries ago people already lit fires on mountains, but for a different reason. On **Hochwachten**, lookout posts on hills, people warned of **danger** with fire and smoke. When a fire was seen, another one was lit on the next hill. In this way a message could travel through the whole country in a short time. The hilltop bonfires on 1 August recall this time.

If it is **dry** for a long time in summer, a fire can quickly spread to woods and meadows. Then cantons or municipalities often issue a **fire ban**. In such years some hilltop bonfires and firework displays are cancelled. You never leave a fire burning on its own. At the end it is **put out properly**, so that no embers are left.

gewusst: 1 August has only been a public holiday off work throughout Switzerland since 1994.
In the past, a warning could reach large parts of the country in a few hours via the Hochwachten.

teile.einleitung: A children's parliament is an assembly in which children discuss topics that affect them. There children contribute ideas for their town or municipality. In doing so, they learn how politics works.
wichtigste: A children's parliament is a parliament for children.
Its members are called children's parliamentarians.
School classes often elect the members; sometimes you simply sign up.
The children make suggestions on how to make their home town more child-friendly.
The ideas go to the authorities of the municipality or town.
In a children's parliament, children practise democracy on a small scale.

abschnitte.text: A **children's parliament** is an assembly in which children **have a say**. They discuss topics that affect them. Children's parliaments exist, for example, in Swiss **towns** and **municipalities**. They are usually made up of children from the **middle years** of primary school. Adults support them but do not decide for them.

Anyone who sits in a children's parliament is called a **children's parliamentarian**. In many children's parliaments, **school classes** elect their members. Sometimes children can also simply **sign up**. Children from the place may take part. That way different schools and neighbourhoods are represented.

Children make suggestions on how to make their home town more **child-friendly**. A good topic is a **safe route to school**. Children know their route to school very well and can show where it is dangerous. Other topics are playgrounds, school playgrounds or nature nearby. The children's parliament writes down its wishes and passes them on to the **authorities**.

In a children's parliament, children practise **democracy** on a small scale. They learn to put concerns into words, to **discuss** and to **vote**. Anyone presenting an idea gives a **speech** in front of many people. That takes courage and can be practised well. The adults of the municipality then check what they can put into practice.

gewusst: Some children's parliaments meet in the real council chamber, where adults normally sit.
Children's right to give their opinion is set out in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

teile.einleitung: A coalition government comes about when several parties govern together because none has a majority in parliament on its own. Such governments exist in many European countries, for example in Germany.
wichtigste: A coalition government is formed jointly by several parties.
Coalitions come about when no party has a majority on its own.
In the coalition agreement, the parties set out their joint plans.
In Germany, the CDU/CSU and the SPD form a “grand coalition”.
The traffic-light coalition of the SPD, Greens and FDP governed from 2021 to 2024.
A minority government has no majority of its own in parliament.

abschnitte.text: To get laws passed and form the government, you need a **majority** in parliament. With **proportional representation**, parties receive seats in proportion to their votes. Then a single party rarely gets more than half. That is why several parties join together to form a **coalition**. They share out the ministerial posts between them.

The **coalition agreement** sets out which goals the partners want to achieve together and who gets which ministries. In Germany there is also the **coalition committee**. Party leaders, parliamentary group chairs and leading members of the government meet there to settle disputes. This body is not provided for in the Basic Law, but it is politically very influential.

In Germany, coalitions are often named after the **party colours**. The **traffic-light coalition** of the SPD (red), the FDP (yellow) and the Greens governed from 2021 until it broke up in November 2024. A **Jamaica coalition** of the Union, the Greens and the FDP recalls the flag of Jamaica; at federal level, negotiations for one failed in 2017. When the CDU/CSU and the SPD govern together, people speak of a **grand coalition**.

A **minority government** has no majority of its own and must look for votes from other parties for every law; this is common, for example, in Denmark and Sweden. An **oversized coalition** includes more parties than would be needed for a majority. In Britain coalitions are rare, but from 2010 to 2015 the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats governed together there.

Members of several big parties sit in the **Federal Council**. This is called **concordance**. Unlike a coalition, however, there is no coalition agreement and no fixed governing majority against an opposition. The parties work together, but in Parliament they still hold their own positions.

gewusst: The word “coalition” comes from the Latin “coalescere”, which means “to grow together”.
The coalition of 2010 was the first coalition government in Britain since the Second World War.

teile.einleitung: The canton of Neuchâtel lies in French-speaking Switzerland between Lake Neuchâtel and the border with France. French is spoken there. It is known for watches, the Jura and an unusual history involving a king.
wichtigste: The capital is the city of Neuchâtel, in German Neuenburg.
Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake that lies entirely within Switzerland.
La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle are watchmaking towns and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Neuchâtel belonged to the King of Prussia for a long time.
The coat of arms is green, white and red.

abschnitte.text: The city of **Neuchâtel** is called **Neuenburg** in German and lies on the shore of the lake. Above the old town stand the castle and the collegiate church. **Lake Neuchâtel** is the largest lake that lies **entirely within Switzerland**. Lake Geneva and Lake Constance are larger, but partly lie abroad. **French** is spoken in the canton.

Neuchâtel has an unusual history. From 1707 the **King of Prussia** was also Prince of Neuchâtel. Even so, from **1815** Neuchâtel was a canton of the Confederation. In **1848** the people of Neuchâtel proclaimed a **republic**. Only in 1857 did the Prussian king finally give up his rights. The **coat of arms** has three vertical stripes in green, white and red, with a small white cross.

High up in the Jura lie **La Chaux-de-Fonds** and **Le Locle**. **Watches** have been made in these towns for a long time. The streets were laid out in a grid so that the workshops got plenty of light. Since 2009 the two towns have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. **Le Corbusier**, one of the best-known architects in the world, was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1887.

The **Creux du Van** is a huge **rock amphitheatre** in the Neuchâtel Jura. Its cliffs are up to 160 metres high and form a semicircle. At the top you can walk along the edge. **Ibex** and chamois also live there. In clear weather you can see as far as the Alps.

gewusst: Absinthe has its home in the Val-de-Travers in the canton of Neuchâtel.
Le Corbusier appeared on the Swiss ten-franc note, which was valid until 2021.

teile.einleitung: A counter-proposal is a proposal of their own by the Federal Council and Parliament in response to a popular initiative. It takes up the aim of the initiative but often goes less far or carries it out in a different way. This gives voters a real choice.
wichtigste: A counter-proposal is Parliament's response to a popular initiative.
With a direct counter-proposal, the initiative and the counter-proposal are voted on together.
You may vote yes to both proposals; this is called a double yes.
With the deciding question, you decide which proposal you prefer if both are approved.
An indirect counter-proposal is a change to a law instead of a change to the Constitution.
The initiators often withdraw their initiative if the counter-proposal is enough for them.
The counter-proposal is a typical tool of direct democracy in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: With a **popular initiative**, 100,000 voters can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. The Federal Council and Parliament sometimes like the aim but find the proposed solution too strict or clumsy. Then they can draw up a **counter-proposal**. It is, so to speak, a compromise proposal by the authorities.

With a **direct counter-proposal**, Parliament proposes a constitutional text of its own. The people then vote on the initiative and the counter-proposal on the same day. Both are on the same ballot paper. For a proposal to be approved, it needs, like any change to the Constitution, a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.

Since 1987 you may vote yes to both the initiative and the counter-proposal; this is the **double yes**. In addition, there is the **deciding question**. There you tick which of the two proposals you would prefer if both are approved. Before that, the yes votes could be split between two proposals, so that in the end both often failed.

With an **indirect counter-proposal**, Parliament changes a law instead of amending the Constitution. It is not voted on at the same time as the initiative. If the initiators withdraw their initiative, the new law can come into force, provided nobody successfully calls a referendum. If the initiative is rejected at the ballot box, the indirect counter-proposal usually still comes into force, if it was decided that way.

The counter-proposal shows that initiatives can have an effect even if they are not approved themselves. In this way the Federal Council and Parliament take the population's concerns seriously. One example is the Responsible Business Initiative of 2020: it failed to win a majority of the cantons, but the indirect counter-proposal with new duties for companies came into force. This is how compromises often come about in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A proposal from the people to change the Federal Constitution, for which 100,000 signatures are needed.
The extra question about which proposal you prefer if the initiative and the counter-proposal are both approved.
The majority of the cantons in a vote.
The initiators give up the vote on their initiative.

gewusst: Until 1987 it was forbidden to vote yes to both the initiative and the counter-proposal at the same time.
Many popular initiatives are withdrawn because a counter-proposal meets some of their demands.
The cantons also have counter-proposals to cantonal popular initiatives.

teile.einleitung: A municipal newsletter is a small newspaper for the people in a municipality. It is published by the municipality and reports on what is happening locally. That way everyone is informed, even those who do not go to every meeting.
wichtigste: The municipal newsletter reports news from the municipality.
It is published by the municipality itself.
It usually comes free of charge to every letterbox.
It is often also called a bulletin or municipal paper.
Planning applications and decisions of the municipal council are announced in it.
Clubs announce their events in it.
Many municipalities also put their news on their website.

abschnitte.text: The **municipal newsletter** is published by the municipality. It comes out, for example, every month or a few times a year. In many municipalities it is also called a **bulletin** or municipal paper. It is usually distributed **free of charge** to all households. That way it reaches all inhabitants, young and old.

abschnitte.titel: What the municipal council has decided
abschnitte.text: The **municipal council** is the government of the municipality. Its meetings are not public. That is why it announces its **decisions** in the municipal newsletter. You find out, for example, that a road is being repaired or that a new playground is planned. The dates of the next **municipal assembly** or vote are often in it too.

Anyone who wants to build a house or make major alterations needs permission. The **planning application** must be made public. The municipal newsletter or the canton's official gazette is often used for this. That way the neighbours can see what is planned. If they do not agree, they can lodge an **objection** within a deadline.

There is also room in the municipal newsletter for **clubs**. They announce concerts, tournaments or festivals. There is often a calendar of events for the coming weeks. Many municipal newsletters congratulate older people on a **special birthday**, for example their 90th. In this way the newsletter becomes a meeting point for the whole village.

Today you can often also find the municipality's news on its **website**. Some municipalities even have their own **app** or an email newsletter. Even so, the printed paper remains popular, especially with older people. If you are well informed, you can **have your say** and help decide better in the municipality.

gewusst: There are over 2,000 municipalities in Switzerland (as of 2024), and many of them have their own bulletin.
Because it comes to every letterbox, it is often the paper read by the most people in the place.

teile.einleitung: Freedom of religion and conscience is a fundamental right in the Swiss Federal Constitution. Every person may decide for themselves whether and what they believe. Both religious and non-religious convictions are protected.
wichtigste: Freedom of religion and conscience is set out in Article 15 of the Federal Constitution.
Every person may freely choose and profess their religion or world view.
Nobody may be forced to belong to a religious community.
People without a religion are protected too.
This right was only guaranteed in general with the constitution of 1874.
The cantons regulate the relationship between church and state.

abschnitte.text: **Article 15** of the Federal Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and conscience. Every person may freely choose their **religion** or **world view**. They may profess it alone or with others. According to paragraph 4, nobody may be forced to join or belong to a religious community or to take part in a **religious act**.

Your **conscience** is the inner voice that tells you what is right and wrong. That is why Article 15 protects not only religious but also **philosophical convictions**. Even people who do not believe in any god are protected. So you may leave a church or not belong to any community at all. The state must remain **neutral** towards religions.

The Federal Constitution of **1848** only provided freedom of worship for the recognised Christian denominations. Only the constitution of **1874** guaranteed freedom of religion and conscience in general. At that time it was in **Article 49**. With the new constitution of 1999 it moved to Article 15. Its content stayed essentially the same.

abschnitte.titel: Church and state in the cantons
abschnitte.text: According to **Article 72 of the Federal Constitution**, the **cantons** regulate the relationship between church and state. That is why there are big differences. In many cantons certain churches are **recognised** under public law and may levy church taxes. Geneva and Neuchâtel separate church and state more strictly. But the Confederation makes sure that religious peace is maintained.

In the 19th century, the constitution still contained special bans on religious groups. One example is the **ban on the Jesuits**. It was removed from the Federal Constitution in a **popular vote in 1973**. At the same time, the ban on founding new monasteries was also dropped. These changes strengthened the equal treatment of religions.

gewusst: From the age of 16, young people in Switzerland may decide on their religious affiliation themselves.
Freedom of conscience was one reason why Switzerland introduced civilian service for those liable for military service.

teile.einleitung: Homework is tasks for school that you do at home. In German-speaking Switzerland many children call it “Ufzgi”. Homework helps you to practise and consolidate what you have learnt.
wichtigste: In Swiss German dialect, homework is often called “Ufzgi”.
Homework is mainly for practice.
You write down what you have to do in your homework diary.
A quiet place helps you to concentrate.
If you do not understand something, you ask.
Children do their homework themselves; parents may help.

abschnitte.text: In German-speaking Switzerland many children call their homework **“Ufzgi”**. The word comes from “Aufgaben”, meaning tasks. So that you do not forget anything, you write it in your **homework diary**. It also says when you have to do it by. The teacher tells you the **deadline**, and you keep to it.

Homework is mainly for **practice**. You go over what you have learnt at school. That way it stays in your head better. Sometimes you also prepare something for the next lesson, for example a short talk. Homework also helps you to work **independently** and to plan your time.

To do your homework well, you need a **quiet place**. There you can **concentrate** better. Loud noises, the television or your mobile phone are distracting. It also helps if everything you need is ready: exercise books, books and pens. Many children like to do their homework at the same time every day.

If you do not understand a task, **asking** is the best solution. You can ask your teacher, your parents or your brothers and sisters. Asking is allowed and good. Parents may help and explain. But **the child must do** the homework **themselves**, because that is the only way they learn something from it.

When your homework is finished, it goes into your **Schulthek**. That is what the school bag is called in Switzerland. It is best to pack your school bag the evening before. Then you will not forget anything in the morning. Some schools also offer **homework help**, where you can do your homework at school with support.

gewusst: Some schools in Switzerland do without homework completely or partly and do more practice in lessons instead.
In French-speaking Switzerland homework is called “les devoirs”.

teile.einleitung: The principle of collegiality is an important rule for the Swiss Federal Council and many other governments in Switzerland. It means that the members make their decisions together and present them in a united way to the outside world. Even those who were against a decision in the meeting stand behind it publicly afterwards.
wichtigste: The principle of collegiality applies to the Federal Council, the cantonal governments and many municipal councils.
Decisions are made together and presented in a united way to the outside world.
The Federal Council has seven members with equal rights.
The President of the Confederation is only first among equals.
The Federal Council's discussions are confidential.
The principle helps parties with different opinions to govern together.

abschnitte.text: A **collegial body** is a group of people with equal rights who carry out a task together. The principle of collegiality means that it is not one single person but the whole group that decides. The Federal Constitution states that the Federal Council decides as a collegial body. Once a decision has been made, all members present it **in a united way** to the outside world.

The **Federal Council** has seven members, each of whom heads a department, for example the Department of Defence or of Foreign Affairs. But they discuss important matters together in their meetings. A Federal Councillor therefore cannot decide everything in their area alone. What is said in the meetings remains **confidential**, so that people can discuss openly.

In many countries there is a head of government or a president with a lot of power. Switzerland is different: the **President of the Confederation** is elected anew every year by the Federal Assembly. The President chairs the meetings and represents Switzerland on special occasions, but has no more power than the others. This is called **primus inter pares**, first among equals.

The Federal Council includes members from several big parties, who often have different opinions. The principle of collegiality makes sure that the government still acts **together** and seems reliable. If every member spoke publicly against their own government, there would be constant arguments and uncertainty. That is why the principle fits well with Switzerland's **concordance democracy**.

Before popular votes, the Federal Council explains its position, and the responsible member must defend it, even if they personally think differently. Sometimes Federal Councillors do not stick to it completely, and then the media speak of a **breach** of the principle of collegiality. Critics say that this way the population does not find out who voted how. Supporters think that this is exactly what protects cooperation and trust.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of people with equal rights who decide together.
Latin for first among equals.
The government, which carries out the laws.
Secret, meant only for those involved.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the few countries that have no single head of government.
The President of the Confederation is only in office for one year.
Many municipal councils in Swiss villages also work according to the principle of collegiality.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who disagrees with a court judgement can often have it reviewed by a higher court. The sequence of courts is called the hierarchy of courts (Instanzenzug). In Switzerland it leads from the canton to the Federal Supreme Court.
wichtigste: The hierarchy of courts is the sequence of courts that examine a case.
In civil cases in Zurich, it leads from the district court via the high court to the Federal Supreme Court.
First-instance civil judgements with a value of 10,000 francs or more can be appealed.
In civil cases you can usually only go to the Federal Supreme Court if the amount in dispute is 30,000 francs or more.
In employment and tenancy cases, the limit is 15,000 francs.
Since 2007 there have been three unified appeals to the Federal Supreme Court.
After the Federal Supreme Court, a complaint in Strasbourg is possible.

abschnitte.text: A **hierarchy of courts** is like a staircase with several steps. Each step is a court, called an **instance**. In the canton of Zurich, in a civil case, after **conciliation** the **district court** examines the case first. After that you can go to the **high court** and finally to the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne. The Federal Supreme Court Act requires that, as a rule, the last cantonal instance is a **higher court**.

A route to a higher court is called a **legal remedy**. Against first-instance final decisions in civil cases with an amount in dispute of **10,000 francs** or more, there is an **appeal**. Below that, only an **objection** (Beschwerde) is possible. This is set out in the Swiss Civil Procedure Code. The higher instance then examines whether the first judgement was correct.

abschnitte.titel: The road to the Federal Supreme Court
abschnitte.text: The **Federal Supreme Court Act** of 2007 provides for three **unified appeals**: in civil cases, in criminal cases and in public-law matters. In civil cases there is usually a **threshold** of **30,000 francs** for the amount in dispute. In employment and tenancy cases it is lower, at **15,000 francs**. If the threshold is not reached, often only the **subsidiary constitutional complaint** remains. With it, you can only complain that constitutional rights have been violated.
