teile.einleitung: The canton of St Gallen lies in eastern Switzerland between Lake Constance and the Alps. It completely surrounds the two Appenzells. The capital is the city of St Gallen, with its famous abbey.
wichtigste: The city of St Gallen is named after the monk Gallus.
The Abbey Library is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
St Gallen sausage is traditionally eaten without mustard.
The OLMA takes place in St Gallen every autumn.
St Gallen became world-famous for its embroidery.

abschnitte.text: About 1400 years ago the monk **Gallus** lived in this place. Later a large **abbey** was built there, and from it grew the city of **St Gallen**. The **Abbey District**, with the cathedral and the **Abbey Library**, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983. The library owns very old handwritten books. Anyone entering the magnificent hall puts on felt slippers to protect the floor.

St Gallen became world-famous for its **embroidery** and **lace**. Around 1900 embroidery was one of Switzerland's most important exports. Many families in eastern Switzerland worked at embroidery machines. Companies in St Gallen still make fine fabrics today. They are even used by well-known fashion houses.

Every October the **OLMA** takes place. It is a big fair for agriculture and food. The **pig races** there are well known. A speciality is the **St Gallen sausage** (Bratwurst). It is pale and made from veal and pork. Traditionally it is eaten **without mustard**, often with a bread roll (Bürli).

The canton was created in **1803**. It stretches from **Lake Constance** at Rorschach through the **Rhine valley** to the mountains in the south. It completely surrounds the two cantons of **Appenzell**. The Walensee and the Churfirsten also lie partly in the canton. You can see the abbreviation **SG** on number plates. The coat of arms shows a **bundle of rods** with an axe.

gewusst: The Abbey Library holds the Plan of St Gall, a famous drawing of an ideal monastery from the early Middle Ages.
The OLMA fair has existed since 1943.

teile.einleitung: On the desk of the President of the National Council stands a small bell. The person chairing the chamber uses it to get attention. The bell is a sign of who is leading the meeting.
wichtigste: A small hand bell stands on the President's desk.
With the bell, the chair asks for quiet and attention.
A session is traditionally opened with the ring of the bell.
The president is elected anew every year.
The person at the head of the National Council is often called the highest Swiss citizen.
If there is a tie, the President has the casting vote.

abschnitte.text: In the National Council chamber, the **President of the National Council** sits at the front at a raised desk. A small **hand bell** stands there. When it gets too noisy in the chamber, the President rings the bell. In this way she asks for **quiet** and attention. The bell works better than shouting.

Parliament meets for **sessions**, normally four times a year for three weeks. At the beginning, the President traditionally rings the bell. In this way the session is **rung in**. Individual meetings or votes are also often announced with the ring of the bell.

The President **chairs the meeting**. She gives members the floor, keeps an eye on speaking time and guides the chamber through the **votes**. Normally she does not vote herself. But if there is a tie, her vote decides. This is called the **casting vote**.

The person at the head of the National Council is often called the **“highest Swiss woman”** or **“highest Swiss man”**. In terms of protocol, the office comes right at the top, even ahead of the Federal Council. The President is elected for **one year** at a time. That way different people and parties take their turn. Re-election the following year is not planned.

At the start of the **2020 spring session**, the little bell had suddenly disappeared. The President of the National Council, **Isabelle Moret**, knew what to do. She **clapped her hands** to get quiet. This little story shows how much the bell is part of the chamber's work.

gewusst: The President of the National Council also chairs the United Federal Assembly, for example when the Federal Council is elected.
The Council of States also has a presidency that changes every year.

teile.einleitung: Every canton has its own constitution. It is the canton's most important law and sets out how the canton is organised. The Federal Constitution sets out which rules every cantonal constitution must follow.
wichtigste: Every canton must give itself a democratic constitution.
The canton's voters must approve the constitution.
The Federal Assembly must guarantee every cantonal constitution.
Federal law takes precedence over cantonal law if they contradict each other.
According to the Federal Constitution, the cantons are sovereign, except where their sovereignty is limited.
Zurich approved a new cantonal constitution in February 2005.

abschnitte.text: The **cantonal constitution** is a canton's highest law. It sets out, for example, how the canton's parliament, government and courts are organised. It also describes the **popular rights** and the tasks of the canton. All other cantonal laws must fit with the constitution. According to **Article 3** of the Federal Constitution, the cantons are **sovereign**, except where the Federal Constitution limits their sovereignty. Whatever has not been given to the Confederation remains a matter for the cantons.

**Article 51** of the Federal Constitution sets out clear rules. Every canton must give itself a **democratic** constitution. So a canton may not, for example, have a king. The canton's **voters** must approve the constitution. In addition, it must be possible to **revise** the constitution if the majority of voters demand it.

Every cantonal constitution needs the **guarantee** of the **Federal Assembly**, the federal Parliament. The Federal Assembly checks whether the constitution contradicts **federal law**. If everything is in order, it is guaranteed. According to **Article 49**, federal law also takes precedence over conflicting cantonal law. This is called the **primacy of federal law**.

Many cantonal constitutions give the people more rights than the Federal Constitution. One example is the **financial referendum**. With it, the people decide on **spending** above a certain amount. This popular right does not exist at federal level. Some cantons also have a popular initiative for new laws, not just for changes to the constitution.

In recent decades many cantons have completely renewed their constitution. Zurich's voters approved a new cantonal constitution in **February 2005**. It replaced the old constitution of **1869**. A new constitution is often drawn up by a **constitutional council** elected by the people. At the end, the people vote on the draft.

gewusst: Switzerland has 27 constitutions: the Federal Constitution and one for each of the 26 cantons.
The constitution of the canton of Jura was drawn up before the canton was founded in 1979.

teile.einleitung: From 2015 the Polish government reorganised the country's judiciary considerably. Supporters spoke of a necessary reform; critics spoke of a danger to the independence of the courts. The dispute led to a long conflict with the European Union.
wichtigste: The Law and Justice party (PiS) governed with an absolute majority from 2015 to 2023.
At first, the Constitutional Tribunal was at the centre of the dispute.
In 2017 the EU Commission launched an Article 7 procedure under the EU Treaty for the first time.
The Disciplinary Chamber created in 2018 was abolished again in 2022.
In 2021 the European Court of Justice imposed a penalty of 1 million euros a day.

abschnitte.text: In a democracy, the **separation of powers** applies: parliament, government and courts check one another. Courts should be **independent** and not steered by the government. The national conservative party **PiS** won the elections in Poland in 2015. It said that the judiciary was slow and still shaped by old networks. Critics at home and abroad accused it of wanting to bring the courts under political control.

abschnitte.titel: Constitutional Tribunal and National Council of the Judiciary
abschnitte.text: First it was about the **Constitutional Tribunal**. The new majority did not recognise judges elected by the old parliament and appointed its own judges. After that, the tribunal lost its role as an independent check. In 2017 the **National Council of the Judiciary** (KRS) was reorganised. It proposes new judges. Previously, judges elected its judge members themselves; afterwards they were chosen by parliament, the **Sejm**.

abschnitte.titel: Disciplinary Chamber and the muzzle law
abschnitte.text: In 2018 a new **Disciplinary Chamber** was created at the Supreme Court. It could punish judges. From 2016 **Zbigniew Ziobro** was both Minister of Justice and Prosecutor General. A law of 2020 threatened judges with sanctions if they questioned the lawfulness of newly appointed judges. Critics called it the **muzzle law**. There were protests against it in many cities.

The EU requires its members to have a functioning **rule of law**. In December 2017 the EU Commission launched an **Article 7 procedure** for the first time in its history. The **European Court of Justice** (CJEU) ruled that the Disciplinary Chamber was not independent enough. Because Poland did not stop it, the Court imposed a penalty of 1 million euros a day in October 2021, which was later halved. In 2022 the chamber was abolished. After the change of government in 2023, the Commission closed the Article 7 procedure in 2024.

gewusst: Poland was the first country against which the EU Commission launched an Article 7 procedure.
Many judges in Poland publicly opposed the reform; some wore their judges' robes at protests.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland the word Gemeinderat does not mean the same thing everywhere. In most municipalities it is the government, but in some towns it is the parliament.
wichtigste: In most small municipalities the Gemeinderat is the executive.
It usually consists of five to nine people.
It is led by the mayor, called Gemeindeammann in some cantons.
In the city of Zurich the Gemeinderat is the parliament and the Stadtrat is the government.
In the city of Bern it is the other way round.
Elections are usually held under the majority system.

abschnitte.text: In most small Swiss municipalities the **Gemeinderat** (municipal council) is the **executive**, meaning the government. It runs the municipality and carries out decisions. It usually has **five to nine members**, and each is responsible for certain areas. It is elected by the municipality's **voters**, at the ballot box or at the municipal assembly.

One member leads the Gemeinderat. In many municipalities this person is called the **mayor** (Gemeindepräsidentin or Gemeindepräsident). They chair the meetings and represent the municipality to the outside world. Depending on the canton the office has a different name; in Aargau, for example, it is **Gemeindeammann** or Stadtammann. But the task is the same.

In the **city of Zurich** the **Stadtrat** is the government, while the Gemeinderat is the **parliament**. In the **city of Bern** it is the other way round: there the government is called the Gemeinderat, and the parliament with 80 seats is called the **Stadtrat**. So when you hear these terms, you always need to know which town is meant.

In small municipalities the councillors usually work **part-time**, alongside their job. This is called the **militia system**. In big towns the office is a full-time job. Elections are usually held under the **majority system**: the people with the most votes are elected. Some towns such as **Bern** or **Biel**, by contrast, elect their executive by **proportional representation**, meaning according to the parties' share of the vote.

gewusst: The same word means the parliament in Zurich and the government in Bern.
The militia system is considered typically Swiss.

teile.einleitung: The canton of Aargau lies in the north of Switzerland between Zurich, Basel and Bern. It is a canton of rivers, castles and baths. Its capital is Aarau.
wichtigste: The name Aargau means “area on the River Aare”.
The canton's abbreviation is AG, and it is also called Rüebliland (carrot country).
The coat of arms shows three white stars and waves for the rivers.
Near Brugg the Aare, Reuss and Limmat flow together: the Wasserschloss.
The Habsburgs' ancestral castle is in Aargau.

abschnitte.text: The canton of Aargau was created in **1803**. Before that, its territories belonged to various rulers, for example to Bern. The capital is **Aarau**, where the government and the parliament, the Grand Council, sit. You can see the abbreviation **AG** on number plates. The **coat of arms** shows three white stars on a blue background, with black and white waves beside them for the rivers.

The **Aare** flows through the middle of the canton and gives it its name. Near **Brugg**, the Aare, the **Reuss** and the **Limmat** flow together. This area is called the **Wasserschloss** (water castle) of Switzerland. A large part of Switzerland's water flows through here. In the north, the **Rhine** forms the border with Germany.

There are many castles in Aargau. **Habsburg Castle** is the ancestral castle of the **Habsburgs**. This family later ruled over Austria and large parts of Europe. **Lenzburg Castle** stands on a hill above the old town of Lenzburg. Today it houses a museum that many families visit.

The town of **Baden** is known for its warm **thermal springs**. The Romans already bathed in the warm water here; today there is a modern thermal bath. Aargau has the nickname **Rüebliland** (carrot country) because many carrots used to be grown there. Aargau carrot cake is still popular today.

gewusst: Near Brugg was the Roman legionary camp of Vindonissa, one of the most important Roman camps north of the Alps.
The monastery church of Königsfelden in Windisch has famous stained glass windows from the 14th century.

teile.einleitung: The pedestrian crossing, also called a zebra crossing, helps you to cross the road safely. In Switzerland it is yellow and there are clear rules.
wichtigste: In Switzerland zebra crossings are yellow.
The name comes from the stripes, like those of a zebra.
At a zebra crossing without traffic lights, pedestrians have priority over cars.
Trams have priority even at zebra crossings.
A saying to remember: “Wheel stops, child goes.”
You walk briskly, but you do not run.

abschnitte.text: A **pedestrian crossing** consists of wide bars painted on the road. Because they look like a **zebra's** coat, it is also called a **zebra crossing**. In Switzerland they are painted **yellow**, while in many other countries they are white. At a zebra crossing, drivers expect pedestrians. That is why it is the safest place to cross the road, not between parked cars or on bends.

At a zebra crossing without traffic lights, **pedestrians have priority**. Cars must stop when someone wants to cross the road. One exception is the **tram**: it cannot swerve and brakes only slowly. That is why it has priority even at zebra crossings. If there are traffic lights, the light signal applies.

Before you set off, you stop at the kerb and look left, right and left again. If a car is coming, remember the saying **“Wheel stops, child goes”**. Only when the wheels have come to a complete stop is it safe. It also helps to make eye contact with the driver. Then you walk **briskly**, but you do not run, because if you run you can trip or not be seen.

On wide roads there is often a **traffic island** in the middle. You can wait there safely. That way you only have to watch one lane and one direction of traffic at a time. This makes crossing easier and safer.

gewusst: Yellow pedestrian crossings are rather rare in Europe.
In Switzerland trams have priority even at zebra crossings.

teile.einleitung: The Kantonsrat is the parliament of a canton. Here elected representatives of the people discuss the canton's laws and money. Depending on the canton, this parliament has a different name.
wichtigste: The Kantonsrat is the parliament of a canton.
Voters elect its members every four or five years.
It passes laws and decides on the canton's budget.
The Zurich Kantonsrat has 180 members and is the largest cantonal parliament.
In Bern, Basel-Stadt and Aargau, the parliament is called the Grand Council.
In Uri, Glarus, Nidwalden and Basel-Landschaft it is called the Landrat.

abschnitte.text: Every canton has its own **parliament**. In many cantons it is called the **Kantonsrat** (cantonal council). It is made up of **representatives of the people** from different parties and regions. They represent the views of the population. Alongside the parliament there is the **cantonal government**, which carries out the decisions. In this way the tasks in the canton are divided, much as at federal level.

The canton's **voters** elect the members of the Kantonsrat. Depending on the canton, this happens every **four or five years**. There are usually **constituencies** for this, for example districts or regions. Each constituency gets a certain number of seats. Those elected usually hold the office alongside their actual job.

Its most important task is to pass **laws**. The Kantonsrat also decides what the canton spends **money** on and approves the **budget**. It also supervises the government and the administration. Members can bring in new ideas with **procedural requests**. For some decisions, the people can call a **referendum** and vote on them.

The parliament is not called the Kantonsrat everywhere. In **Bern**, Basel-Stadt and Aargau it is called the **Grand Council** (Grosser Rat). In **Uri**, Glarus, Nidwalden and Basel-Landschaft it is called the **Landrat**. In Vaud and other French-speaking cantons it is called the **Grand Conseil**, which means “Grand Council”. In Ticino it is called the Gran Consiglio. The **Zurich Kantonsrat** has 180 members, which makes it the largest cantonal parliament in Switzerland.

The meetings usually take place in the **town hall**. There is a large **council chamber** for the members. A president chairs the meetings. The meetings are usually **public**, so you can watch from the public gallery. Many cantons also broadcast the debates on the internet.

gewusst: Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden also have the Landsgemeinde, where the people vote in the open air.
Zurich's town hall stands right on the Limmat.

teile.einleitung: The Helvetic Republic existed from 1798 to 1803. It came about when French troops occupied the old Confederation. For the first time, Switzerland was a unitary state with a shared government.
wichtigste: The Helvetic Republic was proclaimed in Aarau on 12 April 1798.
It was a unitary state; the cantons were only administrative districts.
The first constitution was written by Peter Ochs from Basel, based on the French model.
The government was a Directory with five members.
The subject territories were abolished, and all citizens received equal rights.
The national colours were green, red and yellow.
After the Stecklikrieg of 1802, the republic collapsed.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 18th century, the **French Revolution** changed the whole of Europe. In 1798 French troops marched into the old Confederation. On **12 April 1798**, 121 representatives in **Aarau** proclaimed the Helvetic Republic. Aarau became the first, provisional capital. The constitution had been written by **Peter Ochs** from Basel on behalf of France.

The republic was a **unitary state**. A central government ran the whole country. The cantons lost their **sovereignty** and became administrative districts, each headed by a **government prefect**. The government was called the **Directory** and, as in France, had five members. Parliament consisted of the Senate and the Grand Council.

The constitution brought big changes. The **subject territories** were abolished, and all citizens received **equal rights**. There was now freedom of religion and freedom of the press. The national colours were **green, red and yellow**. Many of these ideas came back later in the federal state of 1848.

Not everyone wanted the new state. **Nidwalden** rejected the constitution, and on 9 September 1798 French troops crushed the uprising. Many people were killed. For the orphans, **Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi** set up an orphanage in **Stans** on behalf of the government. In 1802 opponents drove out the Helvetic troops in the **Stecklikrieg**, and in 1803 Napoleon ended the republic with the **Act of Mediation**.

gewusst: The Stecklikrieg (war of sticks) got its name because many of the rebels were armed only with clubs.
Pestalozzi described his experiences in Stans in the famous “Stans letter”.

teile.einleitung: The Hagenbach-Bischoff method is a way of distributing seats among parties in proportional elections. It is named after the Basel physicist Eduard Hagenbach-Bischoff. In Switzerland it is used, for example, in National Council elections.
wichtigste: Eduard Hagenbach-Bischoff (1833 to 1910) was a physicist from Basel.
He campaigned for proportional representation.
First you calculate the distribution number: votes divided by seats plus one, rounded up.
Each party gets as many seats as the number of times the distribution number fits fully into its votes.
Remaining seats go to the party with the highest figure of votes divided by seats plus one.
The result is always the same as with the D'Hondt method.
Large parties have a slight advantage.

abschnitte.text: **Eduard Hagenbach-Bischoff** lived from 1833 to 1910. He was a Swiss **physicist** and professor in **Basel**. Besides science, he was interested in politics. He campaigned for **proportional representation**, in which seats are distributed according to the share of the vote. For this he developed a method of calculation that now bears his name.

First you count all the valid **party votes**. You divide these by the number of **seats plus one**. The next highest whole number is the **distribution number**. Example: 5 seats and 10,000 votes. 10,000 divided by 6 is 1666.67, so the distribution number is **1667**. Each party gets as many seats as the number of times the distribution number fits fully into its votes. Party A with 4000 votes first gets 2 seats, because 4000 divided by 1667 is 2.4.

Often there are seats left over after the first distribution. Then each party divides its votes by its current **seats plus one**. The party with the highest figure gets the **remaining seat**. Example: A has 4000 votes and 2 seats, B 3000 and 1 seat, C 2000 and 1 seat, D 1000 and no seat. The figures are A 1333, B 1500, C 1000 and D 1000. The last seat goes to **B**.

The Hagenbach-Bischoff method is just another way of calculating the **D'Hondt method**. Both distribute the seats in **exactly the same way**. As with D'Hondt, **large parties** often get a small advantage with the remaining seats. That is why smaller parties often link their lists. Such a **list alliance** is first treated like a single party in the distribution.

In **National Council elections** the method is used in the cantons with several seats. The National Council has been elected by proportional representation since **1919**. Many cantons and municipalities also use the method. However, some cantons have switched to the **double Pukelsheim** for their parliamentary elections. This distributes the seats more precisely according to the share of the vote.

gewusst: With only 2 seats, a party with 6000 of 10,000 votes can win both seats if the others have 2500 and 1500 votes.
The D'Hondt method is named after the Belgian lawyer Victor D'Hondt.

teile.einleitung: On 26 November 1989 Switzerland voted on a popular initiative that wanted to abolish the army. It was rejected but received many more yes votes than expected. The vote set off a big debate about the role of the army.
wichtigste: The initiative came from the Group for a Switzerland without an Army (GSoA).
The GSoA was founded in 1982.
In 1989, 35.6 per cent of voters said yes.
The Federal Council and Parliament clearly rejected the initiative.
The Federal Council based its no on armed neutrality.
Most young voters said yes, older voters clearly said no.
A second attempt in 2001 received only around 22 per cent yes.

abschnitte.text: The **Group for a Switzerland without an Army**, **GSoA** for short, was founded in 1982 in the setting of the peace movement. It wanted to abolish the army and promote a comprehensive peace policy. For this it launched a **popular initiative** and collected the necessary signatures. For many people, even the idea broke a taboo. On 26 November 1989 the initiative went to the ballot box.

The **Federal Council** rejected the initiative. It relied on **armed neutrality**: Switzerland should be able to protect its neutrality militarily. In the **National Council** the rejection was very clear, by 172 votes to 13. The **Council of States** even rejected it unanimously. There was no counter-proposal.

With **35.6 per cent yes**, just over a third of voters said yes. This was far above the expectations of the Federal Council and the initiators. The cantons of **Jura** and **Geneva** even approved the initiative. According to a follow-up survey, most **under-30s** voted yes, while the over-60s very clearly voted no. There were also big differences between the parties: 91 per cent of SVP and FDP supporters rejected it, while there were yes majorities among SP and Green supporters.

Well-known writers such as **Max Frisch** and **Friedrich Dürrenmatt** publicly supported the initiative. Max Frisch wrote the text “Switzerland without an army? A palaver” about it. After the vote, the army was reformed and reduced in size over the following years. A **second attempt** by the GSoA clearly failed in December 2001, with around 78 per cent voting no. The GSoA still campaigns for its goals today with further initiatives.

gewusst: The 1989 vote took place only a few weeks after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
Turnout in 1989 was unusually high, at around 69 per cent.

teile.einleitung: Vaud is a large canton in the west of Switzerland, between Lake Geneva, the Jura and the Alps. French is spoken here, and the capital is Lausanne. The canton is known for vineyards, festivals and international organisations.
wichtigste: Vaud lies in French-speaking Switzerland on the northern shore of Lake Geneva.
The capital is Lausanne; the official language is French.
The people are called Vaudois in French (Waadtländer in German).
The coat of arms is white and green and bears the motto “Liberté et Patrie”.
The International Olympic Committee and the Federal Supreme Court have their seat in Lausanne.
The vineyard terraces of Lavaux have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.
Well-known festivals are the Montreux Jazz Festival and the Paléo Festival in Nyon.

abschnitte.text: Vaud stretches from **Lake Geneva** to the **Jura** and up into the Vaud Alps. It belongs to **Romandy**, French-speaking Switzerland. The capital, **Lausanne**, lies on steep slopes above the lake. Other well-known towns are Montreux, Vevey, Nyon and Yverdon-les-Bains. In terms of population, Vaud is one of the largest cantons in Switzerland.

For a long time Vaud was a **subject territory** of Bern. Only in 1803 did it become a separate canton of Switzerland with equal rights. The **coat of arms** recalls this: white at the top, green at the bottom, with the motto “Liberté et Patrie”, which means “Freedom and Fatherland”. The people of the canton are called **Waadtländer** in German. In French they are called “Vaudois”.

The **International Olympic Committee** has its seat in Lausanne. It organises the Olympic Games. On the lakeshore, the **Olympic Museum** shows the history of the Games. The **Federal Supreme Court**, the highest court in Switzerland, is also in Lausanne. There are also big universities such as the University of Lausanne and the ETH Lausanne, in French EPFL.

Between Lausanne and Vevey lies **Lavaux**. There vines grow on steep **terraces** above the lake, supported by walls. Since 2007 the area has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Near Montreux, **Chillon Castle** stands on a rock in Lake Geneva. It is one of the most visited castles in Switzerland.

Since 1967 the **Montreux Jazz Festival** has taken place every summer. Many famous musicians have performed there. **Nyon** has the **Paléo Festival**, one of the largest open-air festivals in Switzerland. The film star **Charlie Chaplin** spent the last years of his life near Vevey. A statue on the lakeshore at Vevey commemorates him.

gewusst: Chillon Castle does not stand on the shore but on a rock in the water.
The big food company Nestlé has its headquarters in Vevey.
Lausanne has a metro that climbs steep differences in height.

teile.einleitung: Fundamental rights are the most important rights that every person has. In Switzerland they are set out in the Federal Constitution. They protect all people, including children, from injustice and arbitrary action by the state.
wichtigste: Fundamental rights are important rights for all people.
They are set out in the Federal Constitution.
The fundamental rights begin with human dignity in Article 7.
All people are equal before the law.
Children and young people are entitled to special protection.
Freedom of religion and freedom of assembly are fundamental rights.
Anyone in need is entitled to help with the bare essentials.

abschnitte.text: **Fundamental rights** are the most important rights that every person has. They are set out in the **Federal Constitution** and protect everyone. The state must respect them. Right at the beginning is **human dignity** in Article 7: human dignity must be respected and protected. Then comes **equality before the law**: all people are equal before the law.

**Article 11** of the Federal Constitution says that children and young people are **specially protected** and supported. They should be able to develop well. In addition, all children have a right to free **primary education**. The **right to privacy** also applies to children: it protects, for example, their home, their letters and their personal data.

Many fundamental rights are **freedoms**. **Freedom of religion** allows every person to decide for themselves whether and what they believe. **Freedom of expression** allows you to say what you think. **Freedom of assembly** allows people to meet peacefully, for example for a demonstration. And **academic freedom** in Article 20 protects research and teaching.

**Freedom of establishment** allows Swiss citizens to live anywhere in the country. So you may freely choose which municipality you live in. Anyone who is in need and cannot help themselves has a **right to assistance in situations of need**. This includes food, shelter and medical care.

Fundamental rights do not apply without limits. But they may only be **restricted** under strict conditions. There must be a legal basis and a **public interest**, and the restriction must be **proportionate**. The core of a fundamental right may never be touched. Anyone who feels their fundamental rights have been violated can turn to a **court**.

gewusst: The current Federal Constitution has applied since 1 January 2000 and contains 30 articles on fundamental rights.
The European Convention on Human Rights also protects fundamental rights and has applied in Switzerland since 1974.

teile.einleitung: Zug is a small canton in central Switzerland. It lies between Zurich and Lucerne on Lake Zug and Lake Ägeri. The capital is also called Zug.
wichtigste: The canton of Zug is one of the smallest cantons in Switzerland.
The capital is called Zug and lies on the north-eastern shore of Lake Zug.
Other municipalities include, for example, Baar and Cham.
Zug cherry cake is a well-known sweet speciality.
According to tradition, the Battle of Morgarten took place near Lake Ägeri in 1315.
In 1887 part of the suburb of Zug sank into the lake.

abschnitte.text: By area, the canton of Zug is one of the **smallest cantons** in Switzerland. It stretches from **Lake Zug** up into the Ägeri valley. The capital is the town of **Zug**. Well-known municipalities are Baar, Cham, Steinhausen and Unterägeri. Zug has belonged to the Confederation since 1352. Today many international **companies** have their seat in the canton, because taxes there are low.

Many **cherry trees** grow around Zug. The cherries are used, among other things, to make **kirsch**, a spirit. This is used to soak the **Zug cherry cake** (Zuger Kirschtorte), which is named after the canton. It is made of sponge, nut layers and buttercream. The cake is known throughout Switzerland.

According to tradition, the **Battle of Morgarten** took place near **Lake Ägeri** in **1315**. There the Confederates fought against a Habsburg army and won. The battle is considered an important event in the early history of the Confederation. In the old town of Zug stands the **Zytturm** (clock tower). Below the large clock face it has an astronomical clock that shows the day of the week, the month and the **phase of the moon**.

On **5 July 1887** part of the **suburb** of Zug slid into Lake Zug. The ground on the shore was not stable enough. Many houses sank into the water, and people were killed. The event is called the **suburb disaster**. Afterwards the shore was redesigned.

The **Zugerbergbahn**, a funicular, goes up the **Zugerberg**. It starts in Schönegg and takes visitors up to walking paths with views. Near Baar, the **Höllgrotten** caves lie in the Lorze gorge. In these caves you can marvel at many **stalactites and stalagmites**. On Lake Zug you can often see beautiful sunsets.

gewusst: Stalactites grow very slowly, because only tiny amounts of lime are deposited from the water.
Lake Zug also lies partly in the cantons of Schwyz and Lucerne.

teile.einleitung: Hospitality means welcoming visitors in a friendly way so that they feel at home. Children can be good hosts and polite guests too.
wichtigste: You greet visitors in a friendly way, for example with “Welcome!”.
You offer a guest something to drink.
A good host shares their toys.
Before someone comes to visit, you ask your parents.
When you leave, you say thank you for the invitation.

abschnitte.text: When visitors are at the door, you say **“Welcome!”** and ask them in. Their jacket is hung up on the **coat rack** by the entrance. In many Swiss homes people take off their **shoes** when they come in, so that the floor stays clean. You often first offer the guest **something to drink**, for example water, squash or tea.

Before a friend comes round to play, you ask your **parents** whether it suits them. When your friend is there, you **share** your toys. That way you both have fun. If you have played together, you can also **tidy up together**, so that one person does not have to do everything alone.

There are rules for guests too. If something gets broken at someone's house, you **say so honestly** and apologise. Then you can find a solution together. When you leave, you say **“Thank you for having me”**. This shows that you enjoyed the visit.

Hospitality is important in almost all cultures of the world. But the customs are different. In some countries guests are always offered tea; elsewhere the guest brings a small present. If you ask with curiosity, you learn a lot about other cultures.

gewusst: The word “Garderobe” (cloakroom) comes from French and originally meant a room for clothes.
In many cultures it is considered a great honour to host guests.

teile.einleitung: A municipal parliament is the elected representative body of a municipality. Larger towns in particular have such a parliament, while many small municipalities decide at the municipal assembly.
wichtigste: Town parliaments are usually elected by proportional representation.
The names differ depending on the place and the language.
In Bern the town parliament has 80 members, in Winterthur 60.
In Geneva, Lausanne and Ticino, the authorities have French or Italian names.
Article 50 of the Federal Constitution protects municipal autonomy.
Neuchâtel has had voting rights for foreigners at municipal level since 1849.

abschnitte.text: In most small Swiss municipalities, voters decide at the **municipal assembly**. Larger municipalities and towns, on the other hand, have a **municipal parliament**. Its members are elected by the people and decide, for example, on the budget and regulations. Alongside it is the **executive**, the government of the municipality. Almost everywhere, parliaments are elected by **proportional representation**, so parties receive seats in proportion to their votes.

The names are confusingly varied. In **Winterthur** the parliament is called the **Grosser Gemeinderat** and has 60 members, while the government is called the Stadtrat. In **Lucerne** the parliament is called the **Grosser Stadtrat** and the five-member government the Stadtrat. In **Bern** it is the other way round: the parliament with **80 members** is called the Stadtrat. It is elected every four years.

In the **city of Geneva**, the **Conseil administratif** with five members runs the city, and the parliament is called the Conseil municipal. In **Lausanne** the **Municipalité** with seven members forms the government, and the parliament is called the Conseil communal. In **Ticino** the **Municipio** runs the municipality, led by the Sindaco. There the parliament is called the Consiglio comunale.

**Article 50** of the Federal Constitution guarantees **municipal autonomy**, but its extent depends on cantonal law. The Confederation must take into account the effects of its actions on the municipalities. The cantons also decide who may vote. The canton of **Neuchâtel** has had voting rights for foreigners at municipal level since as early as **1849**. Today several cantons in French-speaking Switzerland have similar rules.

gewusst: In the city of Bern the government is called the Gemeinderat and the parliament the Stadtrat.
Neuchâtel introduced voting rights for foreigners in its municipalities shortly after the founding of the federal state.

teile.einleitung: A counter-proposal is Parliament's response to a popular initiative. It takes up the aim but often goes less far than the initiative.
wichtigste: A counter-proposal is also called a counter-draft.
It is drawn up by Parliament, the Federal Assembly.
A counter-proposal is voluntary.
With a direct counter-proposal, you vote on both proposals at the same time.
Since 1987 you may say yes twice; the deciding question settles it.
An indirect counter-proposal usually changes a law.

abschnitte.text: With a **popular initiative**, citizens can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. Parliament can respond with a **counter-proposal**, also called a **counter-draft**. It often does this when it likes the idea but thinks the initiative goes too far. The counter-proposal is then usually milder. It is not compulsory: many initiatives go to the vote without a counter-proposal.

A **direct counter-proposal** also changes the Constitution. That is why the initiative and the counter-proposal are voted on on the same day. An **indirect counter-proposal** usually changes a **law** instead of the Constitution. The people do not vote on it together with the initiative. But a referendum can be called against it.

Since a vote in **1987**, you may say **yes twice** to the initiative and the direct counter-proposal. In addition, there is the **deciding question**: you state which proposal you would prefer if both are approved. This gives a clear result in the end. Because it is about the Constitution, a **majority of the people** and a **majority of the cantons** are needed.

If the **initiative committee** likes the counter-proposal, it can **withdraw** its initiative. With a direct counter-draft, only the counter-draft then goes to the vote, because as a change to the Constitution it is subject to the **mandatory referendum**. With an indirect counter-proposal, a committee often only withdraws its initiative on condition that the counter-proposal comes into force.

gewusst: Before 1987 a double yes was counted as invalid.
Sometimes a committee achieves more with a counter-proposal than it would have achieved with the initiative at the ballot box.

teile.einleitung: In a vote, those entitled to vote decide on a proposal with yes or no. In Switzerland this happens several times a year. Every vote counts, and each question is decided separately.
wichtigste: People who are in favour of a proposal are called supporters.
People who are against it are called opponents.
If the answer is no, everything stays as it was before.
For each question you write only yes or only no; otherwise the vote is invalid.
You decide afresh on each proposal.
Once a ballot paper has been put in the box, it can no longer be changed.
Swiss people living abroad may also vote in federal votes.

abschnitte.text: The **ballot paper** contains a question, for example whether a new law should apply. Whoever writes **yes** is in favour; whoever writes **no** is against. People who are in favour of a proposal are called **supporters**. Those who are against it are **opponents**. You may also put in a blank paper; then the vote counts neither for yes nor for no.

If a change is **rejected**, it is not introduced. Then the **existing law** continues to apply, so things stay as they were. If it is approved, it comes into force later. Changes to the Federal Constitution need a **majority of the people** and a **majority of the cantons**. This means: the majority of voters and the majority of the cantons must say yes.

For each question, you write only **yes** or only **no**. If both appear for the same question, the vote is **invalid**, because it is impossible to tell what the person wants. On a voting Sunday there are often several proposals. Each is about a different topic, which is why you decide on **each one afresh**. Once the ballot paper is in the **ballot box**, you cannot take it back.

In federal votes, Swiss citizens aged **18** and over may take part. **Swiss people living abroad** may also vote. They are sent the documents abroad. Most people today vote **by post** and send their paper before the Sunday. Others go to the polling station on voting day.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are usually four voting dates a year at federal level.
In the canton of Glarus, young people can vote on cantonal questions from the age of 16.

teile.einleitung: The cantonal referendum is a right of the cantons. If eight cantons demand it, a popular vote must be held on a federal act. It is very rarely used, but it is an important sign of Swiss federalism.
wichtigste: With the cantonal referendum, cantons can demand a popular vote on a federal act.
For it to come about, eight cantons must demand the referendum.
The deadline is 100 days after the act is published.
It is set out in Article 141 of the Federal Constitution.
The popular referendum with 50,000 signatures is much more common.
So far a cantonal referendum has come about only once, in 2003.
Each canton decides itself who in the canton makes the decision.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, new federal acts are subject to the **optional referendum**. This means that the people can vote on them if someone demands it. Usually citizens collect 50,000 signatures for this. But there is a second way: if eight cantons demand it, the **cantonal referendum** comes about.

The cantons have 100 days after the act has been published in the **Federal Gazette**. Each canton decides itself who makes the decision; usually it is the **cantonal parliament**. In some cantons the people of the canton can also vote on it. If eight cantons come together, the whole Swiss people votes on the act.

A cantonal referendum came about for the first and so far only time in 2003. At that time eleven cantons opposed the Confederation's **tax package**, because they feared losing too much tax revenue. In May 2004 the people voted on it and clearly rejected the package. So the cantons were successful.

Switzerland is a **federal** state in which the cantons carry a lot of weight. With the cantonal referendum, they can defend themselves if a federal act seriously harms their interests. It complements the **cantonal initiative**, with which a canton can make its own proposal to the federal Parliament. Together with the Council of States, this ensures that the cantons have a say at federal level.

It is difficult to convince eight cantonal parliaments in a short time. In addition, the cantons already have many chances to give their opinion beforehand, for example in the **consultation procedure**. Interest groups prefer to use the popular referendum with signatures. Even so, the cantonal referendum is an important tool for emergencies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A popular vote that only takes place if it is demanded.
A proposal from a canton to the federal Parliament.
A survey by the Confederation of cantons, parties and associations on a planned law.
The Confederation's official publication, in which new laws are published.

gewusst: The cantonal referendum has existed since 1874, but it was only used successfully for the first time around 130 years later.
For the cantonal referendum, every canton counts the same, whether it is large or small.
Besides the cantonal referendum there is also the mandatory referendum, in which the people must vote, for example on changes to the Constitution.

teile.einleitung: The House of Lords is the upper house of the Parliament of the United Kingdom. Unlike the House of Commons, it is not elected by the people. It examines laws and can delay them, but usually cannot stop them.
wichtigste: The House of Lords is the second chamber of the British Parliament.
Its members are not elected by the people.
26 bishops of the Church of England sit there as Lords Spiritual.
Since 1999 most hereditary peers have no longer had a seat.
The upper house can only delay most laws.
Since 2006 the Lord Speaker has chaired the sittings.
Since 2009 the Supreme Court has been the highest court.

abschnitte.text: The British Parliament has two chambers: the elected **House of Commons** and the **House of Lords**. Both sit in the Palace of Westminster in London. The Lords are not elected but are mostly appointed for life. Many of them are experts from science, business or politics. The chamber examines laws closely and proposes changes.

The 26 bishops of the **Church of England** are called the **Lords Spiritual**. They include the Archbishops of Canterbury and York. All the other members are called **Lords Temporal**. In the past, many nobles had an inherited right to a seat. The **House of Lords Act 1999** took away the seats of most **hereditary peers**; only 92 were allowed to stay for the time being, and a newer law also ends their right to sit.

Since the **Parliament Acts** of 1911 and 1949, the upper house can only **delay** most laws. It can hold up normal laws for about a year, and money bills for only a month. After that, the House of Commons can pass them on its own. Under the **Salisbury Convention**, the Lords do not block laws that the governing party announced in its election manifesto. This rule dates from 1945.

The person presiding sits on the **Woolsack**, a large cushion stuffed with wool. It is a reminder of how important the **wool trade** was for England in the Middle Ages. In the past, the Lord Chancellor, a member of the government, chaired the sittings. Since **2006** the Lords have elected their own **Lord Speaker**. Until 2009 the House of Lords was also the highest court; then the **Supreme Court of the United Kingdom** took over.

gewusst: Today the Woolsack is stuffed with wool from several Commonwealth countries.
The House of Lords is one of the largest parliamentary chambers in the world.

teile.einleitung: Gerrymandering is the deliberate drawing of constituency boundaries so that one party wins more seats. With the same number of votes, a completely different result can come out. The practice is best known from the USA.
wichtigste: In gerrymandering, constituencies are drawn to favour one party.
The name comes from Elbridge Gerry and the word salamander.
In cracking, the opponents are spread over many constituencies.
In packing, the opponents are squeezed into a few constituencies.
In the USA, constituencies are redrawn after every census, every 10 years.
Some states, such as California, let an independent commission draw the boundaries.

abschnitte.text: In 1812 **Elbridge Gerry**, Governor of Massachusetts, signed a law on new electoral districts. One of them had a very twisted shape and helped his party. A newspaper compared it to a **salamander**. Gerry and salamander became the word **gerrymander**. Gerry later even became Vice-President of the USA.

There are two main techniques. In **cracking**, the opponent's voters are spread over many constituencies. They then remain a minority everywhere and win nowhere. In **packing**, the opponent's supporters are squeezed into a few constituencies. There the opponent wins by a huge margin, but the surplus votes are missing elsewhere.

Imagine 50 voters divided into 5 constituencies of 10 people each. 30 vote for party A, 20 for party B. To win, B needs at least 6 out of 10 votes. With clever division, B can therefore win **3 constituencies**, because 3 times 6 makes 18. Even though A has the **majority** of votes, B then wins more constituencies.

In the USA the House of Representatives is elected in constituencies with one seat each. After every **census**, every 10 years, the seats are redistributed among the states and the boundaries redrawn. This is called **redistricting**. It is often done by the state legislature. Some states, such as **California**, have an independent commission of citizens do this work.

In 2019 the US Supreme Court ruled in the case **“Rucho v. Common Cause”**. It declared that federal courts cannot review partisan gerrymandering. It said it was a political question. The states and Congress can, however, make their own rules against it. In Switzerland the constituencies for the National Council are the **cantons**, so gerrymandering is hardly possible here.

gewusst: Some constituencies in the USA look like long, winding snakes on the map.
The word gerrymandering is over 200 years old and is now used all over the world.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who stands for election is a candidate. In Switzerland you can stand for many offices, from the municipality to the National Council. So that everything runs in an orderly way, there are clear rules.
wichtigste: You can stand for the National Council from the age of 18 if you are entitled to vote.
In the National Council election, you appear on a list in only one canton.
Besides your name, the list also shows your year of birth, job and place of residence.
New groups need signatures from voters for their list to be valid.
People without a party and Swiss people living abroad may also stand.

abschnitte.text: Anyone **entitled to vote** in federal matters can be elected to the **National Council**. That means Swiss citizens aged 18 and over. There is no higher minimum age. **Swiss people living abroad** who have registered may also stand. Some parties even have their own lists for them. For cantonal and municipal offices, the rules of each canton apply.

In the National Council election, each canton elects its seats. The candidates appear on **electoral lists**. Besides the name, the list shows the year of birth, **job and place of residence**, so that people know who is standing. A person may appear on a list in only one canton, usually their canton of residence. New groups need **signatures** from voters for their list. Parties that already sit in Parliament usually do not.

Most candidates belong to a **party**. Many parties have a **youth party** for young members. Youth parties often stand with their own lists. That way young people can gain their first experience. Anyone who does not belong to a party is **independent**. Independents may also stand for election, but they often find it harder to become known.

Someone who already holds an office and stands again is called an **incumbent** (Bisherige or Bisheriger) in Switzerland. Incumbents are often better known and are frequently re-elected. Anyone standing for the first time is a new candidate. In the **election campaign**, everyone introduces themselves with posters, leaflets, appearances and on the internet. On election day, the voters decide.

gewusst: The National Council has 200 seats and is elected every four years.
When voting, you may mix names from different lists; this is called panachage.

teile.einleitung: HarmoS is an agreement between Swiss cantons. It aligns important key features of compulsory schooling, for example the age at which children start school and the length of the school stages. The name stands for the harmonisation of compulsory schooling.
wichtigste: HarmoS is short for the harmonisation of compulsory schooling.
The concordat came into force in 2009, after ten cantons had joined.
15 cantons have joined; in seven cantons the people said no.
Children start school at four; the cut-off date is 31 July.
The two years of nursery school count too: 1H and 2H.
The cantons that have joined offer block timetables and day-care facilities.
National basic skills set out what almost everyone should be able to do.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the **cantons** are responsible for schools. That is why schools were quite different for a long time. **HarmoS** stands for the **Intercantonal Agreement on the Harmonisation of Compulsory Schooling**. Such an agreement between cantons is called a **concordat**. It aligns important key features, so that moving to another canton becomes easier. It was drawn up by the **EDK**, the Swiss Conference of Cantonal Ministers of Education.

The concordat was to apply as soon as **ten cantons** had joined. The tenth canton was **Ticino**. So HarmoS came into force in **2009**. By the end of the implementation period in **2015**, **15 cantons** had joined. In **seven cantons** the people rejected joining in a vote. Some other cantons suspended joining or did not take it up.

Under HarmoS, children start school once they have **turned four**. The cut-off date is **31 July**: whoever is four by then goes to nursery school. This made **nursery school compulsory**. The two years of nursery school count too; they are called **1H and 2H**. The former 1st year of primary school is therefore **3H**, and compulsory schooling lasts eleven years, up to 11H.

The cantons that have joined commit themselves to **block timetables**. This means that lessons in the morning last the same length of time for all children. There is also a range of **day-care facilities**, for example a **lunch club** and care after school. Using these services is voluntary. This helps many families to combine work and family life.

In **2011** the EDK adopted national education goals in the form of **basic skills**. They describe what almost all pupils should be able to do, for example in the **language of schooling**, in **maths** and in foreign languages. Whether these goals are reached is checked by the **ÜGK**, the assessment of the attainment of basic skills. For this, samples of pupils are tested in all cantons. **PISA**, on the other hand, is an international study by the OECD.

gewusst: In 2006 Swiss voters approved a new education article in the Federal Constitution, which obliges the cantons to harmonise their schools.
In German-speaking Switzerland the Lehrplan 21 curriculum builds on the goals of HarmoS; in French-speaking Switzerland it is the Plan d'études romand.

teile.einleitung: In many cantons the Gymnasium (academic secondary school) is called the Kantonsschule. The canton runs this school, and at the end comes the Matura. With it you can study at a university.
wichtigste: A Kantonsschule is a Gymnasium run by the canton.
Many people call it “Kanti” for short.
At the end you take the Matura exam.
Depending on the canton, the Gymnasium starts after primary or lower secondary school.
You usually need an entrance exam or good marks.
In French-speaking Switzerland the Gymnasium is often called “gymnase”.

abschnitte.text: A **Kantonsschule** is a **Gymnasium**, an academic secondary school. The name comes from the fact that the **canton** runs and pays for the school. In German-speaking Switzerland many pupils call it **“Kanti”** for short. In French-speaking Switzerland the Gymnasium is often called **“gymnase”**, in Ticino “liceo”. All these schools lead to the **Matura**.

Depending on the canton, the Gymnasium begins after **primary school** or after **lower secondary school**. The long-course Gymnasium starts earlier and lasts longer than the short-course Gymnasium. In many cantons you have to pass an **entrance exam**. Sometimes good marks or a recommendation from your teachers are enough. Besides the Gymnasium there are other good paths, for example an **apprenticeship**.

At the Kantonsschule you have many subjects: languages, maths, sciences, history, art and sport. Many schools offer **specialist subjects**, for example languages, economics or biology and chemistry. Towards the end you write your own **Matura paper** on a topic of your choice. Because the schools are run by the cantons, they are not organised in the same way everywhere. The **school holidays** are also set by the cantons and municipalities.

At the end of the Gymnasium comes the **Matura exam**. Anyone who passes receives the **Matura certificate**. With it you may study at a **university** or at the ETH. There you can study, for example, medicine, law, languages or engineering. The Matura is recognised throughout Switzerland.

gewusst: Some Kantonsschulen are very old and have buildings that are over a hundred years old.
The word Matura comes from the Latin word for “ripe”.

teile.einleitung: Karl Popper was an important philosopher of the 20th century. He was born in Vienna in 1902 and was concerned with science and politics. He is known especially for his defence of the open, democratic society.
wichtigste: Karl Popper was born in Vienna in 1902 and died in England in 1994.
His main political work is called “The Open Society and Its Enemies” and was published in 1945.
He wrote it during the Second World War in New Zealand.
For Popper, a democracy exists where you can vote the government out without bloodshed.
In science he called for theories to be falsifiable.
His paradox of tolerance is also well known.

abschnitte.text: **Karl Popper** was born in **Vienna** in **1902**. He studied there and worked as a teacher. Because his family had Jewish roots and National Socialism was growing stronger in Europe, he emigrated to **New Zealand** in **1937**. In **Christchurch** he taught at the university. After the war he moved to **London** and taught at the London School of Economics. He died in England in **1994**.

In his book **“The Logic of Scientific Discovery”**, Popper asked what makes a theory scientific. His answer: a theory must be able to **fail** when tested against experience. This is called **falsifiability**. So you must be able to imagine an experiment or an observation that would disprove the theory. For Popper, science learns above all by finding and correcting **mistakes**.

In **1945** **“The Open Society and Its Enemies”** was published in two volumes. Popper wrote it during the Second World War in New Zealand. In it he defends **liberal democracy** against **totalitarian** ideas. As enemies of freedom, he criticises **Plato**, **Hegel** and **Marx**. He devotes the first volume to Plato and the second to Hegel and Marx. He accuses them of justifying closed societies or inevitable laws of history.

Popper replaced the old question “Who should rule?” with a new one: how do you get rid of bad rulers? For him, the most important feature of a **democracy** is that you can vote the government out **without bloodshed**. Instead of rebuilding the whole of society according to a big plan, he recommended small reforms that can be checked. He called this **piecemeal social engineering**. In this way mistakes can be recognised and corrected.

By **historicism**, Popper meant the belief that the course of history can be predicted according to fixed laws. He considered this unscientific and dangerous for freedom. His **paradox of tolerance** is also well known: anyone who tolerates even the intolerant without limit risks the intolerant abolishing tolerance. An open society may therefore protect itself against its enemies. These ideas are still debated today.

gewusst: Popper was knighted in Britain in 1965 and was then called Sir Karl Popper.
As a young man, Popper also worked as an apprentice cabinetmaker.

teile.einleitung: The climate strike is a protest movement, mainly of young people, that demands more climate protection. It grew in 2018 out of Greta Thunberg's school strike in Sweden and also became very big in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Greta Thunberg began her school strike outside the Swedish parliament in August 2018.
This gave rise to the worldwide movement Fridays for Future.
The Swiss climate strike demands net zero emissions within the country by 2030.
The revised CO2 Act was narrowly rejected on 13 June 2021.
On 18 June 2023 voters approved the Climate and Innovation Act with around 59 per cent.
School strikes raise above all the question of unexcused absences.

abschnitte.text: In August 2018 **Greta Thunberg**, then aged 15, sat down with a sign outside the Riksdag, the parliament in Stockholm. She went on strike during school time for more climate protection. Many young people all over the world followed her example. This gave rise to the movement **Fridays for Future**, which usually organises school strikes and demonstrations on Fridays. Another group is **Extinction Rebellion**, which relies more on civil disobedience.

The **Swiss climate strike** demands that Switzerland reduce its **greenhouse gas emissions** within the country to **net zero** by 2030. Net zero means that no more greenhouse gas is emitted than is removed from the air again. The movement wants to achieve this without offsetting abroad. It also demands **climate justice**, meaning that the burdens are shared fairly.

On 13 June 2021 around 51.6 per cent of voters rejected the revised **CO2 Act**. For the climate movement this was a setback. On 18 June 2023 voters then approved the **Climate and Innovation Act** with around 59 per cent. It was the indirect counter-proposal to the **Glacier Initiative** and sets the goal of net zero by 2050. For the climate strikers this goal does not go far enough; others think it is sufficient or too strict.

In September 2020, activists under the name **“Rise up for Change”** occupied the **Bundesplatz** in Bern. This happened during Parliament's autumn session. During the session, demonstrations there are as a rule not permitted. That is why the police cleared the camp. The action sparked a debate about permitted and forbidden forms of protest.

Anyone who strikes during school time misses lessons. Legally, therefore, the main question is whether this counts as an **unexcused absence**. In Switzerland the rules on this are made by the **cantons**. Schools dealt with it in different ways, from punishment to tolerance. Some teachers also took up the topic of climate in their lessons.

gewusst: Greta Thunberg's sign said “Skolstrejk för klimatet” in Swedish, meaning school strike for the climate.
The Glacier Initiative was withdrawn after Parliament had passed the counter-proposal.

teile.einleitung: An interpellation is a question from members of Parliament to the Federal Council, which the Federal Council must answer. With it, members of Parliament can question the government on a topic and ask for information. It is an important tool with which Parliament keeps a check on the government.
wichtigste: An interpellation is a written question to the Federal Council.
The Federal Council must answer the interpellation.
It can be submitted by members of the National Council or the Council of States, but also by parliamentary groups and committees.
An interpellation only asks for information, not for a change in the law.
For urgent topics there is the urgent interpellation, which is answered more quickly.
Other parliamentary procedures are the motion, the postulate, the question and question time.
Cantonal and municipal parliaments also have interpellations.

abschnitte.text: The word **interpellation** comes from Latin and means something like “interruption” or “addressing someone”. In Swiss politics it is a **parliamentary procedural request** with which members ask the Federal Council questions. For example, a member of the National Council can ask how the Federal Council intends to improve rail links in the mountains. The Federal Council must give an answer.

A member writes down their questions and submits the interpellation during a **session**. The Federal Council usually answers in writing, mostly by the next session. Then the person who submitted the interpellation can say whether they are satisfied with the answer. Sometimes the answer is also discussed in the chamber.

If a topic is very current, an **urgent interpellation** can be submitted. This is dealt with in the same session. This makes sense, for example, in a crisis or after a disaster. Whether a request is urgent is decided by the bureau of the chamber concerned.

The interpellation is only one of several tools of Parliament. With a **motion**, Parliament instructs the Federal Council to draft a law or take a measure. With a **postulate**, it asks the Federal Council to examine something and write a report. An interpellation, by contrast, only asks for an answer, without giving an instruction.

With interpellations, Parliament can keep a check on the work of the **government**. The answers are public and are often taken up by the media. That way the population also finds out what the Federal Council thinks about a topic. Every year several hundred interpellations are submitted in the federal chambers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A proposal or a question submitted by a member of Parliament.
The period when Parliament meets; at federal level four times a year for three weeks.
A binding instruction from Parliament to the government.
An instruction to the government to examine something and report on it.

gewusst: All interpellations and the Federal Council's answers can be read online in the Curia Vista database.
The word interpellation is not only used in Switzerland; parliaments in France and other countries also know this tool.
Parliamentary groups sometimes use interpellations deliberately to get a topic into the headlines.

teile.einleitung: John Stuart Mill was a British philosopher and economist who lived from 1806 to 1873. He wrote about freedom, happiness and democracy. His book “On Liberty” is one of the most important texts of liberalism.
wichtigste: Mill published “On Liberty” in 1859.
Under the harm principle, freedom may only be restricted to protect others.
Like Jeremy Bentham, Mill held the views of utilitarianism.
Even false opinions should not be suppressed.
In 1867 he campaigned for women's suffrage in the House of Commons.
In 1869 “The Subjection of Women” was published.

abschnitte.text: In 1859 **“On Liberty”** was published. In it Mill asks how far the state and society may interfere in the life of the individual. His answer is the **harm principle**. Force is only allowed to prevent **harm to others**. What only affects yourself, you decide alone.

Mill defended **freedom of expression** very firmly. Even a false opinion should not be suppressed. It often contains part of the truth. And without opposition, even a true opinion becomes a **dead dogma** that nobody understands any more. The truth only stays alive in open **debate**.

abschnitte.titel: Happiness for as many as possible
abschnitte.text: Mill was brought up by his father **James Mill** in the tradition of **utilitarianism**, as taught by **Jeremy Bentham**. Utilitarianism judges actions by how much **happiness** they bring to as many people as possible. Mill refined this teaching. He distinguished **higher** pleasures of the mind from **lower** pleasures of the body. It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied, he wrote.

Mill sat for some years as a member of the British **House of Commons**. In 1867 he proposed replacing the word “man” with “person” in the electoral reform bill, so that women could vote too. The proposal failed but was a milestone for **women's suffrage**. In 1869 **“The Subjection of Women”** was published, in which he called for legal equality for women. In his **“Considerations on Representative Government”** he proposed giving educated people extra votes, which was controversial.

gewusst: Mill learnt Ancient Greek when he was still a small child.
Mill named his wife Harriet Taylor Mill as an important source of ideas.

teile.einleitung: A youth party is the party for young people that belongs to a larger parent party. In Switzerland almost all the big parties have a youth party. Youth parties are often louder and bolder than their parent parties and launch their own popular initiatives.
wichtigste: The JUSO is the youth party of the SP.
The FDP's youth party is called the Young Liberals (Jungfreisinnige).
The Centre's youth party is called the Young Centre.
The Young Greens launched the Environmental Responsibility Initiative.
The JUSO's 1:12 Initiative was rejected in 2013.
The Young Liberals' pension initiative was rejected in 2024.
The JUSO's inheritance tax initiative failed in 2025 with around 78 per cent voting no.

abschnitte.text: A **youth party** is aimed at young people, usually up to about 30 or 35. With the **Young Liberals**, for example, you can be a member until 35. Youth parties work together with their **parent party** but often act independently. Sometimes they even hold different positions. Many well-known politicians started out in a youth party.

The **JUSO**, the Young Socialists, belongs to the **SP**. The **Young Liberals** belong to the **FDP** and have a seat on its executive. When the CVP renamed itself **The Centre**, the Young CVP became the **Young Centre**. There are also, among others, the **Young SVP**, the **Young Greens** and the Young Green Liberals. **Tamara Funiciello** from Bern led the JUSO from 2016 to 2019 and was elected to the National Council in 2019.

The **JUSO** launched several popular initiatives. The **1:12 Initiative** wanted the highest wage in a company to be no more than twelve times the lowest. It was clearly rejected in 2013. The **99% Initiative** wanted to tax capital income more heavily and failed in September 2021. On 30 November 2025 around **78 per cent** rejected the **inheritance tax initiative**; not a single canton approved it. The **Young Greens** launched the **Environmental Responsibility Initiative**, which was rejected in February 2025.

Centre-right youth parties also put their own ideas to the vote. The **Young Liberals** launched the **pension initiative**. It wanted to raise the retirement age first to 66 and then link it to **life expectancy**. It was rejected in 2024. Supporters saw it as a way of securing the AVS; opponents feared a retirement age that was too high.

gewusst: Youth parties can launch a popular initiative even without the support of their parent party.

teile.einleitung: The canton of Basel-Stadt consists of the city of Basel and the municipalities of Riehen and Bettingen. It is the smallest canton in Switzerland by area. Basel lies on the Rhine where three countries meet.
wichtigste: Basel borders Germany and France.
The Basel carnival begins with the Morgestraich at 4 o'clock in the morning.
The Rhine ferries have no engine and are powered only by the current.
Basel Zoo, called the Zolli, is the oldest zoo in Switzerland.
Basel Minster is built of red sandstone.

abschnitte.titel: A city where three countries meet
abschnitte.text: Basel lies at the **Dreiländereck**, the point where three countries meet: Switzerland, **Germany** and **France**. Many people commute across the border every day. Basel has an important **Rhine port**; from here ships sail as far as the North Sea. The University of Basel was founded in 1460 and is the oldest in Switzerland. The coat of arms shows a black **Basel crozier**.

The **Basel carnival** (Fasnacht) begins on the Monday after Ash Wednesday. At **4 o'clock in the morning**, at the **Morgestraich**, all the lights in the city go out. Then the **Cliquen** (carnival groups) set off with lanterns, piccolos and drums. For three days the city is full of music and masks. Since 2017 the carnival has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.

The small **Basel ferries** hang from a rope across the Rhine. The **current** pushes them to the other bank without an engine. In summer many people go **swimming in the Rhine**. They pack their clothes in a **Wickelfisch**, a waterproof bag shaped like a fish. Above the Rhine stands **Basel Minster**, made of red sandstone, with its two towers.

**Basel Zoo** is the oldest zoo in Switzerland. People affectionately call it the **Zolli**. In 1977 the artist **Jean Tinguely** built the **Tinguely Fountain**, with machine figures that turn and spray water. **Basler Läckerli** are also well known: hard gingerbreads with honey, nuts and candied fruit. Basel also has many museums.

gewusst: The ferries in Basel are called Wilde Maa, Leu, Vogel Gryff and Ueli, after figures from Basel customs.
Basel-Stadt has only three municipalities: Basel, Riehen and Bettingen.

teile.einleitung: Keystone-SDA is Switzerland's national news agency. It collects news, pictures and videos and sells them to newspapers, radio stations and online portals. Many of the reports you read every day come from it.
wichtigste: Keystone-SDA is the only full news agency in Switzerland.
SDA stands for Schweizerische Depeschenagentur (Swiss Dispatch Agency).
The SDA was founded in 1894.
In 2018 it merged with the picture agency Keystone.
Its headquarters are in Bern.
Its reports appear in German, French and Italian.
The abbreviation “(sda)” shows that a text comes from the agency.

abschnitte.text: A **news agency** collects news from home and abroad. It writes short **reports** and supplies photos and videos with them. Its most important **customers** are newspapers, radio, television and **online portals**. They take over the reports in full or in part. In this way they can also report on events where they have nobody of their own on the spot.

**SDA** stands for **Schweizerische Depeschenagentur**, the Swiss Dispatch Agency. A **dispatch** is an old word for a message sent quickly, for example by **telegram**. Newspaper publishers founded the SDA on 25 September **1894**. From 1895 it also distributed reports from abroad. In **2018** the SDA took over the picture agency **Keystone**. Since then the company has been called **Keystone-SDA** and supplies texts and photos.

Keystone-SDA has its **headquarters in Bern**. Since 2019 the newsroom has been in the **Wankdorf** district. The agency reports in **German**, **French** and **Italian**. The French and Italian service is called **Keystone-ATS**. That way the media in all the main language regions of Switzerland receive reports in their own language.

Keystone-SDA is a **public limited company**. The Austrian news agency **APA**, the Austria Presse Agentur, holds around 30 per cent of the shares. The remaining shares belong mainly to **Swiss media companies**. Because the agency supplies many different media, it is meant to report as **neutrally** and factually as possible.

At the end of many newspaper articles is the abbreviation **“(sda)”**. With it, a newspaper shows that it has taken the report from the agency. That way readers know where the **information** comes from. This is important for being able to judge a **source**. Photos also often carry “Keystone” to show where the picture comes from.

gewusst: Agency reports are often written so that the most important point comes in the first sentence.
Big international news agencies often work with national agencies such as Keystone-SDA.

teile.einleitung: The Control Committees, GPK for short, are committees of the Swiss Parliament. There is one in the National Council and one in the Council of States. They check whether the Federal Council, the federal administration and the federal courts are doing their work properly.
wichtigste: The Control Committees exercise overall supervision of the Federal Council, the administration and the federal courts.
The basis is Article 169 of the Federal Constitution.
They mainly check legality, appropriateness and effectiveness.
The Control Delegation supervises state security and the intelligence services.
The Parliamentary Control of the Administration supports them with evaluations.
The Control Committees work independently of party politics and aim for consensus.

abschnitte.titel: The task of the Control Committees
abschnitte.text: Under **Article 169 of the Federal Constitution**, the Federal Assembly exercises **overall supervision**. This work is done mainly by the Control Committees. They supervise the **Federal Council**, the federal administration and the federal courts. Other bodies that carry out federal tasks are also included. Every year the Control Committees examine the **annual reports** of the Federal Council and the federal courts, which the chambers then approve.

The Control Committees check three things above all: **legality**, **appropriateness** and **effectiveness**. Are the authorities keeping to the law? Is their approach sensible? Does it reach its goal? The checks usually take place **afterwards**. The Control Committees publish reports with **recommendations**, and the authority concerned must respond to them.

The **Control Delegation (GPDel)** is made up of three members from each of the two Control Committees. It supervises **state security** and the **intelligence services**. For this it has particularly extensive rights to information. It was created as a result of the **secret files scandal**: investigations in 1989 and 1990 had revealed serious gaps in supervision. The delegation met for the first time in March 1992.

abschnitte.titel: Support and comparison with a PUK
abschnitte.text: The **Parliamentary Control of the Administration (PCA)** is part of the Parliamentary Services. It carries out scientific **evaluations** on behalf of the Control Committees. The Control Committees have extensive rights to information. But a **Parliamentary Investigation Committee (PUK)** has even greater powers of investigation. That is why a PUK is only set up for events of great significance.

Members of different parties sit on the Control Committees. Even so, they work **independently of party politics** and according to the **consensus principle**. They aim to reach findings that are as unanimous as possible. Only in exceptional cases is an important minority opinion published. This is meant to make their reports credible and stop them being seen as party politics.

gewusst: The Control Committees of the National Council and the Council of States often carry out larger investigations together.
