In the secret files scandal, it became known that state security had kept index cards, so-called “Fichen”, on many people and organisations.

teile.einleitung: Every Swiss canton has its own constitution. For it to apply, the Confederation must guarantee it, meaning confirm that it does not contradict federal law. The Federal Assembly is responsible for this.
wichtigste: Every cantonal constitution needs the Confederation's guarantee.
The Confederation must guarantee it if it does not contradict federal law.
This is set out in Article 51 of the Federal Constitution.
There is no political assessment.
The Federal Assembly's decision is final and cannot be challenged.
The guarantee has only very rarely been refused.

abschnitte.text: According to **Article 51 of the Federal Constitution**, every canton needs a democratic constitution. It must be approved by the people. The Confederation **guarantees** the cantonal constitution if it does not contradict **federal law**. So it only checks whether it fits legally. Whether it likes the content politically does not matter.

The **Federal Assembly**, meaning the National Council and the Council of States, decides on the guarantee. Its decision is **final** and cannot be challenged at the Federal Supreme Court. However, the Federal Supreme Court can later check whether cantonal law is being applied correctly in an individual case. The guarantee is **not constitutive**: it only confirms the law but does not create it. That is why a change can come into force beforehand.

In 1948 the Federal Assembly refused to guarantee articles of the cantons of **Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft** on reunification. It saw them as a violation of the **territorial guarantee**. In 1960 it reversed this decision. The canton of **Jura** also did not receive a guarantee for one article in 1977. Its first constitution planned to take in further areas of the Jura region.

In 2013 the canton of **Schwyz** did not receive a guarantee for its electoral system for the cantonal parliament at the time. The National Council rejected it twice, because the system violated **equal voting rights**. Small constituencies meant that not all votes carried the same weight. Schwyz then introduced the **double Pukelsheim**, a method for a fairer distribution of seats.

If the guarantee is refused, the provision lapses **retroactively**, back to the date it came into force. The canton must then change it. But such cases are very rare. According to the **Parliamentary Services**, the guarantee has only been refused in **five cases** so far (as of 2026). In almost all other cases it was granted.

gewusst: Every year cantons submit changes to their constitutions to the Confederation for guarantee, usually without any discussion.
The double Pukelsheim is named after the German mathematician Friedrich Pukelsheim.

teile.einleitung: The mayor is at the head of a municipality. In many Swiss municipalities they lead the municipal government and are something like the face of the village or town. Whoever holds this office deals with very local things such as school buildings, roads, water and festivals.
wichtigste: The mayor leads the municipal government, the municipal council.
The office is part of the municipality's executive, meaning the authority that carries out decisions.
In most municipalities the person is elected directly by the voters.
In towns the office is usually called town president.
Depending on the canton there are other names, for example Gemeindeammann, Syndic, Maire or Sindaco.
In small municipalities the office is often a part-time role done alongside a job.
The mayor represents the municipality to the outside world, for example towards the canton.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has around 2100 **municipalities**, and each one needs leadership. The mayor chairs the meetings of the **municipal council**, the municipal government. Together with the other members of this body, they run the municipality's business. The office is the highest post in the municipality, but the person cannot decide alone.

Usually the municipality's **voters** elect the mayor directly at the ballot box. In some municipalities the election takes place at the municipal assembly. Depending on the canton, a term of office usually lasts four or five years. After that, you can stand for election again.

Together with the municipal council, the mayor prepares business, for example the **budget** or the building of a new school. In municipalities with a municipal assembly, the mayor often chairs it. They work closely with the municipal administration and the municipal clerk. They also welcome guests, give speeches at the National Day celebration on 1 August and sometimes congratulate very old people on their birthday.

In the canton of Aargau the office is called **Gemeindeammann**. In the French-speaking cantons of Vaud and Fribourg people say Syndic, in Geneva, Neuchâtel and the Jura Maire. In Ticino the person is called Sindaco or Sindaca. In big cities such as Zurich, Bern or Basel people speak of the **town president**, and in Basel of the president of the government, because the city is also a canton there.

In small villages the office is a **militia office**. This means that the person also has a normal job, for example as a farmer, teacher or tradesperson. In larger towns, on the other hand, the post is a full-time job with a proper salary. Some municipalities now find it hard to find people willing to take on such an office.

Hardly any politician is as close to the people as a mayor. You meet them in the shop, at the village festival or on the way to school and can speak to them directly. Many well-known politicians began their career in a **municipality**. That is why the office is a school for democracy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The government of a municipality, with several members. In some big cities, however, this name is used for the municipal parliament.
The authority that carries out decisions and governs.
A political office that you hold alongside your actual job.
The period for which someone is elected to an office.

gewusst: In the city of Zurich the town government is called the Stadtrat, while the town parliament is called the Gemeinderat, exactly the other way round from many villages.
Because the municipality of Basel and the canton of Basel-Stadt are closely linked, the city of Basel has no municipal government of its own.
Some very small municipalities have fewer than 100 inhabitants, but even there someone has to be mayor.

teile.einleitung: The municipality is the place where you live, and at the same time the smallest political unit in Switzerland. It takes care of many things you need every day: school, the playground, the roads and rubbish collection. There are around 2100 municipalities in Switzerland (as of 2026).
wichtigste: The municipality is the smallest political unit in Switzerland.
Switzerland has around 2100 municipalities (as of 2026).
The municipality often looks after the school, playgrounds, roads and rubbish.
It is run by the municipal council, headed by the mayor.
The municipal administration works in the municipal hall.
At the municipal assembly, those entitled to vote meet and help decide.
Large towns have a municipal parliament instead of an assembly.

abschnitte.text: A **municipality** is a village or town with its own administration and its own authorities. Switzerland is divided into three levels: the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities. The municipality is the lowest level and the one closest to the people. Some municipalities have only a few dozen inhabitants; the city of Zurich has over 400,000.

The municipality often builds and maintains school buildings and nursery schools. It looks after playgrounds, municipal roads, parks and sometimes a swimming pool. **Rubbish collection** takes away the waste, and the municipality makes sure there is clean drinking water. It also keeps the register of residents, with which you must register after moving house.

The government of a municipality is usually called the **municipal council**; in some cantons it is also called the town council or municipal executive. At its head is the mayor, often called the town president in towns. In French-speaking Switzerland this person is often called the syndic. The staff of the municipal administration work in the **municipal hall**, or in the town hall in towns.

abschnitte.titel: Having a say in the municipality
abschnitte.text: Many smaller municipalities have a **municipal assembly**. This is a meeting that all voters may attend. There they vote, for example, on the budget, the tax rate or a new school building, usually by show of hands. Larger municipalities and towns have an elected municipal parliament instead.

The municipality raises its own taxes to pay for its tasks. That is why people pay different amounts of tax depending on where they live. Because small municipalities can hardly manage some tasks alone, many join together. These **municipal mergers** are the reason why there are far fewer municipalities today than in the past.

begriffe.erklaerung: The government of the municipality, which runs its day-to-day business.
A meeting of voters at which municipal questions are decided.
A number that sets how high the municipal taxes are.
Two or more municipalities join together to form a new municipality.

gewusst: Around 1850 there were still over 3000 municipalities in Switzerland.
In 2011 the canton of Glarus merged its 25 municipalities into just three large ones.
Every Swiss person has a place of origin, a municipality whose citizenship they hold.

teile.einleitung: A children's rights poster shows at a glance what rights all children have. With pictures and short sentences, every child can understand it, even children who cannot read well yet.
wichtigste: A children's rights poster shows the most important rights of children.
The rights come from the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child of 1989.
Switzerland recognised this Convention in 1997.
Many schools hang such a poster in the classroom.
Pictures help small children and children with a different language.
Each picture stands for a right, for example the school bag for the right to education.

abschnitte.text: In 1989 the United Nations, the **UN** for short, adopted the **Convention on the Rights of the Child**. This is a treaty between many countries that sets out the rights of all children. Almost all the countries in the world have signed it. Switzerland joined in 1997. Every person under 18 counts as a child.

The treaty is long and written in difficult language. A **poster** sums up the most important rights briefly. There is often a simple picture for each right. That way even small children and children who speak a different language understand what is meant. If the poster hangs in the **classroom**, the children see their rights every day.

A **school bag** stands for the right to education: every child may go to school and learn. A **full plate** stands for the right to food; no child should go hungry. A **roof** shows the right to a safe home. A **speech bubble** means that children may give their opinion and adults should listen. Children holding hands stand for **equal treatment**.

abschnitte.titel: All children are worth the same
abschnitte.text: An important principle is: no child may be **put at a disadvantage**. Origin, language, appearance or religion do not matter. The rights apply to every child all over the world. That is why many posters show children from different countries together.

Many classes design their own children's rights poster. The children choose rights that matter to them and draw suitable pictures for them. While doing so, they talk about what these rights mean in everyday life. This is a particularly good way to get to know your own rights.

gewusst: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child is one of the treaties recognised by the most countries in the world.
20 November is the international day of children's rights, because the Convention was adopted on that day in 1989.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is divided into 26 cantons. Between them run cantonal borders. They show where one canton ends and the next begins, and you can cross them freely at any time.
wichtigste: A cantonal border separates two cantons from each other.
You never need a passport to travel to another canton.
In the countryside, borders are often marked with boundary stones.
On roads, a sign with the canton's name and coat of arms often shows the border.
Geneva borders only one other canton, Vaud.
Cantonal borders can also run through the middle of a lake.

abschnitte.text: A **cantonal border** is the line between two cantons. On one side the laws of one canton apply, and on the other those of the neighbouring canton. This concerns, for example, schools, taxes or the **cantonal police**. Because all cantons belong to Switzerland, you can cross the border freely. You never need a **passport** for this.

In the countryside, borders are often marked with **boundary stones**. They show exactly where the border runs. **Coats of arms**, letters or dates are often carved into them. On many roads there is a **sign** at the cantonal border with the name and often the coat of arms of the canton. That way you notice, even in a car or train, that you are entering another canton.

Cantonal borders often follow nature, for example mountain ridges, rivers or lakes. **Lake Zurich** lies in three cantons: Zurich, Schwyz and St Gallen. The borders run through the middle of the water there. Cantonal borders also meet on high mountains. Some borders are very old and go back to earlier lordships.

Some cantons border not only other cantons but also neighbouring countries. **Geneva** borders only one other canton, **Vaud**. Otherwise Geneva is almost completely surrounded by **France**. **Ticino** has a long border with **Italy**. The **Grisons** borders the Austrian states of Vorarlberg and Tyrol, but also Italy and Liechtenstein. St Gallen also borders Austria.

gewusst: Some municipalities lie like small islands in the middle of another canton. This is called an exclave.
If you stand at a boundary stone, you can sometimes stand with one foot in each of two cantons.

teile.einleitung: At a municipal assembly, the voters of a municipality decide directly on its business. Instead of electing representatives, citizens come to a hall themselves and vote by raising their hands. This form of direct democracy is typical of Switzerland.
wichtigste: The municipal assembly is the meeting of a municipality's voters.
In many municipalities it is the highest body, the municipality's legislature.
Voting is usually open, by raising hands.
Only people entitled to vote may take part, not all inhabitants.
Typical business includes the budget, the tax rate, the annual accounts and big building projects.
Most small and medium-sized Swiss municipalities have a municipal assembly.
Larger towns have an elected municipal parliament instead.

abschnitte.text: The **municipal assembly** is a meeting at which all the voters of a municipality may have their say and help decide. It is a form of **direct democracy**, because people decide themselves and not through elected representatives. It usually takes place in the gym, the municipal hall or the multi-purpose hall. It is something like the municipality's parliament.

Those who may take part are **people entitled to vote**, usually Swiss citizens aged 18 or over who live in the municipality. In some cantons, for example Neuchâtel, Jura, Vaud, Fribourg and Geneva, foreigners may also vote at municipal level if they have lived there for some time. Children and young people may often watch as guests but may not vote. If you listen, you learn a lot about how your own municipality works.

The assembly usually takes place twice a year. In winter the **budget** for the following year and the **tax rate** are often decided, and in spring the annual accounts. There are also matters such as a new school building, road repairs or a new regulation. The municipal council prepares everything and sends documents to the voters beforehand.

The mayor chairs the assembly. First each item of business is presented; then everyone may ask questions, make proposals and give their opinion. At the end there is a vote, usually by **raising hands**, and **vote counters** count the hands. For important questions, a secret vote or a ballot-box vote can be demanded.

In larger municipalities there would not be room for everyone in one hall. That is why many towns have a **municipal parliament**, which depending on the canton is called the Einwohnerrat, Stadtrat, Gemeinderat or Conseil communal. In French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino, such parliaments are common in smaller municipalities too. A special relative of the municipal assembly is the Landsgemeinde, which still exists at cantonal level in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.

Although all voters are invited, often only a few per cent come. With controversial issues, however, the hall is sometimes full. In many municipalities, anyone who disagrees with a decision can call a **referendum** and demand a ballot-box vote. That way people who had no time that evening can also have a say.

begriffe.erklaerung: People who may take part in votes and elections.
The people decide on issues themselves.
A number that sets how high the municipal taxes are.
A suggestion that is to be voted on.

gewusst: At many municipal assemblies there is a small apéro at the end, where people can carry on discussing.
A municipal assembly can also refer a matter back; then the municipal council must revise it.
As early as the Middle Ages, the men of a village met to decide on pastures, woods and paths.

teile.einleitung: In a block of flats, many people live close together. So that living together works well, there are house rules. They set out what is allowed in the building and where you need to show consideration.
wichtigste: The house rules apply to all tenants of a building.
They are usually written by the landlord or the property management.
The stairwell must be kept clear, because it is an escape route.
In many buildings, bikes belong in the bike room.
In the stairwell and in the evening, you are quiet and considerate.
You play ball outside, in the playground or on the grass.
The caretaker often looks after order and repairs.

abschnitte.text: **House rules** are a list of rules for a residential building. They are usually set by the **landlord** or the **property management**. They are often part of the tenancy agreement, and everyone in the building must follow them. The rules are meant to make sure that everyone feels comfortable and nobody is disturbed. Each building can have slightly different house rules.

In a building you hear many noises through walls and ceilings. That is why there are often **quiet times**, for example at night and over lunchtime. You are quiet in the **stairwell**, because every sound can be heard there. Ball games belong outside, in the playground or on the grass, because a ball can break something indoors. A friendly **greeting** to the neighbours shows respect and makes living together more pleasant.

The stairwell is an **escape route**. In a fire, everyone must be able to get outside quickly and safely. That is why no shoes, boxes or bikes may be left standing there. Many buildings have a separate **bike room** for bikes. Prams and scooters often have a fixed place too.

Some rooms are shared by everyone in the building, for example the **laundry room**, the cellar or the lift. In many Swiss buildings a **laundry rota** sets out who may do their washing when. Anyone who uses a shared room leaves it clean. If you get stuck in the **lift**, you press the **alarm button** and wait calmly for help. In many large buildings the **caretaker** looks after order and repairs.

gewusst: The laundry rota for the shared laundry room is typical of many blocks of flats in Switzerland.
Lifts have an alarm button that you can use to call for help around the clock.

teile.einleitung: Every canton has a capital. The cantonal government and the cantonal parliament usually work there. The capital is not always the largest town in the canton.
wichtigste: The capital is the seat of a canton's government and parliament.
Chur is the capital of the Grisons.
The capital of Valais is called Sion, or Sitten in German.
Bellinzona is the capital of Ticino, but Lugano is the largest town.
Liestal is the capital of Basel-Landschaft, Stans that of Nidwalden.
Lausanne is the capital of Vaud, Aarau the capital of Aargau.

abschnitte.text: A **cantonal capital** is something like the capital city of a canton. The **cantonal parliament** and the **cantonal government** usually meet there. Many offices of the cantonal administration are there too. The capital often has the same name as the canton, for example Zurich, Bern, Lucerne or Zug. In other cantons the capital has its own name.

The capital is not always the largest town. In Ticino **Bellinzona** is the capital, but the largest town is **Lugano**. Bellinzona is known for its **three castles**. In Basel-Landschaft **Liestal** is the capital, even though **Allschwil** has more inhabitants. And in the Grisons **Chur** is the capital, not the famous resort of Davos.

**Chur** is considered one of the oldest towns in Switzerland. The capital of Valais is called **Sion** in French and **Sitten** in German. It lies in the French-speaking part of the canton. **Stans** is the capital of Nidwalden, and **Sarnen** that of neighbouring Obwalden. In Vaud, **Lausanne** on Lake Geneva is the capital. The Federal Supreme Court also has its seat there.

**Aarau** is the capital of Aargau. In **1798** Aarau was briefly the first capital of the **Helvetic Republic**. After that, the government moved on to Lucerne. By the way, Switzerland itself has no official capital set out in law. **Bern** is called the **federal city**, because the Federal Council and Parliament have their seat there.

gewusst: In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, the capital is simply called Appenzell.
The three castles of Bellinzona are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: When a new law has been passed, it does not apply immediately. Only from the day it comes into force must everyone follow it. This date is set precisely, so that people and authorities can prepare.
wichtigste: From the moment it comes into force, a law must be applied.
The Federal Council usually decides when a federal act comes into force.
New legislation is first published in the Official Compilation.
Many new rules come into force on 1 January.
An urgent federal act can come into force immediately.
Transitional provisions regulate the change from old to new law.
Stricter criminal laws do not apply retroactively.

abschnitte.text: A law **comes into force** when it becomes valid from a particular day. Then the **authorities**, **courts** and everyone must follow it. For federal acts, the **Federal Council** usually sets the date, unless the act itself says otherwise. Before that, the deadline for a **referendum** must have passed or the people must have approved it. A particularly large number of rules come into force on **1 January**, which makes planning easier.

New and amended federal legislation is published in the **Official Compilation of Federal Legislation** (AS). This publication is what counts, and it appears before the law comes into force. That way people can find out about the rules before they apply. The law in force can also be found arranged by subject in the **Classified Compilation** (SR). Both are now available online.

Sometimes a case begins under the old law and is still going on. For such cases there are **transitional provisions**. They set out which law applies when. A law can also come into force **in stages**, if some parts need more preparation. In criminal law, the **ban on retroactivity** applies: only acts that were already forbidden at the time may be punished.

Sometimes things have to happen very quickly. Then Parliament can **declare** a law **urgent**. This requires a **majority of all members** in each chamber, as set out in **Article 165** of the Federal Constitution. An urgent law can come into force immediately and must be **time-limited**. A referendum is still possible, but only afterwards.

gewusst: Since 2016 the Official Compilation has been published in legally binding electronic form.
The Covid-19 Act of 2020 was passed as an urgent federal act and came into force immediately.

teile.einleitung: Child protection means that children can grow up safely, without violence and without danger. Adults are responsible for this: parents, teachers and also authorities such as the KESB.
wichtigste: Child protection means protecting children from violence and danger.
A child is never to blame if someone uses violence against them.
In Switzerland the KESB helps if a child is not safe at home.
Since 2019 professionals such as teachers have had to report a risk to a child.
The foundation Child Protection Switzerland works against violence towards children.
On the internet you do not send photos to strangers, and you tell your parents about strange messages.

abschnitte.text: Every child has the right to grow up without **violence**. This is also set out in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. When a child's well-being is in danger, this is called a **risk to the child's welfare**. This can happen through violence or through **neglect**, meaning when nobody looks after a child properly. Then adults must act.

If a child is hit or treated badly, it is **never their own fault**. The responsibility always lies with the person who does such a thing. It is brave and right to talk about it. You can get help from a **person you trust**, for example your parents, teachers or the school social worker. In Switzerland there is also Pro Juventute's phone number 147 for children and young people.

abschnitte.titel: The KESB and the duty to report
abschnitte.text: **KESB** stands for the Child and Adult Protection Authority. It checks whether a child needs protection and makes sure help is provided. Since 2019 an extended **duty to report** has applied in Switzerland: professionals who work regularly with children, for example teachers, must report an obvious risk to the authority. This is meant to help children in need get help faster.

On the internet you never know for sure who is really writing. That is why you do not send **photos** of yourself to strangers. Pictures can be passed on and used against a child's will. If a stranger wants to **meet**, you show the message straight away to your parents or another adult you trust. You also do not give out personal details such as your address or school.

The foundation **Child Protection Switzerland** works to make sure children grow up without violence. It informs parents, children and professionals and runs campaigns on this topic. There are also many other services that give advice and help. Child protection is a task for the whole of society.

gewusst: Pro Juventute's phone number 147 can be reached by children and young people in Switzerland around the clock.
The KESB has existed in its present form since 2013; before that, in many municipalities, lay people sat on the guardianship authority.

teile.einleitung: The caretaker makes sure that everything works in a school or a block of flats. In many parts of Switzerland the caretaker is also called the Abwart. Without this work, buildings would soon be dirty, cold or broken.
wichtigste: In Switzerland Hauswart and Abwart mean the same thing.
The caretaker often cleans large floors with a cleaning machine.
The caretaker locks the school in the evening and opens it in the morning.
You report broken things in the school to the caretaker.
The caretaker checks the heating and often clears the snow in winter.
In the summer holidays the caretaker cleans the school thoroughly.
The caretaker makes sure that the emergency exits are clear.

abschnitte.text: The **caretaker** looks after a building and its surroundings. He has the **keys**, locks the school in the evening and opens it in the morning. In many parts of Switzerland he is also called the **Abwart**. There are caretakers in schools, housing estates, hospitals and office buildings. Some work alone; in large complexes there are whole teams.

The caretaker often cleans large areas such as corridors and gyms with a **cleaning machine**. It scrubs and dries the floor in one go. In the **summer holidays**, when there are no children, there is a big clean. Then floors, windows and furniture are cleaned thoroughly. He often collects forgotten jackets and gym bags in the **lost property**.

If a light flickers or a door sticks, you report it to the caretaker. He repairs small damage himself or calls a specialist firm. He checks the **heating**, the ventilation and other systems in the building. That way the rooms are warm in winter. Many caretakers have done an apprenticeship in a trade.

In winter the caretaker often clears the **snow** and grits the paths. That way everyone gets into the school safely. He also makes sure that the **emergency exits** are never blocked. In a fire, everyone must be able to get out quickly. Outside, he often looks after the lawn, hedges and open spaces.

gewusst: In Switzerland you can learn the job of “Fachfrau or Fachmann Betriebsunterhalt” (building maintenance specialist) through an apprenticeship.
For experienced caretakers there is further training leading to a federal diploma.

teile.einleitung: Cohabitation literally means “living together”. In France the word describes a situation in which the President and the Prime Minister come from opposing political camps and still have to work together.
wichtigste: In a cohabitation, the President and the Prime Minister come from different camps.
By 2025 there had been three cohabitations in the Fifth Republic.
From 1986 to 1988 Jacques Chirac was Prime Minister under François Mitterrand.
From 1993 to 1995 Édouard Balladur governed as Prime Minister.
From 1997 to 2002 Lionel Jospin was Prime Minister, the longest cohabitation.
Since the “quinquennat”, cohabitations have become much less likely.

abschnitte.text: In France the people elect the **President** directly. Parliament, the National Assembly, is elected separately. If the majority in parliament has a different political direction from the President, he must appoint a **Prime Minister** from that camp. Otherwise parliament could bring down the government. The two must then work together; this is called **cohabitation**.

The first cohabitation was from **1986 to 1988**: the Socialist President **François Mitterrand** appointed the Gaullist **Jacques Chirac** as Prime Minister. From **1993 to 1995** the Gaullist **Édouard Balladur** governed, again under Mitterrand. From **1997 to 2002** it was the other way round: the Socialist **Lionel Jospin** governed for five years alongside the centre-right President Chirac. By 2025 there had been no further cohabitation.

According to Article 20 of the constitution, the **government** determines the policy of the nation. In a cohabitation, therefore, the Prime Minister and his parliamentary majority steer **domestic policy**. **Foreign and defence policy**, on the other hand, are traditionally regarded as the **“domaine réservé”** of the President. He is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and represents France internationally.

In the past, the President's term of office lasted seven years and that of parliament five. A reform shortened the President's term to **five years**, called the **“quinquennat”**. Since 2002 the parliamentary elections have taken place shortly after the presidential election. Voters usually give the new President a majority. That is why a cohabitation has been much less likely since then.

gewusst: Jacques Chirac experienced cohabitation from both sides: first as Prime Minister, later as President.
There is no cohabitation in Switzerland, because the Federal Council is elected by Parliament and several parties govern together.

teile.einleitung: A youth commission is a body that looks after the concerns of children and young people. They exist in many municipalities and also at federal level. They advise the authorities but usually do not decide themselves.
wichtigste: A youth commission advises the municipality on youth questions.
For example, it can propose a new youth centre.
It is good if young people themselves also take part.
At federal level there is the Federal Commission for Child and Youth Affairs (EKKJ).
The members of the EKKJ are elected by the Federal Council.
The Child and Youth Promotion Act supports youth work outside school.

abschnitte.text: Many municipalities have a **youth commission**. It discusses topics that affect children and young people. Then it makes **proposals** to the municipal council. For example, it can propose a **youth centre**, a skate park or an event. The responsible **authority** must then decide.

Many municipalities offer **open youth work**. These are voluntary meeting places and projects for young people in their free time, outside school. Youth work professionals support the young people there. The municipality often pays for these services and is advised on them by the youth commission. That way the services fit better with what young people need.

A youth commission is more credible if **young people** themselves sit on it. That way their experiences flow directly into the proposals. Adults do not always know what matters to young people. By taking part, young people also learn how politics works. This is called **participation**.

The Confederation is advised by the **Federal Commission for Child and Youth Affairs**, **EKKJ** for short. It watches the situation of young people in Switzerland and gives **recommendations** to the Federal Council. The EKKJ is an **extra-parliamentary commission**, an expert body that advises the government and administration. Its members are elected by the **Federal Council**. Since 2013 the **Child and Youth Promotion Act** (KJFG) has also applied; among other things, it supports youth organisations.

gewusst: The Child and Youth Promotion Act was passed in 2011 and came into force in 2013.
The Confederation has dozens of extra-parliamentary commissions on very different topics.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is made up of 26 cantons. Each canton has its own name, a coat of arms and a two-letter abbreviation. The cantons vary greatly in size and have a lot of independence.
wichtigste: Switzerland has 26 cantons.
Each canton has a two-letter abbreviation, for example GR for the Grisons.
Six cantons have only half a cantonal vote.
The Grisons is the canton with the largest area.
Basel-Stadt is the canton with the smallest area.
Zurich has the most inhabitants.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is a **federal state** made up of 26 cantons. The cantons have their own constitutions, parliaments, governments and courts. They decide, for example, on schools, the police and hospitals. The youngest canton is the **Jura**, founded in 1979. German, French, Italian or Romansh is spoken in the cantons; some are multilingual.

Each canton has a two-letter **abbreviation**. You can see it, for example, on **number plates**. The Grisons has **GR**, Nidwalden **NW** and Neuchâtel NE. Some abbreviations come from other languages: **VS** stands for “Valais”, the French name of the Wallis, and **VD** for “Vaud”, the Waadt. **TI** comes from “Ticino”, while Thurgau has TG. Appenzell Ausserrhoden has **AR**, Appenzell Innerrhoden AI and Aargau AG.

In some popular votes, it is not only the majority of the people that counts but also the majority of the cantons, the **Ständemehr**. Each canton has a **cantonal vote**. Six cantons have only **half a cantonal vote**: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden. They used to be called **half-cantons**. They also send only one person instead of two to the Council of States.

The cantons are very different. The **Grisons**, with just over 7100 square kilometres, is the largest canton, larger than Valais and Bern. **Basel-Stadt**, with around 37 square kilometres, is the smallest. Besides the city of Basel, only Riehen and Bettingen belong to it. The most people live in the canton of **Zurich**: over 1.5 million in 2024.

gewusst: The small canton of Basel-Stadt has many more inhabitants than the huge but mountainous canton of Uri.
The Grisons is the only canton with three official languages: German, Romansh and Italian.

teile.einleitung: A youth council is a group of young people who represent the concerns of young people. There are youth councils in municipalities, towns and cantons. There, young people can have their say long before they are allowed to vote.
wichtigste: Young people sit on the youth council.
It brings the ideas and wishes of young people into the municipality.
A youth council can, for example, campaign for a youth centre.
You join a youth council by election or by applying.
The youth council often works together with the municipality.
On the youth council you learn how politics works.

abschnitte.titel: Who sits on the youth council
abschnitte.text: A **youth council** is made up of **young people** from a place. It represents the young people of a municipality, a town or a canton. Some youth councils are **elected**. For others you can sign up or **apply**. Each youth council decides itself exactly who may take part.

The youth council collects young people's **wishes and ideas**. It passes them on to the municipality or carries out its own **projects**. It can campaign, for example, for a **youth centre**, a concert or a safe cycle path. It does not plan big buildings such as hospitals, though. Sometimes a youth council has its own small budget.

A youth council often works closely with the **municipality**. It talks to the authorities so that young people's ideas are put into practice. The **municipal council** is made up of elected adults who decide for the whole municipality. The youth council is made up of young people who contribute their **point of view**. So the youth council advises, and the municipality makes the important decisions.

On the youth council, young people take part in **meetings**, discuss and plan together. They learn to write proposals and to convince others. In this way they find out how **politics** works. Those who have been on a youth council are often interested in politics later too. At national level there is also the **Youth Session**, where young people debate their concerns in the Federal Palace.

gewusst: The Federal Youth Session has taken place regularly in the Federal Palace in Bern since 1991.
Some youth councils may submit official proposals to the municipal council.

teile.einleitung: “Child-friendly municipality” is a label awarded by UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein. Municipalities that make a special effort for children can receive it. Taking part is voluntary.
wichtigste: The label is awarded by UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
The initiative has existed in Switzerland since 2006.
Taking part is voluntary; a municipality must apply itself.
The municipality writes an action plan with concrete measures.
A UNICEF expert jury decides on the award.
The label is valid for four years.

abschnitte.text: **UNICEF** is the UN children's agency. **UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein** awards the label **“Child-friendly municipality”**. The initiative started in Switzerland in **2006** and has existed in Liechtenstein since 2018. Taking part is **voluntary**. A municipality must apply itself if it wants the label.

In a child-friendly municipality, children are asked for their **opinion**. They can **have a say** on matters that affect them. The municipality pays attention to **safe routes to school**, good **playgrounds** and meeting places. Children should feel comfortable and safe there. The basis is the rights set out in the **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child**.

First the municipality carries out an **assessment**, also called a **stocktake**. It looks at what already exists for children and what is missing. Then it sets out in an **action plan** what it wants to improve. After that, a **UNICEF expert jury** decides on the award. According to UNICEF, this process takes around **a year and a half** on average.

The label is valid for **four years**. During this time the municipality carries out its measures. After that it must show what it has achieved in order to receive the label again. That way child-friendliness remains a goal that people keep working on. The **federal city of Bern** was also awarded the title of child-friendly city by UNICEF in 2016.

gewusst: The idea of child-friendly cities exists in many countries around the world.
Small villages can also receive the label, not only big towns.

teile.einleitung: A legal code is a collection of laws on one subject. In it you can look up which rules apply. Switzerland has several important codes, for example the Civil Code and the Criminal Code.
wichtigste: A legal code collects many laws.
Laws are divided into numbered articles.
The Civil Code (ZGB) has applied since 1912.
The Criminal Code (StGB) sets out crimes and punishments.
The Code of Obligations (OR) regulates contracts such as buying and renting.
Federal laws are equally valid in German, French and Italian.
All federal laws can be read free of charge on the internet.

abschnitte.text: A **legal code** collects many rules on one subject in one place. The rules are divided into numbered **articles**, for example Article 1. Long articles often also have **paragraphs**. That way you can find a rule exactly and refer to it. Anyone who says “Article 8 of the Federal Constitution” means one very specific place.

The **ZGB** is the Swiss **Civil Code**. It regulates how people live together, for example family, inheritance and **property**. The ZGB has applied since **1912**, so it is over 100 years old. But it has often been changed since then. It was written mainly by the lawyer **Eugen Huber**.

abschnitte.titel: Code of Obligations and Criminal Code
abschnitte.text: The **Code of Obligations**, OR for short, regulates contracts such as buying, renting and employment. So anyone who buys a bike or rents a flat concludes a contract under the OR. The **Criminal Code**, StGB for short, sets out which acts are forbidden and which punishments apply. The Criminal Code has applied to the whole of Switzerland since 1942.

Besides the big codes, there are many other laws. The **Road Traffic Act**, SVG for short, regulates traffic on the roads. It contains rules for cars, bikes and pedestrians. Above all laws stands the **Federal Constitution**. No law may contradict it.

Federal laws are published in **German, French and Italian**, and all three versions are equally valid. Important texts are also available in **Romansh**. Anyone can read the federal laws free of charge on the internet on the **Fedlex** platform. There they are arranged in the Classified Compilation.

gewusst: The first article of the ZGB says that if there is no rule, a court should decide as it would if it were the legislator making a rule.
The ZGB served as the model for Turkey's Civil Code of 1926.

teile.einleitung: Justice means that everyone is treated fairly and nobody is put at a disadvantage without a reason. It matters in everyday life, for example when sharing, and in the state, for example in court.
wichtigste: Justice means that everyone is treated fairly.
Its best-known symbol is Justitia with scales and a sword.
The blindfold shows that everyone is equal before the law.
Fair does not always mean that everyone gets exactly the same amount.
Sometimes someone needs help so that they have the same chance.
In Switzerland courts decide according to the law.

abschnitte.text: **Justitia** is a female figure who stands for justice. Her name comes from Latin. In one hand she holds **scales**: both sides are examined carefully. In the other hand she holds a **sword**: the judgement is also enforced. She often wears a **blindfold**, because she judges without regard to the person, whether someone is rich or poor.

Justitia often stands outside courts or on fountains. In the old town of Bern there is the **Fountain of Justice**, on which Justitia stands. The street there is also called Gerechtigkeitsgasse (Justice Street). Similar figures can be found in many other Swiss towns. They remind people that the law should apply to everyone.

In everyday life it is often about **sharing**. If three children share 12 cherries, each gets 4 cherries. With a piece of cake, a trick helps: one child cuts and the other chooses first. That way the first child makes an effort to cut pieces of the same size. And if someone has forgotten their mid-morning snack, it is fair and kind to give them some of yours.

Justice does not always mean that everyone is **treated exactly the same**. A child with a broken leg may, for example, start later on sports day. Otherwise they would not have **the same chance**. This is also called **equality of opportunity**. It is about making up for disadvantages so that everyone has a fair chance.

In Switzerland the **courts** make sure that disputes are decided fairly. They examine what happened and judge according to the **law**. The Federal Constitution says that all people are equal before the law. This is called **equality before the law**. People have been thinking about what exactly is just since ancient times.

gewusst: The Fountain of Justice in Bern dates from the 16th century.
Justitia did not always have a blindfold; it was only added over time.

teile.einleitung: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was a philosopher and writer from Geneva. He lived from 1712 to 1778. With his ideas on freedom, equality and the sovereignty of the people, he shaped the French Revolution and thinking about democracy.
wichtigste: Rousseau was born in the Republic of Geneva in 1712.
In 1762 “The Social Contract” and “Emile” were published.
“The Social Contract” begins with the sentence that man is born free and everywhere he is in chains.
The general will aims at the common good, not at private interests.
For Rousseau, the sovereignty of the people cannot be represented.
For him, inequality began with private property.

abschnitte.text: Rousseau was born in 1712 in what was then the **Republic of Geneva**. He did not have a long school education and taught himself a great deal. Later he lived in France, among other places. On the title page of “The Social Contract” he proudly calls himself **“citoyen de Genève”**, citizen of Geneva. He is considered one of the most important thinkers of the **Enlightenment**, even though he criticised many Enlightenment thinkers.

In 1762 **“Du contrat social”**, The Social Contract, was published. The first chapter begins with the famous sentence: “L'homme est né libre, et partout il est dans les fers.” So man is born free, but everywhere he is in chains. Rousseau asks what a **legitimate order** could look like. His answer: people join together and give themselves the laws.

Rousseau distinguishes the **general will** (“volonté générale”) from the **will of all** (“volonté de tous”). The will of all is only the sum of private interests; the general will is directed at the **common good**. For him, the **sovereignty** of the people is inalienable and **cannot be represented**. Members of Parliament may only be agents. He mocked that the English people were only free when electing Parliament.

In his discourse on **inequality**, Rousseau describes the first person who fenced in a piece of land and called it “mine”. For him, competition and inequality arose with **private property**. In the novel **“Emile, or On Education”** he describes an education of a child in harmony with nature. This book was also published in 1762. In Geneva, “Emile” and “The Social Contract” were banned and burned.

gewusst: Rousseau also composed music, including an opera.
Rousseau is buried in the Panthéon in Paris, where France honours its great figures.

teile.einleitung: Children have their own rights, which are set out in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Switzerland has adopted this Convention and must keep to it. Swiss laws such as the Civil Code also protect children's rights.
wichtigste: The Convention on the Rights of the Child came into force for Switzerland on 26 March 1997.
To ratify means that a country officially accepts a treaty.
With its public state schools, Switzerland fulfils the right to education.
The Civil Code regulates the rights and duties of parents and children.
From the age of 16, a child decides on their religion themselves.
Since 1 July 2026 the law has required parents to bring up their children without violence.
Switzerland reports regularly to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child.

abschnitte.titel: The Convention on the Rights of the Child
abschnitte.text: The **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child** is an international treaty on the rights of children. The UN adopted it in 1989. Almost all the countries in the world have accepted it. Switzerland **ratified** the Convention on 24 February **1997**. To ratify means that a country officially accepts a treaty and promises to keep to it. It came into force for Switzerland on **26 March 1997**.

An important children's right is the **right to education**. In Switzerland there is a public **state school** for all children. It is compulsory and free for the children. In this way Switzerland fulfils this right. Other children's rights include, for example, the right to **protection**, to health, to play and free time, and the right to give your own **opinion**.

The **Civil Code**, **ZGB** for short, regulates family life throughout Switzerland. It describes, for example, the **duties of parents**. According to the ZGB, from the age of **16** a child decides on their **religious affiliation** themselves. Since **1 July 2026** the law has stated that parents must bring up their children **without violence**. That means without physical punishment and without other degrading treatment.

The Convention on the Rights of the Child obliges above all the **state**, meaning the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities. But **parents**, schools and all **adults** should also respect children's rights. If a child needs help, there is, for example, the **Child and Adult Protection Authority**, **KESB** for short. Children can also turn to advice services such as the **147** helpline.

Every country that has accepted the Convention must **report** regularly on how it is putting children's rights into practice. Switzerland sends its reports to the **UN Committee on the Rights of the Child**. The committee examines the reports and then gives **recommendations**. Organisations from Switzerland can also give the committee their view. This is how it is checked whether the rights really apply in everyday life.

gewusst: 20 November is the international day of children's rights, because the UN adopted the Convention on that day in 1989.
The Convention on the Rights of the Child applies to everyone under the age of 18.

teile.einleitung: In law, immunity means special protection against prosecution. Members of Parliament are protected against certain prosecutions during their term of office, so that they can speak and work freely. But immunity is not a licence to break the law.
wichtigste: Immunity is legal protection against prosecution for certain people.
Members of Parliament are protected against certain prosecutions during their term of office.
Members of the National Council and the Council of States cannot be sued for what they say in Parliament.
For other accusations connected with their office, Parliament must first allow a prosecution.
Parliament can lift the immunity; then an investigation may go ahead.
Diplomats also have special immunity.
The aim is that nobody can stop politicians from working by making false complaints.

abschnitte.text: The word **immunity** comes from the Latin “immunis” and means something like “free from burdens”. In medicine it means that the body is protected against a disease. In law it means that certain people are protected against **prosecution**. This protection does not apply to everyone, only to certain offices.

Members of the Federal Assembly cannot be held legally responsible for what they say in the chamber and in committees. This is called **absolute immunity**. So they may make sharp criticisms without fearing a lawsuit. This rule is in the Federal Constitution and also applies to members of the Federal Council and the Federal Chancellor.

If a member of Parliament is reported for a crime connected with their office, the police may not simply investigate. First the responsible **committees** of Parliament must give permission. This is called **relative immunity**. The committees decide whether the immunity is lifted.

Immunity does not protect against everything. Anyone who, for example, drives too fast or commits a theft is punished like everyone else, if the act has nothing to do with their office. Even if the immunity is lifted, a person is still presumed innocent until a **court** decides otherwise. The protection is meant to protect the work of Parliament, not individual people.

Another form is **diplomatic immunity**. Ambassadors and diplomats of other countries may in principle not be arrested or put on trial in the host country. This is set out in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations of 1961. This is especially important for Switzerland, because many international organisations such as the UN have their seat in Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: When the police and the public prosecutor investigate whether someone has committed a crime.
Complete protection for statements made in Parliament.
Protection that can be lifted by Parliament.
A person who officially represents their country in another country.

gewusst: The idea of immunity comes partly from England, where members of Parliament were meant to be protected from the king.
In Switzerland both chambers of Parliament usually have to decide on lifting immunity, not just one.
Many cantons also have immunity for members of the cantonal parliament.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland it is not only federal courts that decide; above all, the cantonal courts decide on disputes and crimes. Each canton organises its courts itself. That is why they have different names depending on the canton.
wichtigste: In principle, the cantons decide how their courts are organised.
Since 2011 the same Civil Procedure Code and Criminal Procedure Code have applied throughout Switzerland.
There are usually two cantonal instances: a first instance and a higher court.
In the canton of Zurich the high court (Obergericht) is the highest civil and criminal court.
Only Zurich, Bern, Aargau and St Gallen have a commercial court.
Decisions of the higher cantonal courts can often be taken to the Federal Supreme Court.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the cantons are responsible for **organising the courts**. They decide how many courts there are and what they are called. Since **2011**, however, the **Civil Procedure Code** (ZPO) and the **Criminal Procedure Code** (StPO) have applied to procedure throughout Switzerland. So the procedure is the same everywhere; only the structure of the courts differs. At the very top, for everyone, is the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne.

An **instance** is a level in the court system. First, a court of **first instance** decides. In the canton of Bern these courts are called **regional courts**; other cantons call them, for example, district or circuit courts. Anyone who disagrees with the judgement can take it to the **second instance**. This **appeal court** examines the judgement again.

In the canton of Zurich the **Obergericht** (high court) is the highest civil and criminal court. It decides on appeals and objections against decisions of the district courts. In Ticino the higher instance is called the **Tribunale d'appello**, and the first-instance civil courts there are called Pretura. In Geneva the **Cour de justice** is the highest cantonal court. It must not be confused with the Tribunal fédéral, the Federal Supreme Court.

Some cantons have special courts. **Commercial courts** exist only in Zurich, Bern, Aargau and St Gallen. They decide disputes between companies that are entered in the **commercial register**. Zurich also has its own **administrative court** for appeals against decisions of the cantonal administration. There is also a **social insurance court**, for example for disputes about insurance benefits.

In the past, each canton had its own rules for trials. Some cantons had a third cantonal instance, a **court of cassation**. With the new Civil and Criminal Procedure Codes of 2011, this level was dropped. That is why the courts of cassation, for example in **Zurich** and St Gallen, were **abolished**. Today the route after the cantonal instances leads directly to the Federal Supreme Court.

gewusst: Many judges at cantonal courts are elected by the people or by the cantonal parliament.
Because the cantons name their courts themselves, there are a great many different court names in Switzerland.
